title: Birthday party, empty seat beside you
text: You're at a friend's birthday party and someone you've never met sits down next to you. They smile and seem to be waiting for someone to say hello first.
explanation: This is a casual first meeting in a relaxed social setting. A brief, friendly self-introduction is exactly right, and "Meeting Someone New" covers each step.

title: Campus open day, ambassador approaching
text: You've gone to an open day at a college you're considering joining. A student ambassador walks up to you and smiles. You've never spoken to them before.
explanation: Even on campus, this is a relaxed first conversation with someone new, not an official check-in. "Meeting Someone New" gives you the right casual opening.

title: Conference table, pre-session pause
text: You're attending a professional conference. You arrive at the morning session and sit down at a table where one other person is already seated. There's a long gap before the talk starts.
explanation: The room is formal, but the moment is a low-key one-to-one opener with a stranger, not a structured go-around. "Meeting Someone New" fits this pause before the session.

title: New street, bins at curbside
text: You've just moved in next door and you see the person from the house beside yours putting their bins out as you step outside. They notice you and make brief eye contact.
explanation: This is a quick neighbourly moment that doesn't need a full conversation, a small wave and a brief hello is exactly right. "Greeting a Neighbour" covers this.

title: Dog walk, wave across street
text: You're walking your dog and the person across the street is also outside. They wave at you first.
explanation: They've already opened the exchange, a wave back and a quick hello keeps it friendly without overcommitting. "Greeting a Neighbour" is this situation.

title: Driveway arrival, morning pass-by
text: You're doing your morning walk and the person from the house next door pulls into their driveway just as you pass. They get out of the car and spot you.
explanation: A passing hello between people who live nearby, you didn't plan a chat and it doesn't need to be long. "Greeting a Neighbour" keeps it appropriate and easy.

title: Lift lobby, monday morning pass
text: You step out of the lift at work on a Monday morning and a colleague from your team walks past. They glance up from their phone.
explanation: A brief, low-key morning exchange with someone you work with is what "Greeting a Coworker" is designed for, with no long conversation needed.

title: Office kitchen, coffee machine pause
text: You're making coffee in the office kitchen and a colleague from your team walks in behind you. They haven't said anything yet.
explanation: A brief, low-key morning exchange with a familiar colleague is what "Greeting a Coworker" is built for, with no long conversation needed, just a friendly acknowledgement.

title: Desk row, one earbud removed
text: You arrive at the office on a Monday after a long weekend. A colleague you see every day is already at their desk with headphones on. They pull one earphone out when they notice you.
explanation: Brief and low-key is perfect here, they're working and you don't want to interrupt much. "Greeting a Coworker" keeps it short and natural.

title: Bookshop aisle, familiar face spotted
text: You're browsing in a bookshop and recognise someone you've met once or twice at a mutual friend's house. They're walking down the same aisle and seem to have noticed you.
explanation: You know this person a little but not well, a nod or brief hello if they come over, and a natural exit if you need one. "Seeing an Acquaintance in Public" is the right script.

title: School pickup, wave from car park
text: You're picking your child up from school and another parent you've chatted to a few times waves at you from across the car park.
explanation: You know this person a little but not closely, a wave back, maybe a quick hello if they come over, and a natural exit. "Seeing an Acquaintance in Public" is exactly right.

title: High street errand, familiar face
text: You're running an errand and walk past someone you used to live beside years ago. They see you and their face lights up.
explanation: You know them, you haven't seen them in a while, but a full catch-up isn't the context. "Seeing an Acquaintance in Public" fits a brief, friendly stop in passing.

title: Entryway, courier with parcel
text: You're at home and the doorbell rings. Through the window you can see someone in a delivery uniform holding a package.
explanation: You need to open safely, say a brief hello, and handle the delivery, not a long visit. "Answering the Door" walks through checking first and what to say.

title: Entryway, invited guest waiting
text: A friend you invited over rings the doorbell. You can see them through the glass, smiling and holding a bag.
explanation: Someone you know is at the door, welcome them in with a warm hello and step aside. "Answering the Door" covers both familiar visitors and brief exchanges.

title: Peephole view, clipboard and lanyard
text: The doorbell rings while you're making dinner. Through the peephole you see someone with a clipboard and a lanyard you don't recognise.
explanation: An unexpected visitor at your door calls for checking who it is first, then a short response, including saying no thanks if you need to. "Answering the Door" has those steps.

title: Shopping centre, familiar voice behind
text: You're at the shopping centre and someone calls your name. You turn around and realise it's a friend from secondary school you haven't seen in years.
explanation: This is someone you know well but haven't seen in a long time, warmth, a comment about how long it's been, then a simple question. "Greeting Someone After a Long Time Apart" fits.

title: Family reunion, cousin crossing room
text: You're at a family reunion and a cousin you used to spend holidays with walks over from across the room. They open their arms as if for a hug.
explanation: Reconnecting with family after a long gap can feel awkward, a warm hello and asking how they've been is the right start. "Greeting Someone After a Long Time Apart" covers this.

title: Cafe queue, former teammate ahead
text: You're in line at a café and the person in front of you turns around. It's a former teammate from a job you left two years ago, and they look surprised too.
explanation: Bumping into someone you worked with but haven't seen in ages calls for a warm reconnect, not a formal round-table intro. "Greeting Someone After a Long Time Apart" is the right fit.

title: Interview lobby, handshake at doorway
text: You've arrived at a job interview and the receptionist calls through to say you're here. The hiring manager walks out to meet you for the first time and extends their hand.
explanation: This is a formal professional first meeting, standing, offering a handshake, and using your full name. "Formal Introduction" has every step.

title: Team desk area, escorted newcomer
text: You arrive at work and your team has a new person starting today. Your manager brings them over to your desk to meet you.
explanation: Meeting a new colleague in a professional introduction context calls for a handshake and a proper introduction. "Formal Introduction" is the right script here.

title: Conference networking area, badge glance
text: You're at a conference networking session. You spot someone whose name badge says they work in the same field as you. They're standing alone.
explanation: In a professional networking context you're approaching a peer you don't know. A confident handshake and a formal introduction sets the right tone. "Formal Introduction" is exactly this.

title: First day, reception desk ahead
text: It's your first day somewhere you've never studied before. You walk through the front doors and can see a staff member sitting behind the welcome desk.
explanation: You need to tell someone official that you're new and find out where to go. "Introducing Yourself at a New School" is exactly this situation.

title: Campus admin office, mid-semester arrival
text: You're transferring to a new college mid-semester. You arrive in the main building and can see an admin office with someone inside.
explanation: You need to announce yourself to a staff member in an institutional setting and find out where to go. "Introducing Yourself at a New School" fits exactly.

title: Orientation hallway, line moving forward
text: It's orientation day at a new school. You're standing in a hallway with a line of other new students, and a staff member is calling people forward one at a time.
explanation: You need to tell an official person that you're new and get directed to the right place. "Introducing Yourself at a New School" covers name, status, and asking what to do next.

title: New team circle, your turn next
text: You've just joined a new team at work. It's your first group meeting and the manager says "Let's quickly go around and introduce ourselves."
explanation: You've been asked to introduce yourself to a room of people in a structured setting. "Introducing Yourself in a Meeting" is the right fit, keep it short and on-topic.

title: Volunteer circle, your turn approaching
text: You're at a volunteer group meeting and the facilitator asks everyone to briefly say their name and why they joined. It's nearly your turn.
explanation: You're being asked to introduce yourself in a structured group context, one sentence about who you are and why you're there. "Introducing Yourself in a Meeting" is the right script.

title: Support circle, one-word check-in
text: You're attending your first session of a community mental health support group. The facilitator opens by asking each person to share their first name and one word about how they're feeling.
explanation: Even in a supportive informal group, this is a structured go-around intro. "Introducing Yourself in a Meeting" is the right framework for waiting your turn and keeping it short.

title: Evening course room, early arrival
text: It's the first week of a new evening class. You arrive early and the person at the front is setting up. No one else is in the room yet.
explanation: A brief hello to your instructor before class, your name and that it's your first time, sets things up well. "Greeting a New Teacher or Instructor" covers this.

title: Lecture hall doorway, front desk pause
text: You stayed after a university lecture because you have a question. The person at the front is packing their bag near the door and looks up when you approach.
explanation: Approaching an instructor in a respectful, brief way, who you are and why you're there, is what "Greeting a New Teacher or Instructor" is built for.

title: Workshop front, newcomer call-up
text: You've signed up for a workshop and the facilitator asks newcomers to come to the front for a quick hello before the session starts.
explanation: Introducing yourself to an instructor in a learning setting, name, first time in their class, optional note about how you learn, is what "Greeting a New Teacher or Instructor" covers.

title: Family barbecue, time to leave
text: You've been at a family barbecue for a couple of hours and you're ready to leave. Your aunt (the host) is nearby chatting. There's a gap in her conversation.
explanation: You need to signal you're leaving, thank the host, and say goodbye, without it becoming a long drawn-out exit. "Leaving a Social Event" covers this step by step.

title: After-hours gathering, colleagues near exit
text: You've been at a work social evening. It's been a long day and you're ready to head home, but a small group of colleagues are still standing near the exit.
explanation: Even with work colleagues, this is a social event context, a brief goodbye round and a graceful exit. "Leaving a Social Event" has the right steps.

title: House party, host in kitchen
text: You're at a house party and after a good conversation with a small group, you feel it's the right time to head home. The host is in the kitchen.
explanation: This calls for a graceful exit: a quick goodbye to the group, a thank-you to the host, and leaving without a drawn-out farewell. "Leaving a Social Event" is this script.

title: Street corner split, two directions
text: You've been walking and chatting with a friend for a while. You've reached the street where you need to head home and they need to go the other way.
explanation: This is a simple, friendly parting between just two people. "Ending a Chat with a Friend" is the low-key goodbye this moment calls for.

title: Phone call, pause before sign-off
text: You've just finished a phone call with a friend and there's an awkward silence before either of you says goodbye.
explanation: This is the same closing energy as ending a face-to-face chat. "Ending a Chat with a Friend" works just as well on the phone, a short, warm, decisive close.

title: Film night, doorway send-off
text: You're at a friend's place watching a film. When it finishes you're the only one leaving. Your friend walks you to the door.
explanation: Saying goodbye to a friend at the door is a warm, low-key close, one-to-one, no audience. "Ending a Chat with a Friend" is simpler and more natural here than a full event goodbye.

title: Clock near five, desks occupied
text: It's nearly 5:30pm and your work for the day is done. Several teammates are still at their desks as you start packing up your bag to leave.
explanation: A brief wave or "See you tomorrow" as you pack up is the right call here. "Leaving Work at the End of the Day" makes this moment feel easy.

title: Remote wrap-up, laptop closing now
text: You're finishing a remote work session and say goodbye as you close the laptop. Several team members are still talking.
explanation: Wrapping up a workday, even a remote one, with a low-key farewell to the team is what "Leaving Work at the End of the Day" covers.

title: Friday afternoon, first one out
text: It's a Friday afternoon and you're one of the first on your team to finish for the week. Others are still at their desks. You're heading out for the weekend.
explanation: A quick "Have a good weekend!" as you leave is exactly the right register here. "Leaving Work at the End of the Day" applies whether it's a weekday or Friday.

title: Study link opens, faces already there
text: You click the link for an online study session. A moment later the call opens and you can see three other people already looking at the screen.
explanation: Joining a video call has its own etiquette: mute, wave, look at the camera. "Starting a Video Call" walks through each step.

title: Family screen, everyone already visible
text: Your family's group video call is starting. You tap the link and suddenly everyone's faces appear on screen. They all look up when you connect.
explanation: Video calls need a different kind of opening, a wave to the camera, checking your mute button, and waiting your turn. "Starting a Video Call" handles this perfectly.

title: Screen entry, room already active
text: You log into a work video meeting a minute late. Everyone is already on the call and they look up when your face appears.
explanation: Joining late is a common situation, a quiet wave, check your mute, and hold back until there's a natural gap. "Starting a Video Call" covers joining the call gracefully.

title: Messaging app, classmate thread open
text: You need to ask a classmate about tomorrow's homework. You open your messaging app and their chat is at the top of the list.
explanation: Opening a text chat calls for a short hello and your reason in one message, then waiting for a reply. "Starting a Chat Message" has those steps.

title: Work inbox, direct thread open
text: You want to check whether a coworker is free for a quick call later. You open your work chat app and start typing in their direct message thread.
explanation: A work message needs a brief opener plus what you need, not a video-call wave. "Starting a Chat Message" covers typing a hello and stating your reason clearly.

title: Club thread, quiet morning feed
text: You're in a group chat for a club project and need to ask where everyone wants to meet. The thread has been quiet all morning.
explanation: Starting a group message thread is the same pattern, a short hello, your question in the same message, then wait. "Starting a Chat Message" fits this.

title: Lift ride, bright sun through glass
text: You're in the lift with your neighbour on the way up to your floor. Bright sunshine is pouring through the glass and neither of you has spoken yet.
explanation: A short remark about what you can see outside is a safe, friendly opener here. "Weather Chat" gives you simple lines and a natural way to respond.

title: Bus stop, dark clouds rolling in
text: You're waiting at a bus stop and the person beside you looks up at the dark clouds rolling in. They shift their umbrella and glance your way.
explanation: Commenting on what is happening in the sky is a classic low-pressure opener. "Weather Chat" fits this moment better than trying to fill a silence or ask for help.

title: Office kitchen, first snowfall outside
text: You're in the office kitchen and a colleague from another team is staring out the window at the first snowfall of the year. They turn and catch your eye with a small smile.
explanation: A brief observation about what is outside is enough to start a light exchange. "Weather Chat" is built for exactly this kind of shared glance out the window.

title: Staff room, local story mention
text: You're eating lunch in the staff room and a coworker mentions a story they saw on TV about a local charity run. They seem open to a short back-and-forth.
explanation: They raised a neutral public story, and you can listen and react without debating. "Chatting About the News" covers picking a safe topic and responding briefly.

title: Waiting room, magazine headline comment
text: You're in a dentist waiting room and the person in the chair next to yours taps a magazine cover showing a new park opening. They make a casual comment about it to you.
explanation: This is light chat about something in the shared environment, not leaving or a dental procedure. "Chatting About the News" helps you join in without needing strong opinions.

title: School gate, local radio mention
text: You're standing at the school gate after pickup and another parent mentions a festival that was covered on the local radio this morning. They pause as if expecting a reply.
explanation: They brought up a general community story, not a greeting or a stalled silence. "Chatting About the News" is the right framework for listening and reacting briefly.

title: Thursday desk, week winding down
text: It's Thursday afternoon at work and a teammate is slowly packing their bag at their desk. The week feels like it is winding down and they look relaxed.
explanation: This is a natural moment to ask what someone is doing in the next few days off. "Weekend Plans" covers asking, listening, and keeping it light.

title: Friday classroom, bags zipping up
text: Your last class on Friday has just ended and a classmate you sit near is zipping their bag at the desk beside yours. You have a minute before you both head out.
explanation: A friendly question about the days ahead fits this pause between class and leaving. "Weekend Plans" is about sharing upcoming time off, not praising someone or classroom tasks.

title: Front garden, bin return moment
text: You're bringing your bins in on a Friday evening and your neighbour is watering their front plants. They wave and seem happy to stand and talk for a moment.
explanation: They are open to chat and the timing points toward what is coming up over the next couple of days. "Weekend Plans" matches this better than wrapping up or only saying hello.

title: Lunch table, interest question
text: You're on lunch with a new teammate and they ask what you like to do when you are not at work. They lean in as if they genuinely want to know.
explanation: They asked about your personal interests, not a news story or a formal introduction. "Talking About a Hobby" helps you share one thing simply and ask them back.

title: Cafe table, host asks interests
text: You're at a board-game café for the first time and the host at your table asks what kinds of games you usually enjoy. Everyone else is waiting for your answer.
explanation: They want to know what you personally enjoy doing in your free time. "Talking About a Hobby" fits sharing an interest briefly, not current events or joining a game already running.

title: Volunteer orientation, circle almost yours
text: You've signed in at a volunteer orientation and the coordinator asks each person what drew them to the group. It is almost your turn in the circle.
explanation: You are being asked to share something about yourself and your interests, not to praise someone else or ask for school help. "Talking About a Hobby" gives a simple way to answer and turn it back politely.

title: Corridor pause, slide praise
text: After a team meeting, a coworker stops you in the corridor and says your slides were really clear today. They are looking at you, waiting for a response.
explanation: Someone praised your work and you need a brief, comfortable reply. "Receiving a Compliment" covers accepting it without deflecting or over-explaining.

title: Cafe meet-up, haircut praise
text: You're meeting a friend at a café and they say your new haircut looks great as you sit down. They smile and hold your eye for a moment.
explanation: They said something kind about you and paused for a response, not to end the visit. "Receiving a Compliment" is the right script for a simple thank-you and moving on.

title: Classroom handback, public praise moment
text: Your instructor hands back an assignment and says aloud that your work has improved a lot since last term. A few students glance over.
explanation: You were praised directly and need a short reply in front of others. "Receiving a Compliment" helps you accept it calmly without changing the subject or filling a silence.

title: Printer corner, patterned scarf notice
text: A coworker you see every day is wearing a scarf with a pattern you genuinely like. They are at the printer and seem in a good mood.
explanation: You noticed something specific you want to acknowledge warmly and briefly. "Giving a Compliment" is for speaking up with a genuine, simple line.

title: Dinner table, homemade dish arrives
text: You're at a friend's house for dinner and they bring a dish to the table that looks and smells amazing. They watch your reaction as they set it down.
explanation: You want to say something kind about what they made, not comment on the sky or order food. "Giving a Compliment" fits praising their effort in one short sentence.

title: Classroom wall, poster finishing touches
text: In class, a classmate's poster on the wall is laid out in a way that makes the information easy to follow. They are standing nearby adjusting the last pin.
explanation: You want to tell them something positive about their work before you move on. "Giving a Compliment" is for a brief, specific kind word, not leaving a group or asking the teacher for help.

title: Corridor pause, clock check moment
text: You've been chatting with a colleague in the office corridor for a few minutes. You glance at the clock and your next meeting starts in five minutes.
explanation: You need a polite way to close a one-to-one chat and get moving. "Ending Small Talk Naturally" covers a brief sign-off without sounding abrupt.

title: Supermarket line, payment turn
text: You've had a friendly exchange in the supermarket queue with someone you know slightly. The cashier calls you forward and it is your turn to pay.
explanation: The chat was pleasant but something else now needs your attention. "Ending Small Talk Naturally" helps you wrap up warmly before you step away.

title: Park bench, leash pulling homeward
text: You're on a park bench talking with a neighbour you ran into. Your dog is pulling on the lead and you need to get home to feed them.
explanation: You want to close a casual chat with one person, not respond to praise or leave a whole event. "Ending Small Talk Naturally" fits a short goodbye and moving on.

title: Break room circle, desk call soon
text: Four coworkers are standing in the break room sharing stories and laughing. You need to join a video call at your desk in two minutes.
explanation: You are stepping away from several people at once, not starting a topic or leaving a whole party. "Excusing Yourself from a Group" covers a brief line and a wave.

title: Kitchen circle, tired energy rising
text: You're at a house gathering and a circle in the kitchen is deep in conversation about recipes. You are tired and want to head upstairs soon.
explanation: You need to slip out of an ongoing group chat without a long explanation. "Excusing Yourself from a Group" is built for a simple exit from several people.

title: Library table, coat already on
text: Your study group is whispering around a library table and the conversation keeps going in circles. You need to catch an early bus and your coat is already on.
explanation: You are leaving a small group mid-conversation, not giving praise or talking to the teacher. "Excusing Yourself from a Group" gives you a short line and a clean exit.

title: Doorstep monologue, appointment approaching
text: Your neighbour is still talking on your doorstep ten minutes after you answered the door. You have an appointment to get to and they have just started a new story.
explanation: The chat has run long and you need a firmer but still kind close. "When a Conversation Goes On Too Long" covers signalling you are leaving even if they keep talking.

title: Desk-side monologue, deadline on screen
text: A coworker has been at your desk recounting their weekend for twenty minutes while you have a deadline on screen. They pause only to take a breath before continuing.
explanation: You need to end a one-sided chat that is still going, not join a new topic or do routine end-of-day goodbyes. "When a Conversation Goes On Too Long" helps you head off clearly.

title: Family video call, overtime chatter
text: You're on a video call with a relative and it is twenty minutes past when you agreed to finish. They launch into another topic just as you were about to sign off.
explanation: The call is stretching on and you need to end it even if they add more. "When a Conversation Goes On Too Long" fits standing up to leaving when the other person keeps going.

title: Cafe table, shared quiet pause
text: You're sitting at a café table with someone you know from a class. Neither of you has said anything for half a minute and you both look up from your drinks.
explanation: The pause feels uncomfortable and you want a light way to restart or close. "Getting Out of an Awkward Silence" offers simple topics or a polite exit.

title: Quiet lift ride, floors ticking
text: You're in a quiet lift with a coworker you barely know. The floors tick by and neither of you has spoken since you got in.
explanation: The stillness is the problem, not asking about days off or a morning hello. "Getting Out of an Awkward Silence" helps you break the pause or end it gracefully.

title: Clinic waiting room, long quiet pause
text: You're in a clinic waiting room with a classmate before your appointments. You both looked at your phones, then looked up at the same time and neither spoke.
explanation: You are stuck in a lull with one other person, not ready to ask about their days off on purpose. "Getting Out of an Awkward Silence" is for restarting light chat or bowing out kindly.

title: After-school pickup, tired sibling
text: You're picking up your younger sibling from an after-school club and they walk out looking tired. You have a short walk home together.
explanation: You are reconnecting after their day and a caring check-in fits. "Asking "How Was Your Day?"" covers asking, listening, and responding briefly.

title: Hallway bag drop, kitchen pause
text: Your roommate comes in from work, drops their bag in the hallway, and sits at the kitchen table. You have not spoken since this morning.
explanation: This is a natural moment to check in on how their day went, not to jump ahead to days off or school paperwork. "Asking "How Was Your Day?"" is the right fit.

title: Living room arrival, deep exhale
text: Your parent gets home from a long shift and sits down in the living room with a deep breath. You are in the same room and have a few quiet minutes.
explanation: They may want to share how the day felt, and you can ask with genuine interest. "Asking "How Was Your Day?"" guides that back-and-forth without jumping to praise or email.

title: Monday kitchen, tea and calm
text: It's Monday morning in the office kitchen and a teammate you often see is making tea. They seem relaxed and open to a quick chat.
explanation: Monday is a natural time to ask how the last couple of days went. "Asking About Someone's Weekend" fits this better than commenting on the sky or routine work tasks.

title: Friday lockers, corridor walkout
text: It's Friday after the last bell and a friend is at their locker in the corridor. You are walking out together and have a minute to talk.
explanation: Friday is a common moment to ask what someone is doing over the next few days. "Asking About Someone's Weekend" covers that light question and listening.

title: Sunday video call, packed days
text: You're on a Sunday video call with a cousin who mentions they have had a packed few days. They lean back as if ready to keep talking.
explanation: They opened the door to talk about recent days, and a weekend check-in fits. "Asking About Someone's Weekend" matches better than giving praise or a reunion-style hello.

title: Desk stop, saturday event ask
text: A coworker stops by your desk and asks if you can come to their birthday dinner on Saturday. You already have quiet plans you want to keep.
explanation: You heard the full ask and want to decline kindly without over-explaining. "Declining an Invitation" covers thanking them and saying you cannot make it this time.

title: Message thread, concert ticket offer
text: A friend messages asking if you want tickets to a concert next month. You like them but do not want to go.
explanation: This is a future event you are choosing not to attend, not a moment where someone is making you feel guilty. "Declining an Invitation" fits a polite no with optional "maybe another time" if you mean it.

title: Door knock, street cookout request
text: Your neighbour knocks and asks if you can join a street barbecue on Sunday afternoon. You would rather have a restful day at home.
explanation: Someone invited you to an event and you want to say no without a long excuse. "Declining an Invitation" is for this kind of social ask, not explaining sensory needs ahead of a visit.

title: Shift end nearing, cover ask
text: Your manager messages two hours before your shift ends asking if you can cover someone tonight. You had planned a quiet evening.
explanation: The ask came with very little notice and you need to refuse clearly. "Saying No to a Last-Minute Request" helps you stay kind and firm without a detailed excuse.

title: Phone ring, urgent babysit favor
text: A friend calls and asks if you can babysit in about an hour. You are not free and did not agree to be on call.
explanation: This is a sudden favour with almost no warning, not a general boundary about behaviour over time. "Saying No to a Last-Minute Request" fits saying it does not work for you right now.

title: Late-night message, morning slot swap
text: A classmate messages late at night asking you to swap into their presentation slot tomorrow morning. You are not prepared to take it on.
explanation: You need to refuse a rushed academic favour, not shut down a personal question. "Saying No to a Last-Minute Request" covers appreciating the ask while holding your no.

title: Family table, second helping offered
text: You are at a family dinner and your host keeps offering a second helping and sliding the dish toward your plate. You are full and do not want more.
explanation: You want to refuse more food politely without eating to please someone. "Saying No to an Offer of Food or Drink" is built for a simple no thank you.

title: Office kitchen, coffee cup offered
text: A coworker in the kitchen offers you a cup of coffee you do not want. They are already pouring and looking at you.
explanation: This is about declining something to eat or drink, not asking someone to turn down volume. "Saying No to an Offer of Food or Drink" covers a brief, polite refusal.

title: Family gathering, dessert plate extended
text: At a gathering your aunt insists you try a dessert she made and holds the plate out to you. You would rather pass.
explanation: Someone is pushing food on you and you want to stay polite but firm. "Saying No to an Offer of Food or Drink" fits even when they ask why, without a long explanation.

title: Shared charger, repeated taking pattern
text: A friend keeps taking your phone charger from your bag without asking. It has happened several times and you want it to stop.
explanation: A repeated behaviour is crossing a line for you and you need to name it calmly. "Setting a Personal Boundary" covers saying you are not comfortable and that you need space.

title: Office mug, repeated borrowing
text: A coworker keeps using your favourite mug at the office even after you have mentioned it. They laugh it off each time.
explanation: You need to state a limit about how others treat your things, not explain sensory preferences in advance. "Setting a Personal Boundary" helps you stay calm and clear.

title: Relative visit, backpack privacy line
text: When you visit a relative, they keep opening your backpack to look inside without asking. You want that to change.
explanation: This is about ongoing behaviour you need to stop, not answering the same repeated favour again. "Setting a Personal Boundary" fits telling them you are not comfortable and may need to step away.

title: Kitchen study time, loud television
text: Your roommate is watching TV at a high volume while you are trying to study at the kitchen table. You can hear it through the wall.
explanation: You need to ask for less noise in the moment, not give a long advance talk about sensitivity. "Asking for Quiet or Less Noise" has calm wording for lowering volume or adjusting.

title: Open office, desk music playing
text: In an open-plan office a colleague is playing music from their desk without headphones. Several people are trying to focus nearby.
explanation: The issue is sound level where you work, not declining food or drink. "Asking for Quiet or Less Noise" covers approaching them calmly and asking to adjust.

title: Family barbecue, loud cousins nearby
text: At a family barbecue you are sitting near where young cousins are shouting and running. The noise is making it hard for you to stay seated.
explanation: You want relief from noise around you, not to repeat a no to the same favour again and again. "Asking for Quiet or Less Noise" is the right script for this setting.

title: Queue line, breath at shoulder
text: You are in a shop queue and the person behind you is standing so close you can feel their breath. They do not seem to notice.
explanation: You need more physical distance in a public line, not to respond to someone who already touched you. "Telling Someone They're Too Close" covers asking for space or stepping back yourself.

title: Desk screen, shoulder hover
text: A coworker leans over your shoulder to read your screen from inches away. You did not invite them into your space.
explanation: This is about personal space at your desk, not refusing a sudden work favour. "Telling Someone They're Too Close" lets you ask for more room without a long explanation.

title: Crowded stop, phone user pressing
text: At a crowded bus stop someone steps right into your space while looking at their phone. You feel boxed in.
explanation: You need distance from someone near you in public, not to decline a hug greeting. "Telling Someone They're Too Close" fits a short request for more space.

title: Party music, intrusive question lands
text: Someone you just met at a party asks whether you are seeing anyone. The music is loud and they are waiting for an answer.
explanation: They asked about a private topic you do not want to discuss with a new acquaintance. "Setting Limits on Personal Questions" helps you decline and optionally change the subject.

title: Lunch table, salary question lands
text: A coworker at lunch asks how much you earn. Others at the table go quiet and look at you.
explanation: This is a boundary around private information, not repeating no to the same repeated favour. "Setting Limits on Personal Questions" covers keeping topics private without apologising.

title: Family meal, medical details asked
text: At a family meal a relative asks detailed questions about your medical history. Several people are listening.
explanation: You want to shut down a personal topic at the table, not manage guilt about a decision. "Setting Limits on Personal Questions" is for keeping health and private life off the menu.

title: Repeated money ask, this month
text: A friend has asked you to lend them money five times this month after you already said no. They are asking again today.
explanation: Your answer has not changed and they keep returning to the same ask. "When Someone Keeps Asking" covers repeating your no and ending the discussion if needed.

title: Hallway stop, shift-cover request again
text: A coworker has asked you to cover their weekend shifts twice after you declined. They stop you in the hallway to ask a third time.
explanation: They are pushing the same request again rather than naming a general limit about your belongings. "When Someone Keeps Asking" fits holding your line until they stop.

title: Family visit, housing topic returns
text: A relative brings up moving in with them at every visit even though you have said no before. They start the topic again as you arrive.
explanation: This is the same pressure coming back, not a single event invite you are declining for the first time. "When Someone Keeps Asking" helps you say your answer is not going to change.

title: Hangout circle, repeated dare pushing
text: At a hangout friends keep urging you to try something you have already said you do not want to do. They laugh and pass it closer to you.
explanation: You feel pushed toward something that does not feel right and need a clear stop. "Being Pressured to Do Something Uncomfortable" covers trusting that feeling and saying no firmly, not setting a boundary about belongings.

title: Office request, login share push
text: A coworker pressures you to share a login for a system you are not allowed to share. They say it will only take a minute.
explanation: You are being pushed to do something that crosses a rule or risk line, not to dodge a personal question. "Being Pressured to Do Something Uncomfortable" fits a direct no that stays final.

title: Party cup, repeated glass pushing
text: At a party someone keeps pushing a drink toward you after you have already refused twice. They say you are being boring.
explanation: The pressure is about doing something you do not want, not a single polite offer of food or drink. "Being Pressured to Do Something Uncomfortable" is for when they will not accept your no.

title: Family talk, guilt-heavy appeal
text: A parent says you are letting the family down because you will not attend an event you do not want to go to. Their voice is upset.
explanation: They are trying to make you feel guilty about a boundary you already set. "When You Feel Manipulated or Guilted" helps you stay calm and keep your answer no.

title: Favour refusal, guilt-laden reply
text: A friend says a real friend would help them after you declined to do a favour. They look hurt on purpose.
explanation: This is emotional pressure about your decision, not deflecting a nosy question at the table. "When You Feel Manipulated or Guilted" covers hearing their upset while holding your no.

title: Team guilt line, late stay
text: A coworker sighs and says everyone on the team will suffer if you do not stay late, after you already said you cannot.
explanation: They are loading guilt onto your no, not asking for the first time with little notice. "When You Feel Manipulated or Guilted" fits staying firm without long justification.

title: Visit arrival, open arms approaching
text: A relative opens their arms wide when you arrive for a visit at their house. They are walking toward you for an embrace.
explanation: You want to connect without a hug and need a polite way to say so. "Saying No to a Hug" covers stepping back, offering a handshake, or a warm line that sets your preference.

title: Friday sign-off, arms outstretched
text: A new colleague you have only known a week moves in for an embrace at the end of Friday. Others nearby are saying goodbye.
explanation: This is about physical greeting, not declining coffee or food. "Saying No to a Hug" lets you keep things friendly while choosing a handshake or wave instead.

title: Cafe spotting, arms spread approach
text: A friend spots you at a café and walks over with arms out before you have sat down. They look excited to see you.
explanation: They are moving in for contact you do not want in a greeting, not asking for space after someone is already too near. "Saying No to a Hug" is the right script for this hello moment.

title: Shop aisle, shoulder tap surprise
text: A stranger in a shop pats your shoulder to squeeze past you without saying anything first. You flinch and they look surprised.
explanation: Someone made contact without consent and you need to speak up clearly. "When Someone Touches You Without Permission" covers telling them to stop and moving away.

title: Desk prank, hair touched suddenly
text: A coworker ruffles your hair as a joke while you are at your desk. They did not ask first and you froze.
explanation: Unwanted touch happened at work and you need to address it directly. "When Someone Touches You Without Permission" is for clear words and distance, not asking for quieter noise.

title: Group photo, wrist grab moment
text: An acquaintance grabs your arm to pull you into a group photo. Their hand is tight and you did not agree.
explanation: They touched you to move you without permission, not to pressure you into an activity with words. "When Someone Touches You Without Permission" fits saying stop and stepping away.

title: Overnight stay, late-TV note beforehand
text: You are about to stay overnight at a friend's place and want to explain that loud TV late at night is hard for you. They are relaxed and listening.
explanation: You are giving someone a heads-up about your needs before the visit, not asking them to turn something down in the moment. "Telling Someone About Your Sensory Needs" covers a calm advance conversation.

title: New flatmate, evening lights issue
text: You have a new roommate and want to tell them that bright overhead lights in the evening bother you. You catch them in the kitchen alone.
explanation: This is proactive sharing about sensitivity, not refusing a plate of food. "Telling Someone About Your Sensory Needs" helps you explain what helps and when you may step away.

title: Pre-visit call, early exit heads-up
text: Before a big family visit you want relatives to know you may leave early if the house gets overwhelming. Your aunt is on the phone.
explanation: You are explaining how overstimulation affects you ahead of time, not responding to guilt in the moment. "Telling Someone About Your Sensory Needs" is for that calm heads-up.

title: Hardware aisle, screw size missing
text: You are in a large hardware shop looking for a specific screw size. The aisles all look the same and a person in a staff vest is restocking shelves nearby.
explanation: You need a staff member to point you to the right aisle for a product on the shelves. "Finding an Item in a Store" walks through approaching them and naming what you need.

title: Pharmacy aisle, tablets hard locate
text: You are at a pharmacy trying to locate allergy tablets. You have walked the same row twice and an employee is tidying a display at the end of the aisle.
explanation: You are inside a shop and need someone who works there to show you where a product is kept. "Finding an Item in a Store" fits better than stopping a stranger for route guidance.

title: Garden centre, product location confusion
text: You are at a garden centre with a list on your phone. The potting soil bags are not where you expected and a worker is walking past with a trolley.
explanation: You already have the product in mind and need to know where it is in the building, not ask someone to repeat themselves. "Finding an Item in a Store" covers asking staff to guide you to the right section.

title: Shoe shop shelf, size unavailable
text: You are in a shoe shop and the trainers you wanted are not on the shelf. A staff member is folding clothes near the stockroom door.
explanation: You want to know whether they still have that item available, possibly in the back. "Checking if Something Is in Stock" is for that question to an employee.

title: Bookshop shelf gap, staff nearby
text: You are at a bookshop and the novel you came for has an empty gap on the shelf. The person at the counter is free and looking up.
explanation: The title you want may still be in storage even if it is not on display. "Checking if Something Is in Stock" helps you ask calmly and listen to their answer.

title: Cereal aisle, shelf gap confusion
text: You are in a supermarket and your usual cereal is missing from its normal spot. An employee with a name tag is facing the aisle.
explanation: You need to find out if the shop still carries that product, not ask someone to repeat words you missed. "Checking if Something Is in Stock" matches this shelf moment.

title: Department store, unpriced box item
text: You are in a department store holding a kitchen gadget with no price tag on the box. A staff member is walking toward the service desk.
explanation: You already have the item in hand and need to know what it costs before you decide. "Asking for a Price Check" is built for showing the product and waiting while they look it up.

title: Market stall, unpriced fruit
text: You are at an outdoor market stall and a basket of fruit has no sign with a number on it. The seller is serving another customer and will be free in a moment.
explanation: You need the cost of something you might buy, not directions to another part of the building. "Asking for a Price Check" fits a quick question to the person running the stall.

title: Self-checkout alert, unknown item
text: You are at self-checkout and the screen shows an unknown item after you scanned a barcode. A supervisor in a different uniform is standing nearby.
explanation: The machine did not show a clear price and you need a person to confirm it. "Asking for a Price Check" covers approaching staff and pointing to what you are holding.

title: Maths desk, one problem stuck
text: You are in a maths lesson working through problems on your own. You are stuck on one question and the instructor is walking between the desks.
explanation: You need to raise your hand or catch them at a quiet moment to ask about the work in front of you. "Asking a Teacher for Help" covers waiting for the right time and stating your question clearly.

title: Lab bench mismatch, next step
text: You are in a science lab and the next step on your worksheet does not match what is on the bench. The person leading the session is at the far end of the room.
explanation: You need academic support from the person running the class, not just a repeat of words you did not hear. "Asking a Teacher for Help" fits approaching them when they are not mid-lecture.

title: History brief, final paragraph unclear
text: Your history instructor has just explained a long-term assignment. You are unsure what they want in the final paragraph and they are at the front desk packing papers.
explanation: You need clarification on schoolwork from the person who set the task. "Asking a Teacher for Help" is the right framework, not asking a parent whether you may go somewhere.

title: New software screen, nearby teammate
text: You have just been given access to new software at your desk. The screen looks unfamiliar and a teammate at the next workstation does not have headphones on.
explanation: You need a quick show-how from someone on your team who may know the tool. "Asking a Colleague for Help" covers checking they are free and explaining what you are stuck on.

title: Staff kitchen, labels location unclear
text: You are in the staff kitchen at work and cannot find where they keep the food labels. Someone from your shift is cooking and seems relaxed.
explanation: This is a small workplace question for a peer, not route guidance from a stranger on the street. "Asking a Colleague for Help" fits asking if they have a moment and naming the task.

title: Warehouse scanner, unfamiliar buttons
text: You are in a warehouse and the handheld scanner has several buttons you have never used. An experienced coworker is standing a few metres away.
explanation: You need a coworker to walk you through equipment at work, not a shop employee to find a product aisle. "Asking a Colleague for Help" matches this on-the-job moment.

title: After bell, homework confusion remains
text: The bell has just rung and most students are leaving the room. You are still confused about tonight's homework and the instructor is putting papers in a folder.
explanation: You need a quiet moment after the lesson to ask about the assignment. "Asking Your Teacher for Help After Class" is for when the room is calmer and you can be specific.

title: Lecture end, slide still unclear
text: You stayed behind when a university lecture ended. Slide four still does not make sense to you and the person at the podium is unplugging their laptop.
explanation: You want one focused question before they leave, not a repeat of something said over a bad connection. "Asking Your Teacher for Help After Class" covers waiting for a quiet moment and thanking them.

title: Tutoring wrap-up, private question pending
text: A tutoring session is ending and you still have a private question about the practice sheet. The tutor is putting on their coat by the door.
explanation: This is follow-up on learning right as the session closes, not asking a guardian whether you may do an activity. "Asking Your Teacher for Help After Class" fits catching them before they go.

title: Dead phone, bus stop map
text: You are in an unfamiliar city and your phone battery is dead. A person at the bus stop is reading a local timetable and looks unhurried.
explanation: You need to reach a place and must ask someone nearby how to get there on foot or by transit. "Asking for Directions" covers choosing someone approachable and listening carefully.

title: Mall map mismatch, guard nearby
text: You are inside a shopping centre and the map on the wall does not match where you are standing. A security person is at a desk a few metres away.
explanation: You are trying to reach an exit or shop, not locate facilities inside the building. "Asking for Directions" fits asking how to get to a named place.

title: Hospital wing mix-up, volunteer nearby
text: You are visiting someone in a hospital and realise you are in the wrong wing. A volunteer with a lanyard is walking toward you in the corridor.
explanation: You need wayfinding inside a large building from someone who knows the layout. "Asking for Directions" is for that, not a classroom question about homework.

title: Appointment ahead, map app unopened
text: You have an appointment across town in forty minutes. You are still on your street with a full battery and have not started walking yet.
explanation: You can plan the route on your device before you set off. "Using Your Phone for Directions" covers opening the maps app, entering the address, and choosing how you will travel.

title: Trailhead start, route check screen
text: You are at a trailhead with a downloaded route saved. You are about to start walking and want to confirm the path on your screen matches the signpost.
explanation: You are navigating with technology in your hand, not asking a person to repeat something. "Using Your Phone for Directions" fits checking the map before you continue.

title: Transfer station, two platforms listed
text: You have just arrived at a train station for a transfer. Two platforms are listed on the departures board and you open your maps app before moving.
explanation: You are using your device to follow a route through a station, not learning where facilities are in general. "Using Your Phone for Directions" helps you pick the right mode and follow turn-by-turn guidance.

title: Busy cafe, words lost in noise
text: You are in a busy café with a friend. The espresso machine runs and their lips move, but you did not hear the words.
explanation: You missed what they said because of noise, not because you need a lesson explained. "Asking Someone to Repeat Themselves" gives you a polite line to hear it again.

title: Video call glitch, missed instruction
text: You are on a work video call and your manager gives a short instruction. The audio glitches for a second and their mouth is still moving.
explanation: You need the words said again, not a coworker to walk you through a new tool. "Asking Someone to Repeat Themselves" fits when you genuinely did not catch what was spoken.

title: Reception desk, masked time unclear
text: You are at a dental reception desk. The person behind the counter says your appointment time through a mask and you only caught part of it.
explanation: You need them to say the time again clearly, not ask where facilities are in the building. "Asking Someone to Repeat Themselves" covers a brief request to hear it once more.

title: Expense email, portal step unclear
text: Your manager sent an email with several steps for submitting expenses. The third step mentions a portal name you do not recognise.
explanation: You understand part of the process but need to clarify one specific step before you proceed. "Not Understanding Instructions" helps you name what is unclear and confirm what they meant.

title: Flat-pack diagram, piece mismatch
text: You are assembling flat-pack furniture at home. The diagram shows a piece that does not match anything laid out on the floor.
explanation: You are working from written steps that do not line up, not planning a walk with a maps app. "Not Understanding Instructions" fits pinning down which part of the guide is confusing.

title: Discharge leaflet, timing still unclear
text: A nurse explained your home medication routine quickly before you left the ward. You have the leaflet but two timings seem to contradict each other.
explanation: You need to clarify spoken care steps, not the price of something in a shop. "Not Understanding Instructions" covers asking what they meant by a specific part of the routine.

title: Lunch table, sudden quiet mood
text: You are at lunch with a friend and they go quiet right after something you said. They are looking at their plate and the mood feels different.
explanation: Something shifted in the conversation and you are not sure what they meant or felt. "When You Miss a Social Cue" helps you ask gently without panicking.

title: Shared flat, plans meet silence
text: Your roommate sighs heavily when you mention your plans for Saturday. They turn toward the window and stop talking.
explanation: Their reaction suggests you may have missed a signal, not that someone wants you to share contact details. "When You Miss a Social Cue" fits checking what they meant or how they feel.

title: Office desk, topic abruptly shifts
text: A coworker changes the subject right after you ask about their project. They glance at the clock and start typing again.
explanation: You may have stepped past a signal to wrap up, not need a demo of workplace software. "When You Miss a Social Cue" is for when you sense something unspoken happened.

title: Family dinner, mixed reactions table
text: Your sibling comments on dinner in a flat voice while rolling their eyes. Everyone else at the table smiles but you are not sure how to read it.
explanation: You are unsure whether they were serious or playing with tone. "When You Don't Understand Sarcasm or a Joke" gives you a calm way to ask if they meant it literally.

title: Spreadsheet error, room laughs softly
text: After a spreadsheet mistake, a teammate says "great job" slowly and looks at the screen. Others in the room laugh quietly.
explanation: The words sound positive but the delivery does not match. "When You Don't Understand Sarcasm or a Joke" fits checking whether they were being serious.

title: Cold weather comment, uncertain laughter
text: A classmate laughs right after a comment about how cold it is outside. You are not sure whether they were making fun of the weather or of you.
explanation: You need to know if they were joking before you respond, not ask a stranger how to get somewhere. "When You Don't Understand Sarcasm or a Joke" covers asking plainly.

title: Film night, host in kitchen
text: You are at a friend's flat for a film night. You need to use the facilities and they are chatting in the kitchen while snacks are on the table.
explanation: You are a guest in someone's home and need to ask politely during a pause. "Asking to Use the Bathroom at Someone's House" covers waiting for a natural break and asking where to go.

title: Family dinner, host nearby chatting
text: You are at a family dinner that has been going for an hour. You need to slip away quietly and the host is nearby in the dining room.
explanation: This is a private home visit, not asking a guardian whether you may go out. "Asking to Use the Bathroom at Someone's House" fits a brief polite request to the person who lives there.

title: Client home, quiet lounge pause
text: You are babysitting in a client's home. The child is asleep and you need the facilities while the parent is on a call in the lounge.
explanation: You need to ask the adult whose home you are in, not request permission to go out somewhere. "Asking to Use the Bathroom at Someone's House" is the right script for this moment.

title: Coffee place entrance, staff waiting
text: You have just walked into a coffee shop and need the facilities before you order. The person behind the counter is free and looking up.
explanation: You need a staff member to tell you where the customer facilities are in this business. "Asking to Use the Bathroom in a Restaurant, Café, or Shop" covers a quick question at the counter.

title: Fast-food table, corridor signs missing
text: You have finished eating at a fast-food restaurant. You cannot see any signs on the walls and a cleaner with a mop is near the corridor.
explanation: You need to locate facilities inside the venue, not get directions to another building. "Asking to Use the Bathroom in a Restaurant, Café, or Shop" fits asking staff where to go.

title: Clothing racks, till assistant nearby
text: You have been browsing in a clothing shop for a while. You need the facilities and an assistant is folding shirts near the till.
explanation: You are asking where to go in the building, not whether an item is still available. "Asking to Use the Bathroom in a Restaurant, Café, or Shop" works in shops as well as eateries.

title: Seminar room, seated discomfort building
text: You are in a university seminar and feel uncomfortable staying seated much longer. The person at the front has paused for questions.
explanation: You need to be excused briefly in a formal group setting. "Asking for a Bathroom Break During Class or a Meeting" covers raising your hand or catching their attention quietly.

title: Long screen session, discomfort rising
text: You are on a long work video call that has run two hours without a break. You need to step away from the screen for a few minutes.
explanation: You are in a structured meeting and need a formal brief exit, not a classroom question about coursework. "Asking for a Bathroom Break During Class or a Meeting" fits signalling you will be back shortly.

title: Evening workshop, live demo underway
text: You are in an evening community class during a live demonstration. You need to step out mid-session without disrupting everyone.
explanation: You need permission to leave the room briefly while a session is running. "Asking for a Bathroom Break During Class or a Meeting" is for that, not asking café staff where to go.

title: Cinema interval, corridor signs ahead
text: It is your first visit to a cinema and the interval is approaching. You are not sure which corridor the signs point to and want to plan ahead.
explanation: You are learning how facilities are usually marked in this type of venue before you need them urgently. "Knowing Where to Find Bathrooms in Different Places" covers looking for signs and when to ask staff.

title: Coach boarding, onboard layout unknown
text: You are about to board a long bus trip. You want to understand the layout on board before departure so you are not caught off guard later.
explanation: This is about knowing what to expect in different transport settings, not excusing yourself from a classroom. "Knowing Where to Find Bathrooms in Different Places" includes asking the driver or guard when needed.

title: Library entrance, facilities mapped early
text: You have just entered a large library building for a long study session. You want to spot where facilities are early so you do not search later under pressure.
explanation: You are planning ahead in a public building, not hunting for a product on a shelf. "Knowing Where to Find Bathrooms in Different Places" fits scanning for signs near entrances and knowing it is fine to ask.

title: Study group, spare pencil nearby
text: You are in a study group and realise you forgot a pencil. Your friend's case is open on the table beside you.
explanation: You want to use something that belongs to them for a short time. "Asking Permission to Borrow Something" covers asking the owner directly before you take it.

title: Front garden, ladder in driveway
text: You need to trim a hedge and your neighbour's ladder is visible in their driveway. They are gardening in the front garden.
explanation: You need their yes before using their equipment, not before sharing their phone number with someone else. "Asking Permission to Borrow Something" fits naming the item and returning it when agreed.

title: Rainy office, umbrella by desk
text: Rain has started heavily outside the office window. A coworker's umbrella is leaning against their desk and they are in a meeting room.
explanation: You need to ask the owner before using their belonging, not ask them to explain software. "Asking Permission to Borrow Something" is for a clear borrow request and thank-you when you return it.

title: Quiet house, park outing idea
text: You want to walk to the park on your own this afternoon. Your parent is reading on the sofa and the house is quiet.
explanation: You need an adult to agree to an activity or outing, not borrow a physical object. "Asking an Adult for Permission" covers choosing a calm moment and stating your request clearly.

title: Dinner prep, overnight visit request
text: You want to sleep over at a friend's house this weekend. Your guardian is cooking dinner and seems relaxed.
explanation: You are asking whether you may do something, not whether you may pass their contact details to someone. "Asking an Adult for Permission" fits a clear question and waiting for their answer.

title: Calm office, early finish request
text: You would like to leave work two hours early today. Your manager is at the water cooler and the office is calm.
explanation: You need approval from someone in charge, not a teammate to show you a task. "Asking an Adult for Permission" works for any authority figure when you need a yes or no.

title: Group chat, private number requested
text: A friend gave you their new mobile number in private. In a group chat, someone else asks you to share it so they can invite them.
explanation: Their contact details belong to them and you should check before passing them on. "Asking Before Sharing Someone's Information" covers asking if it is okay to share with a named person.

title: Party photos, posting decision moment
text: You took photos at a party and want to post one online. A friend is clearly visible in the background and has not said anything about it.
explanation: Sharing their image is personal information too. "Asking Before Sharing Someone's Information" fits checking before you post, not asking to borrow something they own.

title: Lunch table, confidential news pressed
text: A coworker told you confidentially that they are job hunting. Another colleague asks you at lunch whether you have heard anything about it.
explanation: News about their life is theirs to share, not yours to pass on without consent. "Asking Before Sharing Someone's Information" reminds you to check with the person first, even at work.

title: Home desk, clinic number ready
text: You have had a sore throat for several days and your usual clinic's website says new patients should ring the front desk to request a time. You are at home with the number written on a sticky note.
explanation: You still need to arrange a visit before you go anywhere. "Making a Doctor's Appointment" walks you through what to say on the line and what details to have ready.

title: Reception line, routine checkup call
text: Your dentist sent a card with a surgery number on it because you are due for a routine check-up. You tap the number and after a few rings a receptionist answers and asks how they can help.
explanation: Someone is on the line ready to find you a time, so you need your details and what you need ready to say aloud. "Making a Doctor's Appointment" covers that live conversation; drafting a formal note in your inbox is a different channel.

title: New town, practice registration call
text: You moved towns and need to register with a new GP practice. The welcome leaflet lists a main line that rings for a long time before someone from reception answers.
explanation: This is about setting up care at a clinic, not fixing a product you bought. "Making a Doctor's Appointment" fits when you need to give your details and ask for an available time with a clinician.

title: Desk letter, Thursday clash appears
text: You booked a Thursday afternoon with a specialist, but your employer just scheduled mandatory training that afternoon. The clinic's number is on the confirmation letter on your desk.
explanation: Your existing slot no longer works, so you need to change or drop it with the clinic directly. "Cancelling or Rescheduling an Appointment" covers calling early, stating the date you had, and what you need instead.

title: Calendar conflict, clinic slot overlap
text: Your child has a passport office visit on the same morning as an orthodontist visit you set up last month. The orthodontist's office is open and you have their number saved.
explanation: You already have a time booked and need to move or remove it, not start from scratch. "Cancelling or Rescheduling an Appointment" is built for that; booking a brand-new slot is what "Making a Doctor's Appointment" is for.

title: Morning fever, same-day slot conflict
text: You woke up with a fever on the morning of a hygienist visit you scheduled for later today. The practice voicemail says to call if you cannot attend for health reasons.
explanation: You need to let the practice know you cannot make today's slot, ideally before you are due. "Cancelling or Rescheduling an Appointment" fits a same-day change; a formal written note to a professor is a different kind of contact.

title: Thursday evening, coffee plan check-in
text: You and a friend agreed to meet for coffee on Saturday. It is Thursday evening and they have not mentioned it since you last spoke on Monday.
explanation: You are reaching out first with the day, time, and place so nothing gets forgotten. "Reminding Someone About an Appointment or Event" is for that friendly heads-up, not answering a question they already sent you.

title: Project chat, Tuesday library ping
text: Your group project is meeting at the library on Tuesday at four. One teammate has been quiet in the chat channel since you picked the time.
explanation: A short written nudge with the plan and a check that it still suits them is what you need here. "Reminding Someone About an Appointment or Event" covers that; returning a missed call is a different kind of message.

title: Friday night, airport pickup details
text: Your cousin is flying in on Sunday and you offered to pick them up from the airport. It is Friday and you want to confirm the flight time and terminal before you drive.
explanation: You already have a plan together and just need to jog their memory and confirm details. "Reminding Someone About an Appointment or Event" fits a warm check-in; writing to an official you do not know is closer to "Writing a Formal Email."

title: Home kitchen, takeaway menu open
text: Your favourite pizza place still takes requests by voice only, and their paper menu is on the fridge. You are hungry at home and have your card ready.
explanation: You are placing a meal to be brought to your address, not reporting a faulty product. "Ordering Food Delivery by Phone" walks through stating items, your address, and confirming the total.

title: Kitchen drawer, takeaway flyer ready
text: Your parents asked you to sort dinner because the delivery app on your phone keeps crashing. A local Indian takeaway number is printed on a flyer in the kitchen drawer.
explanation: This is a restaurant line for a meal tonight, not a medical reception desk. "Ordering Food Delivery by Phone" is the right script when you list dishes and give where to bring them.

title: Rainy evening, drop-off menu leaflet
text: It is raining hard and you do not want to go out. A leaflet for a nearby Chinese kitchen arrived today with a number to ring for home drop-off.
explanation: You want hot food sent to you, which means naming what you want and where you live. "Ordering Food Delivery by Phone" covers that flow; leaving a message for a hiring team is a different kind of call.

title: School line, recorded tone prompt
text: You rang your child's school office during lunch and nobody picked up. After several rings, a recorded voice asks you to state your name and reason, then wait for the tone.
explanation: No person is on the line, so you need a short, clear spoken note they can play back later. "Leaving a Voicemail" covers name, purpose, and a number to reach you; navigating a company's billing menu is a different script.

title: After-hours hiring line, recorded message
text: You applied for a job last week and the hiring line goes to an after-hours message. You want to follow up about whether they received your documents.
explanation: You are leaving a professional message for someone who was not available to talk live. "Leaving a Voicemail" fits that moment; drafting a long message in your inbox is what "Writing a Formal Email" is for.

title: Maintenance line, flat details recording
text: You called your landlord's maintenance line about a dripping tap. Hold music plays for a minute, then you hear instructions to record your flat number and the problem after the signal.
explanation: You need to leave structured information on a recording, not book a clinic slot. "Leaving a Voicemail" gives you the steps for a clear spoken note; arranging a GP visit uses a different opening and details.

title: Missed clinic call, afternoon availability
text: You notice a missed call from your dental surgery while you were in the shower. You do not know what they wanted, but you are free this afternoon if they ring again.
explanation: You are returning their attempt to reach you and saying when you are available. "Leaving a Voicemail for a Callback" is short and casual; ringing a clinic to request a new time slot is a different kind of call.

title: Silent phone, missed calls log
text: A friend tried you twice while your phone was on silent during a film. You see their name on the call log and want them to know you saw it.
explanation: You missed their live call and only need to say who you are and that you will answer if they try again. "Leaving a Voicemail for a Callback" fits that; replying to a written question they sent is what "Responding to an Important Text or Email" covers.

title: Meeting break, recruiter call missed
text: A recruiter rang once during a meeting and you could not speak. You have their direct line and want them to know afternoons work best for you this week.
explanation: This is a quick return call note, not a complaint about a purchase. "Leaving a Voicemail for a Callback" keeps it brief with your name, availability, and number; explaining a billing issue to a company line is a different conversation.

title: Damaged parcel, helpline number ready
text: A parcel arrived yesterday but the box inside was crushed and the item inside is cracked. The shop's helpline is printed on your receipt.
explanation: Something you already paid for arrived damaged, so you need to explain the problem and ask what they can do. "Calling Customer Support" covers preparing details and staying on the line until you understand the options.

title: Bank app, duplicate charge spotted
text: You checked your bank app and the same streaming service charged you twice this month. Their website lists a support number under billing questions.
explanation: You are reporting a billing mistake to the company that took the payment, not leaving a general message for a person who called you. "Calling Customer Support" fits describing the charge and asking how they will fix it.

title: Home router offline, agent connected
text: Your home internet has been down for three days even though you restarted the router. The provider's automated system finally connects you to a human agent.
explanation: You need help with a service you pay for, including account details and what you already tried. "Calling Customer Support" is built for that; ringing a GP surgery to request a visit is a different kind of call.

title: Refund delay, frontline answer repeats
text: You were promised a refund two weeks ago after a faulty kettle return. The person on the line keeps saying it is still processing and cannot give a date.
explanation: You already explained the issue to the first agent and need someone with authority to move it forward. "Asking to Speak to a Manager" fits after you have tried the first person calmly; leaving a general recorded message when nobody answered is a different step.

title: Hotel bill, unexplained charge remains
text: You stayed at a hotel last weekend and your bill shows a room service charge you never used. The front desk clerk on the phone says only a supervisor can remove charges.
explanation: The first person has told you they cannot fix the charge, so the next step is a polite request to speak with someone higher up. "Asking to Speak to a Manager" covers that; leaving a recorded message when nobody answered is a different situation.

title: Warranty tracking stalled, policy loop
text: You sent a laptop for warranty repair six weeks ago and the tracking page has not changed. The agent reads the same policy paragraph for the third time without offering a solution.
explanation: You have stated the problem clearly and need escalation, not a new channel of contact. "Asking to Speak to a Manager" is for when the first helper cannot resolve it; writing a structured note to a professor is not the same need.

title: Desk draft, tutor inbox message
text: Your course tutor posted office hours by inbox only and you need to ask whether you may submit your essay one day late. You are at your desk with their address copied.
explanation: This needs a polite written request with a clear subject and short body, not a call to a clinic. "Writing a Formal Email" walks you through opening, stating your purpose, and signing off properly.

title: Cold flat, agency message draft
text: The heating in your flat has been off for two days and the letting agency asks tenants to contact them in writing with the flat number. You open a new draft on your phone.
explanation: They want a written record of the issue, which calls for a structured message with your details up front. "Writing a Formal Email" fits that; ringing a shop helpline about a product is a different format and tone.

title: Volunteer follow-up, coordinator inbox note
text: You volunteered at a community centre and the coordinator asked you to confirm in writing that you can help at the spring fair. You need to sound professional in a few sentences.
explanation: You are composing a respectful written yes or question, not speaking into a machine after a tone. "Writing a Formal Email" covers subject line, greeting, and closing; a spoken note on an answering machine is a different script.

title: Family chat, travel question pending
text: Your aunt messaged yesterday asking which train you arrive on Sunday. You opened the chat hours ago but have not typed anything yet.
explanation: They asked you something directly and are waiting for a clear answer. "Responding to an Important Text or Email" helps you read fully, reply to the actual question, and keep it brief.

title: Work inbox, briefing confirmation needed
text: Your supervisor sent a note this morning: "Can you confirm you will attend the Monday briefing?" The notification is still sitting unread in your work inbox.
explanation: You need a direct yes or no (or a short delay notice), not a heads-up about a plan they already know. "Responding to an Important Text or Email" fits answering what they asked; nudging someone about a date you agreed earlier uses a different script.

title: Kitchen counter, teacher note awaiting
text: Your child's teacher sent a note that the permission slip is due tomorrow. You have the form on the counter and need to tell them you will send it tonight.
explanation: This is a straightforward reply to their request, not reporting a faulty purchase to a company line. "Responding to an Important Text or Email" covers answering the question clearly; calling a shop helpline about a product is a different situation.

title: Unknown number, cruel thread saved
text: Last night an unknown number sent several cruel comments about how you look. You saved the thread and your hands are shaking when you open your phone again.
explanation: The priority is to pause, protect yourself, and get support before you type anything back. "When You Receive an Unwanted or Upsetting Message" covers stepping away, saving evidence if needed, and talking to someone you trust.

title: Morning screen, angry paragraph waiting
text: Someone you used to date sent a long angry paragraph this morning after you stopped replying last week. You feel flooded and are tempted to type a defence right away.
explanation: Reacting while you are still flooded often makes things worse. "When You Receive an Unwanted or Upsetting Message" helps you step back first; placing a takeaway order by phone is unrelated to what you are feeling right now.

title: Group chat, mocking tag appears
