text: In a group chat, someone tagged you in a meme that mocks your accent. Other people have reacted with laughing emojis and your chest feels tight.
explanation: You need space and a plan before you respond, including whether to save, mute, or tell someone safe. "When You Receive an Unwanted or Upsetting Message" is for that; calling a shop about a broken product is unrelated.

title: Morning phone, birthday lunch fallout
text: You forgot your close friend's birthday lunch yesterday and they sent a short note saying they felt hurt. You want to reach out this morning in writing.
explanation: You are owning what happened and keeping it brief without excuses. "Sending an Apology by Text or Email" is for that written repair; a quick spoken note on their answering machine is a different format.

title: After argument, sibling silence lingers
text: You snapped at your sibling last night over noise and they went quiet. After sleeping on it, you want to send them a few honest lines on your phone.
explanation: A short written sorry you can edit before sending fits better than a quick return call. "Sending an Apology by Text or Email" covers saying what you regret without a "but"; saying sorry face to face in the moment is what "How to Say Sorry to a Friend" is for.

title: Deadline miss, colleague stayed late
text: You missed a team deadline and a colleague had to stay late to finish your part. They messaged that they were disappointed, and you want to acknowledge it today.
explanation: You need to express regret for the impact on them, not just nudge them about a plan you already made. "Sending an Apology by Text or Email" focuses on a genuine written sorry; a friendly heads-up about an event uses a different script.

title: Saturday list, supermarket entrance rush
text: It is Saturday morning and you need milk, pasta, and fruit for the week. You are standing at the entrance of your usual supermarket with a list on your phone.
explanation: You are doing a full shop from start to finish, not a quick chat with floor staff. "Getting Through a Grocery Shop" covers working through sections, finding items, and reaching the tills.

title: New supermarket layout, rice hunt
text: You moved recently and this supermarket layout is new to you. You have been walking the aisles for ten minutes and still have not found the rice.
explanation: You are still inside the store working through what you need, including asking for help with shelves. "Getting Through a Grocery Shop" fits the whole visit; asking whether a vehicle goes to a destination is a different setting.

title: After work, dinner ingredients run
text: You stopped in after work to pick up dinner ingredients before the kitchen closes. The store is busy and you want to move through without forgetting anything.
explanation: You are gathering several items across the store, not stepping up to a café counter for one drink. "Getting Through a Grocery Shop" helps you stay organised from basket to tills.

title: Front line, belt loading moment
text: You have reached the front of the line and the person ahead is packing their bags. You place your items on the belt as they finish.
explanation: You are at the till now, ready to pay and respond when staff speak to you. "At the Checkout" covers this moment; ordering one drink at a café counter is a shorter exchange.

title: Self-service till, payment prompt beeping
text: You are at a self-service till and the screen is asking you to insert your card. Your bags are full and the machine is beeping for payment.
explanation: You are finishing a purchase you are keeping, not bringing something back for money off. "At the Checkout" fits paying and leaving; going to a returns desk with a receipt is a different process.

title: Express lane, cashier eye contact
text: You joined the express lane with a few items and the cashier looks up. They seem about to ask whether you found what you needed.
explanation: This is the paying moment at a supermarket till, not a chair in a salon. "At the Checkout" walks you through what to say and having payment ready.

title: Rack picks, curtained room ahead
text: You picked up two jumpers in a clothing shop and are not sure which size fits. You walk toward the curtained area near the back with them over your arm.
explanation: You need a private space to test fit before you buy. "Trying on Clothes in a Store" covers asking for a room and handing back what you do not want; telling a floor worker you are only browsing is a lighter interaction.

title: Fitting area, numbered tag ready
text: A shop worker near the fitting rooms smiles and holds up a numbered tag. You are holding three shirts on hangers you want to test.
explanation: They are about to count your items and let you into a changing room. "Trying on Clothes in a Store" fits that handover; bringing something back to a returns desk is for after you have already bought it.

title: Trouser length check, mirror test
text: You found trousers on the rack that might be too long in the leg. You want to see them on before you carry them to the till.
explanation: You are checking fit in a changing room, not sitting for a trim. "Trying on Clothes in a Store" is the right script for asking to use a room and returning what does not work.

title: Table menus, server with notepad
text: You are seated at a table in a sit-down restaurant and have had a few minutes with the menu. A server is walking toward you with a notepad.
explanation: They are ready to take your meal and drink choices from the table. "Ordering at a Restaurant" covers stating what you want and any dietary questions; paying at a supermarket belt is a different flow.

title: Celebration dinner, server waits patiently
text: It is your friend's birthday dinner and everyone has menus open. The server stops at your end of the table and looks at you first.
explanation: You need to choose food and drinks for this table, not tell a shop worker you are just browsing racks. "Ordering at a Restaurant" fits naming dishes politely when they are ready to write them down.

title: Pasta question, server pen raised
text: You are eating out and need to check whether a pasta dish contains dairy before anyone writes your order down. The server is waiting with their pen raised.
explanation: This is the moment to ask about ingredients as you choose your meal. "Ordering at a Restaurant" includes raising dietary needs when you order; asking whether a vehicle stops near you is unrelated.

title: Counter line, barista awaiting choice
text: You are third in line at a café counter and the barista has just finished with the person ahead. They turn to you and meet your eyes.
explanation: You need to name a drink size and type and then pay at the counter. "Ordering Coffee or a Drink" fits this quick exchange; unloading a trolley at a supermarket till is a longer step.

title: Bakery front, hot cup choices
text: You stepped inside a bakery that sells hot drinks at the front. A screen shows sizes and the person behind the glass is waiting for your choice.
explanation: You are buying one beverage to take away, not sitting down for a full meal or a trim. "Ordering Coffee or a Drink" covers saying your order clearly and moving aside to wait.

title: Station kiosk, cup name requested
text: You are at a train station kiosk that sells tea and snacks. When your turn comes, they ask for your name to write on the cup.
explanation: You are at a counter choosing a drink, not boarding a vehicle yet. "Ordering Coffee or a Drink" fits giving your order and name; tapping on when you enter a bus is a later step.

title: Wrong sauce, server passing nearby
text: Your plate arrived ten minutes ago but the sauce on the chicken is not what you chose on the menu. The server passes nearby with empty hands.
explanation: Something is wrong with what was brought to your table while you are still eating out. "Sending Food Back" covers catching their attention and explaining the mix-up calmly; taking an item to a shop desk with a receipt is a different setting.

title: Nut topping present, allergy risk
text: You ordered a hot meal without nuts because of an allergy, but the bowl in front of you has crushed peanuts on top. You need the kitchen to fix it before you eat.
explanation: This is unsafe food at your table right now, not a gadget that broke after you got home. "Sending Food Back" fits telling staff there has been a mistake with what you received; returning faulty goods to a high-street shop later uses a different script.

title: Vegetarian dish, bacon pieces visible
text: You asked for a vegetarian main course but the dish that arrived has bacon pieces visible on top. The dining room is quiet enough to get the server's attention.
explanation: You need staff to correct what was served while you are still at the table. "Sending Food Back" is for that moment; finishing payment at a grocery till assumes you are keeping everything you scanned.

title: Service desk, faulty headphones boxed
text: You bought headphones last week and the left side has stopped working. You have the box, the receipt, and the item in your bag at the customer service desk.
explanation: You are at the returns counter with proof of purchase, asking what they can do. "Returning an Item to a Shop" covers stating you want to bring something back; explaining a fault that appeared days after buying uses similar words but this script is the standard returns desk flow.

title: Entrance counter, wrong-colour jacket tags
text: A jacket you ordered online is the wrong colour and still has tags on it. The shop has a returns counter near the entrance and you printed the delivery note.
explanation: You are bringing an unwanted purchase to the store, not sending a plate back in a dining room. "Returning an Item to a Shop" fits asking for a refund or exchange with your paperwork.

title: Retail desk, missing part appliance
text: You opened a kitchen appliance at home and a piece was missing from the box. You drove back to the retailer with everything packed as it arrived.
explanation: You need the returns or service desk, not a changing room. "Returning an Item to a Shop" walks you through what to say at the counter; trying on outfits before you buy is a different part of the store.

title: Sports aisle, staff offer arrives
text: You are looking at trainers on a shelf in a sports shop when a staff member walks over. They smile and say they can help you find anything.
explanation: You decide whether you want help locating something or prefer to browse alone. "When a Sales Associate Approaches You" covers a simple yes or a polite "just looking"; planning a whole food shop from aisle to aisle is a bigger task.

title: Homeware section, uniformed help offer
text: You are waiting for a friend in a department store and skimming the homeware section. A person in a shop uniform stops beside you and asks if you need assistance.
explanation: You only need a brief answer about whether you want their help right now. "When a Sales Associate Approaches You" fits that; describing how you want your hair cut happens once you are in the chair.

title: Phone-case display, helper appears
text: You came in to compare phone cases and are still deciding. A sales associate appears from behind a display and asks what you are looking for today.
explanation: They are offering shop-floor help, not taking a meal order. "When a Sales Associate Approaches You" lets you accept help or decline without a long explanation; choosing dishes from a menu at a table is a different interaction.

title: Salon chair, reference photo ready
text: You saved a photo on your phone of the length you want. You have just sat down in the salon chair and the stylist is combing your hair before they start.
explanation: You are here for a cut and need to show or describe the style. "Getting a Haircut" covers sharing a picture and checking the mirror at the end; telling a shop worker you are only browsing happens on the sales floor, not in the chair.

title: Barber chair, tidy-up preference check
text: Your usual barber calls you to the chair and asks how much you want off today. You have been growing it out and only want a small tidy-up.
explanation: You are describing length and style while someone cuts your hair. "Getting a Haircut" fits showing with fingers or saying "just a trim"; a shop worker asking if you need help on the sales floor is not the same moment.

title: New salon, back mirror check
text: It is your first visit to a new salon and the stylist holds up a mirror to the back of your head. They ask whether the shape looks right so far.
explanation: You are mid-appointment checking the result in the mirror. "Getting a Haircut" includes saying when it looks good; trying on trousers in a retail changing room happens before you pay, not in a salon.

title: Salon dryers, pre-cut comfort check
text: You have a salon booking in twenty minutes and loud dryers make your shoulders tense. Before the stylist picks up the scissors, they ask if everything is okay.
explanation: You need them to know about touch around your head before they begin. "Telling the Hairdresser You're Sensitive to Touch" is for that heads-up; trying on clothes in a changing room is a different kind of private space.

title: Barber cape, neck discomfort rising
text: You are in the chair at a barber shop and capes brushing your neck bother you. The barber is about to start clipping the sides.
explanation: This is the moment to ask for gentleness and warnings before contact starts. "Telling the Hairdresser You're Sensitive to Touch" fits that conversation; declining help from a shop assistant on the sales floor is unrelated.

title: Spray bottle ready, ear-area concern
text: A new hairdresser at your usual place is introducing themselves and reaching for the spray bottle. You feel anxious about water and touch near your ears.
explanation: You should let them know about sensitivity before they touch your head, not order food. "Telling the Hairdresser You're Sensitive to Touch" gives the words for that; picking dishes from a menu at a table is a different setting.

title: Boxed lamp, snapped switch discovered
text: You bought a desk lamp three days ago and the switch snapped off in your hand. You still have the receipt and the lamp is in the box in your car outside the shop.
explanation: Something failed soon after you paid and you are back at the retailer to ask what they will do. "When Something Breaks Quickly After Buying It" covers explaining how long you have had it and asking about a replacement; the returns desk script overlaps, but this one focuses on faults that appear right away.

title: Service counter, kettle stopped heating
text: A kettle you purchased last weekend no longer heats water. You are standing at the shop's service counter with the receipt and the kettle in its original packaging.
explanation: The item stopped working almost immediately and you need the store to fix it under consumer rules. "When Something Breaks Quickly After Buying It" fits that calm explanation; telling a server your meal is wrong at a table is not the same context.

title: Electronics visit, silent headphones proof
text: Your new pair of headphones worked once and then went silent. The electronics store is still open and you have the proof of purchase on your phone.
explanation: You are asking the seller to honour your rights on faulty goods, not paying for new groceries. "When Something Breaks Quickly After Buying It" is built for this; scanning items at a supermarket till assumes you are keeping them.

title: City stop, route number arrives
text: You are at a city bus stop and the vehicle pulling in shows the number you planned to take. People are stepping off through the front doors.
explanation: You need to board in the right order and pay or show your ticket. "Getting on a Bus" covers checking the route number, letting others off first, and finding a seat; buying a drink at a counter is a different setting.

title: Window seat, two stops ahead
text: You tapped your travel card as you got on and found a seat near the window. The map on your phone shows your street is two stops ahead.
explanation: You are already on board and need to signal before your stop and exit politely. "Getting on a Bus" includes pressing the stop button and letting others off; walking supermarket aisles with a list is unrelated.

title: New town stop, card ready
text: You are visiting a new town and found the local bus timetable online. The next bus is due and you are first in the queue with your card ready.
explanation: You are about to enter public transport, not buy a drink at a counter. "Getting on a Bus" walks you through matching the route and boarding safely; ordering at a café happens in a fixed building.

title: Unfamiliar streets, seatmate looks up
text: You boarded a bus in an unfamiliar part of town and the street names outside are not ones you recognise. The person beside you looks up from their book.
explanation: You need to confirm you are on the right service or when to get off. "Asking for Help on Public Transport" fits a short question to a passenger or driver; telling a shop worker you are just browsing is unrelated.

title: Train carriage, map still unclear
text: You are on a train and the map above the door is confusing. A uniformed staff member walks through the carriage checking tickets.
explanation: You are unsure whether this service stops where you need and can ask someone official. "Asking for Help on Public Transport" is for that; a shop worker offering help on a sales floor is a different environment.

title: Multiple transfers, terminus name unfamiliar
text: You changed buses twice and now the display shows a terminus you do not recognise. You want to know if you have missed your stop.
explanation: You need information while you are still travelling, not at a shop till. "Asking for Help on Public Transport" covers polite questions about destinations and stops; asking a passer-by for walking directions on the street is a different setting.

title: Clinic desk, weekday arrival early
text: You have a weekday slot at a community clinic and you arrive a few minutes early. A staff member behind the glass smiles and gestures you toward the desk.
explanation: You are at the front desk to confirm who you are and that you are expected, not to collect medicine. "Checking In at a Doctor's Office" covers giving your name and waiting to be called.

title: GP waiting area, screen call-up
text: You are in the waiting area of a GP practice and your name appears on the screen as next. The person at reception looks up and makes eye contact with you.
explanation: This is a planned visit at a clinic desk, not urgent hospital intake. "Checking In at a Doctor's Office" walks you through confirming your details and taking a seat until you are called.

title: Medical centre, first-time desk queue
text: It is your first visit to this medical centre and a clipboard with a form is on the chair beside you. The queue board shows you are due at the desk soon.
explanation: You need to register at reception and wait in the seating area, not open a counselling conversation yet. "Checking In at a Doctor's Office" fits the desk and waiting-room steps.

title: Consult room, notes open discussion
text: You are in a small consultation room and the clinician has closed the door. They look at your notes and ask what you would like to discuss today.
explanation: You are raising a health concern and following up with questions, not only rating a single sensation. "Talking to Your Doctor About a Problem" helps you lead with your main issue and ask what happens next.

title: Phone list, clinician waiting calmly
text: You brought a short list on your phone because several things have been bothering you for weeks. The clinician nods and waits for you to begin.
explanation: This is a structured medical conversation about ongoing issues, not casual chat about your day. "Talking to Your Doctor About a Problem" is built for stating concerns clearly and checking you understand the plan.

title: Home video visit, main concern
text: You joined a video call from home and your image is on screen in a private room. The clinician on the other end asks you to share your main issue first.
explanation: Even on a screen, this is a clinical visit about a health issue, not your first counselling intake. "Talking to Your Doctor About a Problem" covers preparing concerns and asking questions before you leave.

title: Follow-up visit, scan option raised
text: You have been managing knee discomfort for months and today's visit is a routine follow-up. The clinician suggests waiting longer, but you think a scan might help.
explanation: You want to request a specific next step such as a referral or investigation, not only describe how something feels. "Asking for a Referral or Test" helps you ask clearly and understand the response.

title: GP room, onward care letter
text: Your GP mentions that a specialist could review your skin, but does not offer a letter. You would like that arranged before you leave the room.
explanation: You are asking the clinician to arrange onward care, not posing a question at a medicine counter. "Asking for a Referral or Test" fits requesting a referral and noting any next steps.

title: Visit wrap-up, insurer paperwork need
text: Physiotherapy was suggested at your last visit and you want it in writing for your insurer. The clinician is wrapping up and reaching for the door handle.
explanation: You need a formal request or test arranged through the clinic, not information about tablets you already have. "Asking for a Referral or Test" is for that advocacy moment before you go.

title: Bright waiting room, chair invite
text: You are sitting in a bright waiting room with posters of teeth on the wall and your name was called a moment ago. The hygienist opens a door and welcomes you in.
explanation: This is an oral health visit with chair and equipment, not collecting medicine at a high street counter. "Your First Dental Visit" covers telling staff it is new for you and asking for breaks in the chair.

title: Reception clipboard, equipment humming nearby
text: Your parent booked today's slot and you are filling in a clipboard in the reception area. The sound of equipment hums from a corridor nearby.
explanation: You are arriving for oral care with unfamiliar tools and routines, not a talking therapy session. "Your First Dental Visit" helps you tell staff you are new and ask what is happening during the exam.

title: New practice, tray prepared ahead
text: You have not been to this practice before and the receptionist asks whether you have visited them previously. A mask and goggles are laid out on a tray down the hall.
explanation: The setting is an oral health clinic with a chair exam ahead, not a general medical waiting room check-in alone. "Your First Dental Visit" is for that first-time visit flow.

title: Chair lamp, sharp molar sensation
text: You are reclined under a bright lamp and a tool is touching a back molar. A sharp feeling makes you tense and the hygienist continues without pausing.
explanation: You need to signal discomfort during an oral exam and ask for gentler work, not describe symptoms to a GP in a consultation room. "Telling the Dentist You're in Pain" uses hand signals and clear words in the chair.

title: Cold spray, jaw suddenly tight
text: Cold water was sprayed a moment ago and your whole jaw tightened. The person working on your teeth looks up, waiting to continue.
explanation: This moment is during active dental work where you can raise your hand, not a sit-down chat about a general health problem. "Telling the Dentist You're in Pain" fits speaking up in the chair.

title: X-ray holder, gum pressure rises
text: You are holding a plastic holder for an X-ray and the edge is pressing hard on your gum. The clinician is adjusting the machine and counting down.
explanation: You need to pause oral treatment and point to where it hurts, not give feedback about a counselling technique. "Telling the Dentist You're in Pain" covers asking for a gentler approach or numbing if needed.

title: Chemist queue, collection sign visible
text: You received a text that your tablets are ready at the high street chemist. The dedicated counter has a short queue and a sign about collection.
explanation: You are collecting something already prescribed at the pharmacy window, not registering for a clinic visit. "Picking Up a Prescription" tells you which counter to use and what to say when asked.

title: Surname bag, window opens
text: A white bag with your surname printed on it is waiting behind the glass at the chemist. The staff member slides the window open and looks at you.
explanation: Your medicine has already been prepared for collection, not chosen from open shelves. "Picking Up a Prescription" fits confirming your identity and taking the bag.

title: After-work chemist, code ready
text: You are at the supermarket chemist after work and the screen by the counter shows one item ready. You have your card and the confirmation code on your phone.
explanation: You are finishing a collection that was ordered earlier, not starting a new question about a product on the shelf. "Picking Up a Prescription" covers the collection counter steps.

title: Counter turn, two boxes compared
text: You are at the chemist counter with two boxes in your hand and you are unsure whether they can be taken together. The person behind the desk finishes with another customer and turns to you.
explanation: You need a short, specific question at the pharmacy about a product you are holding, not a full clinic visit about side effects in general. "Asking the Pharmacist a Question" helps you show the packet and ask clearly.

title: Consult window, label timing doubt
text: You started a new tablet yesterday and the label mentions taking it with food. You walk back to the same chemist where you collected it and wait at the consultation window.
explanation: This is a quick medicines question to the person behind the pharmacy counter, not raising a new health problem with a GP. "Asking the Pharmacist a Question" fits showing the pack and asking one clear thing.

title: Duty staff, blister pack expiry
text: A relative gave you a blister pack and you want to know if it is still safe to use. The staff member on duty is organising leaflets near the till.
explanation: You are seeking advice before using a medicine, not picking up an order that is already waiting. "Asking the Pharmacist a Question" is for waiting your turn and naming the product.

title: Exam couch, shoulder scale prompt
text: You are on an examination couch and the clinician asks you to rate how uncomfortable your shoulder feels. They wait with a pen ready to write.
explanation: You need to put words to location, intensity, and how long it has been happening in a medical exam, not signal during dental work. "Describing Pain to a Doctor" gives you scales and descriptive words to use.

title: Phone review, ache location asked
text: During a telephone review the nurse asks you to point to where the ache is worst even though they cannot see you. You are standing in your kitchen holding the phone.
explanation: The focus is explaining a physical sensation clearly, not listing every concern you have about your health. "Describing Pain to a Doctor" helps you say where, how strong, and what it feels like.

title: Wrist flare, sharp-or-dull check
text: You have been asked to show the clinician the spot on your wrist that flares when you type. They lean closer and ask whether it is sharp or dull.
explanation: You are describing a bodily sensation in detail for assessment, not discussing mood or daily stress over weeks. "Describing Pain to a Doctor" matches this focused symptom description.

title: Quiet room, mood question today
text: You are in a quiet clinic room and the clinician asks how your mood has been since your last visit. You have been finding it hard to get out of bed most mornings.
explanation: You are sharing emotional symptoms with a medical clinician to explore support options, not starting a weekly therapy hour. "Talking About Mental Health Symptoms" helps you describe what you feel and ask about options.

title: Notebook grip, anxiety check-in
text: Your GP mentions a counselling service and asks whether you have felt anxious lately. You notice your hands are tight around your notebook.
explanation: This conversation is about emotional wellbeing over time, not locating a physical ache on a scale. "Talking About Mental Health Symptoms" fits describing feelings and how they affect daily life.

title: Long slot, sleep strain discussed
text: You booked a longer slot because sleep has been poor and everything feels overwhelming. The clinician closes their laptop and gives you their full attention.
explanation: You are opening up about stress and mood with a clinician, not walking through a list of unrelated physical complaints. "Talking About Mental Health Symptoms" supports sharing at your own pace and asking what help exists.

title: Small office, opening prompt pause
text: You arrive at a small office with a sofa and a box of tissues on the side table. The person you are meeting opens the door and asks what you would like to focus on today.
explanation: This is the opening of a talking therapy hour, not a medical appointment about mood with a GP. "Starting a Therapy Session" helps you respond when you are unsure where to begin.

title: Shared building, early arrival list
text: You are five minutes early for a session in a shared health building and you can hear quiet music from the room inside. Your name is on a list taped to the reception desk.
explanation: You are about to begin counselling, not check in for a physical health slot at a GP desk. "Starting a Therapy Session" fits the first questions and sharing one main topic.

title: Video room, first words pending
text: You logged into a secure video room from your bedroom and the other person appears on screen. They smile and leave a pause for you to speak first.
explanation: This is the start of a therapy conversation, not explaining camouflaging to a professional. "Starting a Therapy Session" covers saying you are not sure where to start and asking about confidentiality if needed.

title: Thought diary, evening strain rising
text: You were asked to keep a thought diary between sessions and it has made you more anxious each evening. The person you see each week asks how the homework went.
explanation: You want to give honest feedback about a therapy tool, not introduce masking for the first time. "Telling Your Therapist Something Is Not Helping" helps you say a technique is not working and ask for alternatives.

title: Breathing task, light-headed afterward
text: Last week's breathing exercise left you light-headed and you avoided practising it. The person you see each week waits for your thoughts on the exercise.
explanation: You are responding to a specific counselling activity that did not suit you, not describing weeks of low mood to a GP. "Telling Your Therapist Something Is Not Helping" is for that feedback conversation.

title: Role-play repeat, drained feeling lingers
text: A role-play about conflict felt unrealistic and you left the last session drained. Today they ask whether you would like to try the same activity again.
explanation: You are adjusting how therapy is going with the person you see regularly, not asking another clinician for a duplicate medical opinion. "Telling Your Therapist Something Is Not Helping" welcomes speaking up about methods.

title: Hospital window, fall injury intake
text: You have come to the hospital after a fall and your arm is sore to move. A clerk at the front window points to a sign that says assessment first.
explanation: You need urgent hospital intake at the assessment desk, not a routine clinic check-in for a booked slot. "Arriving at the Emergency Room" covers stating that you need to be seen and giving key details.

title: Plastic chairs, triage desk call
text: You are sitting in plastic chairs near a reception area with a TV showing numbers. A nurse calls you forward to a small desk with a computer.
explanation: Staff need a short summary of what is happening right now in the hospital pathway, not a detailed pain description during a routine exam. "Arriving at the Emergency Room" fits triage and waiting steps.

title: Hospital entrance, brief incident summary
text: Someone drove you to the hospital entrance and you are holding paperwork from your usual clinic. The person at the window asks one brief question about what happened today.
explanation: This is hospital urgent care intake, not a standard appointment where you list concerns from a notebook. "Arriving at the Emergency Room" helps you answer clearly and wait until called.

title: Night before visit, notes planning
text: You have a clinic visit tomorrow morning and the building layout is unfamiliar. Tonight you are at your desk with a blank page and a list of things that have been worrying you.
explanation: You are getting ready before the visit, including notes and support options, not already in the room answering the clinician's questions. "Preparing a Health Appointment as an Autistic Person" covers planning and communication needs.

title: Bag packed, light sensitivity plan
text: Bright lights at the surgery bother you and you want written instructions after the visit. Your support person has agreed to come with you and you are packing your bag.
explanation: You are arranging accommodations and materials ahead of a medical visit, not explaining camouflaging during therapy. "Preparing a Health Appointment as an Autistic Person" includes bringing someone and asking for written summaries.

title: Home practice, repeat-needed script
text: You saved screenshots of your sleep tracker because words are hard when you are put on the spot. Before leaving home you practise saying you may need information repeated.
explanation: This is preparation and self-advocacy before the appointment, not the moment at the reception desk when you arrive. "Preparing a Health Appointment as an Autistic Person" helps you plan what to share and how.

title: Health aisle, hay fever options
text: You are in the supermarket health aisle and there are several boxes for hay fever with different strengths. You are not sure which is right for you.
explanation: You are choosing and buying something off the shelf, not asking about tablets you already have at home. "Buying Over-the-Counter Medication" covers reading labels and asking staff if unsure.

title: Chemist shelf, lozenge choices compared
text: You have a sore throat and the chemist has three types of lozenges at different prices. A shop assistant walks past and asks if you need help.
explanation: You are selecting a non-prescription product in the shop, not collecting a bag waiting behind the counter. "Buying Over-the-Counter Medication" helps you compare options and ask whether it fits your situation.

title: Daily tablets, headache relief check
text: You take a daily tablet for blood pressure and you want to buy something for a headache today. A staff member on the shop floor is restocking nearby.
explanation: You need to check an over-the-counter product is safe with what you already take, not ask about side effects of a prescription you were given yesterday. "Buying Over-the-Counter Medication" includes telling them what else you use.

title: Post-event fatigue, hidden strain explained
text: You leave social events exhausted even when they seemed to go well. In counselling you want the person opposite you to understand that you often hide how stressed you are.
explanation: You are explaining camouflaging and its impact to a professional, not only listing anxious feelings for a medical record. "Telling a Professional About Masking or Camouflaging" gives language for that specific topic.

title: Work mimicry, evening energy crash
text: At work you copy others' expressions and later feel drained at home. Your clinician asks what tends to wear you out during the week.
explanation: You want to name masking as a pattern, not only request appointment accommodations in advance. "Telling a Professional About Masking or Camouflaging" helps you introduce the idea and ask for strategies.

title: Session honesty, performed confidence drops
text: You have been pretending things are fine in sessions because it feels safer. Today you decided to explain that you often perform confidence when you are overwhelmed.
explanation: You are opening up about hiding autistic traits, not saying a homework task failed. "Telling a Professional About Masking or Camouflaging" supports describing the impact and asking for support.

title: New tablets, leaflet questions pending
text: You were given a new bottle of tablets yesterday and the leaflet uses small print. You are back at the chemist and want to know what reactions to watch for.
explanation: You are asking what to monitor while taking a prescribed medicine, not a general question about two products on a shelf. "Asking About Side Effects of a Medication" covers what to notice and when to contact someone.

title: Added tablet, normal-versus-risk doubts
text: Your GP added a second tablet to your routine and you are unsure what is normal versus worrying. The clinician has a few minutes left and looks at the clock.
explanation: You need information about effects of what you are taking, not to introduce a brand-new health problem from scratch. "Asking About Side Effects of a Medication" fits asking what to expect and when to get in touch.

title: Consult desk, dizziness after capsules
text: You noticed dizziness since you started the capsules and you kept the packaging in your bag. A voice calls your name to the consultation desk.
explanation: You are reporting a reaction and asking what to do, not simply collecting a ready order. "Asking About Side Effects of a Medication" helps you ask what matters and write down the answers.

title: Specialist letter, review decision pending
text: The specialist's letter suggests surgery and you want another clinician to review the plan. Your usual GP has a few minutes at the end of your visit.
explanation: You are asking how to obtain another medical view on a decision, not requesting a new test or referral for the first time. "Getting a Second Opinion" covers asking politely and gathering your records.

title: Conflicting consultant advice, records ready
text: A friend saw a different consultant for the same condition and their advice was not the same as yours. You have your test results on your phone and an open slot today.
explanation: You want another clinician to look at an existing diagnosis or plan, not list symptoms for a first assessment. "Getting a Second Opinion" is for that request and copying records.

title: Long treatment, file review request
text: Treatment has not improved your symptoms after several months and you wonder whether someone else should look at your file. The clinician is summarising before you stand to leave.
explanation: You are seeking another medical perspective on care you are already receiving, not giving feedback about a counselling technique. "Getting a Second Opinion" supports asking how to arrange that review.

title: Home floor collapse, phone ready
text: You are at home and the person with you has collapsed on the floor and is not responding. Your mobile is in your pocket and the street address is on the fridge magnet.
explanation: Someone needs urgent professional help right now, and you must reach the national number and give where you are. "Calling 911 (or Local Emergency Line)" walks you through staying on the line and answering questions.

title: Hallway smoke alarm, doorway pause
text: You smell smoke in your apartment hallway and hear an alarm farther down the corridor. You are alone with your phone near the front door.
explanation: This needs an immediate call to the national helpline with your location, not a chat with shop staff about a hazard. "Calling 911 (or Local Emergency Line)" covers describing what is happening in one sentence and staying on the line.

title: Roadside crash scene, junction sign
text: You have pulled over after seeing a car hit a lamp post on a quiet road. No one else has stopped yet and you have a clear view of the junction name sign.
explanation: You are reporting a serious incident to get professional help sent, not working out your own route on a map. "Calling 911 (or Local Emergency Line)" fits dialling, stating what you see, and giving the exact place.

title: Choking episode, keypad already lit
text: Something is stuck in your throat and you cannot get words out, but you can still reach your phone on the counter. The keypad is lit and the call is connecting.
explanation: When speech is not possible, staying on an open line or using text options can still bring help. "Calling 911 If You Can't Speak" is for keeping the connection and using alternatives like keypad prompts or location texts.

title: Locked bedroom, uninvited sounds outside
text: You are in your bedroom with the door closed and you hear someone in the flat who should not be there. You want help without making noise and your phone is on silent.
explanation: You may need to summon help quietly without a spoken conversation. "Calling 911 If You Can't Speak" covers staying on the line and using text or keypad options when talking is not safe.

title: Rapid swelling, voice fading quickly
text: Your lips are swelling quickly after a bite of food and your voice is very faint. You have opened the phone app with shaking hands.
explanation: Speech may fail even when you still need urgent dispatch; the line itself matters. "Calling 911 If You Can't Speak" focuses on methods when you cannot describe everything out loud.

title: Night walk, same follower behind
text: You are walking home after dark and the same person has been behind you for several blocks. A shop ahead has lights on and a staff member visible through the window.
explanation: You need to tell a nearby trusted person that you do not feel okay and stay with them, not place a national emergency call unless the danger is immediate and clear. "Telling Someone You Feel Unsafe" fits approaching someone and saying you need help.

title: House gathering, distance repeatedly crossed
text: At a house gathering someone you do not know well keeps standing very close despite you stepping away. Your friend is in the kitchen and has offered you a lift home.
explanation: This is telling someone you trust that you need support right now, not asking a stranger in a busy place to help you cope with noise. "Telling Someone You Feel Unsafe" helps you say clearly that you need help and stay with them.

title: Flat corridor shouting, sibling nearby
text: Your flatmate's guest has been arguing loudly outside your door for ten minutes. Your sibling is on the phone in the next room and you want to go to them.
explanation: You are seeking safety with a trusted person nearby, not managing bright lights and noise in a public space. "Telling Someone You Feel Unsafe" is for saying you need help and letting them guide next steps.

title: Lunchroom teasing, tutor door open
text: In the lunchroom two classmates keep taking items from your tray and laughing when you object. Your form tutor is on duty today and has an open door.
explanation: Ongoing mistreatment at school needs a report to a responsible adult with details, not only stopping on a street corner to check a map. "Getting Help if You're Being Bullied" covers speaking up and writing down what happened.

title: Team remarks repeated, manager slot
text: A colleague has made pointed comments about you in team meetings for several weeks. Your manager has a weekly one-to-one slot listed on the door.
explanation: Repeated harmful behaviour at work should be raised with someone in authority who can act, not only reported as a one-off incident to a random uniformed person. "Getting Help if You're Being Bullied" fits telling a trusted adult or manager and escalating if needed.

title: Evening messages, parent downstairs waiting
text: You keep receiving mean messages from the same account every evening after school. Your parent is downstairs and has asked you to come talk if anything is bothering you.
explanation: Persistent harassment needs a trusted adult involved and a record of events, not an immediate national emergency call unless you are in immediate physical danger. "Getting Help if You're Being Bullied" supports telling someone and documenting what happened.

title: Supermarket spill, no warning sign
text: You are in a supermarket aisle and the floor is wet with no warning sign nearby. A person in a branded vest is stacking shelves a few metres away.
explanation: You need to tell an on-site staff member what you observed so they can act, not ask for directions to an exit. "Reporting a Problem to a Staff Member" covers finding someone with ID and describing what happened clearly.

title: Library table theft, desk nearby
text: Someone took your backpack from under the library table while you were printing. The help desk at the entrance has a staff member looking at a screen.
explanation: This is a factual report to venue staff about theft, not telling a friend you feel nervous. "Reporting a Problem to a Staff Member" helps you state what happened, where, and when, and ask what happens next.

title: Stalled lift, security at landing
text: The lift in a shopping centre has stopped between floors with three people inside. When the doors open on the next level, a security officer is waiting outside.
explanation: You are informing on-site staff about a problem they can log and handle, not placing the initial national emergency call yourself unless someone is hurt. "Reporting a Problem to a Staff Member" fits a clear, calm description to someone in uniform.

title: Checkout beeps, lights pressing in
text: You are in a supermarket and the fluorescent lights and checkout beeps feel like they are pressing in from every side. Your chest is tight and you need to get away from the noise.
explanation: Your first step is to reduce input and steady yourself in a quieter spot, not only tell someone you feel wary of another person. "Sensory Overload in a Public Place" covers moving aside, blocking sound, and slowing your breathing.

title: Concert foyer, echoes and crowds
text: You are in the foyer of a concert venue after the support act and the crowd noise is bouncing off the walls. Your ears hurt and you cannot think clearly enough to read signs.
explanation: The trigger is too much sensory input right now, not being unsure of your route on a map. "Sensory Overload in a Public Place" helps you find a corner, cover your ears, and wait until you can move again.

title: Platform delay loop, crowding edge
text: On a train platform the delay announcement keeps repeating and people are crowding near the yellow line. You feel shaky and need somewhere with fewer voices.
explanation: This is an in-the-moment coping situation, not sitting at home writing a plan for later. "Sensory Overload in a Public Place" fits stepping away, reducing noise, and texting someone if you need support.

title: Food court overload, calm stranger nearby
text: You are in a busy food court and everything feels too loud and bright to move on your own. A calm-looking person at the next table is reading and has not put in earbuds.
explanation: You need another person to help you reach a quieter area, not placing a national emergency call when no one is injured. "Asking a Stranger for Help During Overload" covers a short request or showing a message on your phone.

title: Museum hall overload, lanyard desk nearby
text: On a school museum trip the group moved on while you were reading a label and now the hall feels overwhelming. A museum worker in a lanyard is nearby at a small desk.
explanation: You are too flooded to navigate alone and need someone to help you get to a quieter place or find staff, not only stop and check a map. "Asking a Stranger for Help During Overload" fits asking for help getting somewhere quieter.

title: Airport gate noise, seats packed
text: At the airport gate area the PA keeps changing and the seats are full. Your hands will not stay still and you need to get away from the speakers.
explanation: You are asking for practical help because input is too much, not telling someone you fear another person. "Asking a Stranger for Help During Overload" supports a brief approach or a card on your phone.

title: Kitchen table, notebook safety prep
text: You are at your kitchen table on a quiet evening with a notebook open. A stressful week is coming and you want steps ready before you are already struggling in public.
explanation: You are preparing ahead by writing signs, tools, and contacts, not managing a crisis in a shop right now. "Creating a Personal Safety Plan" helps you list what helps and keep the plan accessible.

title: Colored pens, coping page draft
text: After a difficult day last month your counsellor suggested putting coping ideas on one page. You have coloured pens and want to finish it before your next session.
explanation: This is proactive planning for future overwhelm, not reporting mistreatment to an authority figure. "Creating a Personal Safety Plan" covers warning signs, regulation tools, and people to contact.

title: Quiet-exit list, phone and wallet
text: Your parent is helping you list quiet exits for the cinema, the mall, and school after you found last weekend hard. You are saving the list on your phone and in your wallet.
explanation: You are building a personal reference for next time, not asking reception for directions in the moment. "Creating a Personal Safety Plan" fits writing strategies and keeping them easy to reach.

title: Unknown bus stop, late meetup
text: The bus dropped you off at a stop you do not recognise and the street names are unfamiliar. You were meant to meet someone at the library ten minutes ago.
explanation: When you are unsure where you are outdoors, stopping and using your phone or asking a shop worker beats wandering farther. "What to Do If You Get Lost" covers staying put, checking a map, and asking for help clearly.

title: Trail fork, faded sign arrows
text: On a walking trail the path splits and the signpost arrows are worn away. Your group is ahead somewhere but you are not sure which fork they took.
explanation: You need to pause and work out location or contact someone, not mainly block out noise in a corner. "What to Do If You Get Lost" fits stopping, checking where you are, and asking a worker if needed.

title: Outdoor market, family out of sight
text: You wandered away from your family at an outdoor market and the stalls all look similar. You have your phone but the meeting point banner is out of sight.
explanation: The problem is not knowing where you are relative to your plan, not needing a stranger because lights and sounds are too much. "What to Do If You Get Lost" helps you stay in one place and ask for help getting back.

title: Hospital corridor maze, entrance unclear
text: You left a clinic room and every corridor in the hospital looks the same. Wall signs point to wards but not to the main entrance you came through.
explanation: Inside a big building you look for maps, reception, or security and ask for directions step by step. "Getting Lost in a Large Building" fits finding an information point rather than staying on a street corner.

title: Campus wings map, room uncertainty
text: Your lecture was moved to a different room and the campus building has floors labelled A, B, and C. You are standing by a lift that only lists wings you do not need.
explanation: You need building navigation help from staff or signage, not sensory coping because the foyer is too loud. "Getting Lost in a Large Building" covers directories and asking clearly for a room or exit.

title: Car park level, matching stairwells
text: You parked on level four of a multi-storey car park and now the stairwell doors all look identical. A map near the lift shows colours but not where you entered.
explanation: You are orienting inside a complex building, not reporting a hazard to staff. "Getting Lost in a Large Building" helps you head toward reception or security and ask one step at a time.

title: Evening prep, office visit tomorrow
text: You have a formal meeting at a company office tomorrow morning. Tonight you are at your desk with printed notes about the organisation and a short list of points you want to remember.
explanation: The moment is about getting ready before you walk in, not speaking up in a room full of people yet. "Preparing for a Job Interview" covers research, practise, and what to bring.

title: Reception wait, folder on lap
text: You are sitting in a reception area with your folder on your lap. Other people are also waiting, and the front desk has your name on a list.
explanation: You are still in the arrival-and-readiness phase: checking in, staying calm, and having your materials ready. "Preparing for a Job Interview" includes what to do before the conversation starts.

title: Early video room, preview only
text: You joined a video call ten minutes early and only see your own camera preview. The link works, but no one from the company has appeared yet.
explanation: Testing your setup, reviewing notes, and staying composed while you wait are all part of getting ready. "Preparing for a Job Interview" helps you use this time well before anyone speaks.

title: Panel room, background prompt asked
text: You are in a small meeting room with two people from the hiring team. One of them smiles and asks you to walk them through your background.
explanation: They have asked for a short, structured overview of who you are and why you fit the role. "Answering \"Tell Me About Yourself\"" gives you a clear order for that opening.

title: Recruiter call, quick overview request
text: You are on a phone call with a recruiter who has already confirmed your name. They say, "Before we go deeper, can you give me a quick overview of your experience?"
explanation: This is the classic opening overview, not a request for ongoing updates from your boss. "Answering \"Tell Me About Yourself\"" keeps your answer focused and about a minute long.

title: Second-round table, senior joins
text: You are in a second-round visit and a senior leader you have not met joins the table. They open by asking where you would like to begin with your background.
explanation: A new person wants the same concise self-summary others already heard. "Answering \"Tell Me About Yourself\"" helps you repeat the structure without rambling.

title: Mid-interview, support options asked
text: You are midway through a hiring conversation in a quiet meeting room. The interviewer pauses and asks whether you need any support to do your best today.
explanation: They opened space for you to share how you work and what helps you succeed in that setting. "Disclosing Your Autism in an Interview" frames that choice positively and professionally.

title: Hiring chat, setup needs discussed
text: You are explaining how you stay focused on detailed tasks during a hiring conversation. The hiring manager nods and asks what kind of workplace setup helps you perform well.
explanation: The conversation turned toward your needs and strengths in a formal hiring context. "Disclosing Your Autism in an Interview" covers how to name your neurotype and link it to reliability and focus.

title: Previsit form, access field open
text: You received a form to complete before an on-site visit. One section asks whether you want to mention any accessibility needs ahead of time.
explanation: You are deciding what to share before the day, not asking a teacher to repeat a lesson. "Disclosing Your Autism in an Interview" helps you answer honestly and frame accommodations as reasonable.

title: Application silence, draft follow-up open
text: You submitted an online form for a role two weeks ago and have heard nothing back. You are looking at a blank draft message to the contact address on the posting.
explanation: You are checking in politely after applying, not calling out sick for today's shift. "Following Up After a Job Application" gives you a short, professional email structure.

title: Monday inbox, promised update absent
text: A recruiter told you they would update candidates by Friday. It is now Monday morning and your inbox has no reply.
explanation: The timeline has passed and you need a brief status check, not a question during a live team call. "Following Up After a Job Application" keeps the tone interested and respectful.

title: Missed unknown call, role voicemail
text: You missed a call from a number you do not recognise. The voicemail asks you to call back about a role you applied for last month.
explanation: They may want to move your hiring process forward, and you need a clear, professional response. "Following Up After a Job Application" also applies when you re-establish contact after silence.

title: Client-file bullets, two meanings possible
text: You received an email from your supervisor with bullet points about a client file, but two items could mean different tasks. The deadline is this afternoon.
explanation: You need to confirm what they meant before you begin a different task. "Asking Your Manager for Clarification" shows how to check one detail at a time without sounding difficult.

title: Passing supervisor, report note unclear
text: You are at your desk when your supervisor walks past. They mention the report and keep moving toward the lift before you can respond.
explanation: The instruction was too quick to act on safely. "Asking Your Manager for Clarification" helps you catch them and restate what you heard before you begin.

title: Team chat, folder label ambiguity
text: A message in your team chat says "handle the onboarding folder" with no further detail. Three folders on the shared drive have similar names.
explanation: Guessing which folder could waste hours. "Asking Your Manager for Clarification" is for exactly this kind of vague work instruction from your supervisor.

title: Cubicle drop-in, deadline pressure
text: You are typing against a tight deadline when a coworker appears at the opening of your cubicle. They look like they want to talk about something non-urgent.
explanation: You need to protect focus without being rude. "Telling a Colleague You're Busy" offers a polite delay and a time to reconnect.

title: Floor chat ping, unsafe pause
text: A chat notification pops up from someone on your floor. The message asks if you have a moment, but you are halfway through a task that cannot pause safely.
explanation: This is a peer interruption, not a performance review. "Telling a Colleague You're Busy" lets you set a short boundary and offer a later time.

title: Focus room knock, coffee visitor
text: Someone knocks on the door of the small focus room you booked. Through the glass you see a teammate holding coffee and waiting to come in.
explanation: You reserved the room to concentrate, not to host a chat right now. "Telling a Colleague You're Busy" covers spoken and written ways to defer the conversation.

title: Fever morning, shift starts soon
text: Your alarm goes off and you have a fever and sore throat. Your shift at the store starts in two hours.
explanation: You need to notify work that you cannot come in today, with brief facts only. "Calling in Sick" walks you through contacting your supervisor before the shift starts.

title: Migraine daylight, office day ahead
text: You woke with a migraine and light hurts your eyes. It is mid-morning on a day you were due at the office.
explanation: Staying home is a workplace absence message, not signing in for the day. "Calling in Sick" covers what to say without over-explaining your symptoms.

title: Policy reminder, supervisor number open
text: You are looking at your supervisor's number on your phone. Company policy says you must let them know before noon if you cannot work today.
explanation: The task is to report an absence, not to schedule a regular one-to-one. "Calling in Sick" includes optional questions about urgent handover.

title: Desk moved floors, boxes waiting
text: You arrived at the office and found your desk moved to another floor over the weekend. Boxes with your name are stacked by a window you have never sat near.
explanation: A sudden layout change is overwhelming, and you need calm steps to understand what is new. "Dealing with an Unexpected Change at Work" helps you pause, gather facts, and decide what to ask.

title: Group post, project pivot announced
text: Your team lead posted in the group chat about a project pivot. The project you have been building for a month will switch to a different product next week.
explanation: The news changes your daily tasks, not an alarm telling you to leave the building. "Dealing with an Unexpected Change at Work" focuses on breathing first and asking what the change means for you.

title: Temporary lead, task plan shifted
text: Your usual supervisor is on leave and a temporary lead has taken over. They assign you tasks that do not match the plan you were following yesterday.
explanation: The workflow shifted without your input, and you need to regroup before reacting out loud. "Dealing with an Unexpected Change at Work" supports asking practical questions and focusing on what you can control.

title: Staff entrance tablet, coat hooks
text: You have just walked into a retail store where you work part-time. A tablet by the staff entrance asks you to sign in, and two coworkers are hanging up their coats.
explanation: The start of the day includes signing in, a brief hello, and checking for updates. "Starting and Ending a Work Shift" covers those opening routines.

title: Warehouse briefing, machines still silent
text: You are on a warehouse floor before the machines start. Your supervisor is gathering the small team for a quick briefing by the notice board.
explanation: This is the opening of your work period, not staying home due to illness. "Starting and Ending a Work Shift" helps you arrive ready and catch any messages before tasks begin.

title: Locker area, clock near close
text: Your paid hours end in ten minutes. You are at the locker area while coworkers pack bags and the time clock shows your shift closing.
explanation: Wrapping up includes handover, logging out, and a short goodbye. "Starting and Ending a Work Shift" describes how to close the day cleanly.

title: One-to-one note, report gaps raised
text: You are in a one-to-one with your supervisor in a small office. They say your last report missed several details they had asked for.
explanation: They are pointing out a gap in your work and expecting you to listen before responding. "Receiving Critical Feedback" helps you stay calm, thank them, and ask for examples.

title: Video review, structure critique given
text: During a project review on a video call, a senior colleague addresses your section. They say it was hard to follow and needs a clearer structure next time.
explanation: This is input on how you performed, not a request to explain a vague instruction. "Receiving Critical Feedback" guides you to hear the full point and ask what to do differently.

title: Written note, dated issues listed
text: Your manager sends a written note about two habits that are slowing the team down. The note includes specific dates when issues happened.
explanation: Written criticism still needs the same steady listening approach. "Receiving Critical Feedback" reminds you that notes can sting without meaning you failed as a person.

title: Timestamp evidence, response speed questioned
text: Your supervisor says you were late responding to emails. You have timestamps showing you replied within the agreed window.
explanation: You need to share your view without escalating the tone. "Disagreeing with Feedback Professionally" shows how to ask permission and use facts calmly.

title: Review discussion, process sheet conflict
text: In a performance conversation, your manager claims you ignored a client request. You remember following the process sheet step by step.
explanation: You believe their picture of events is incomplete, not that no conversation should happen. "Disagreeing with Feedback Professionally" helps you offer your perspective and stay team-focused.

title: Team chat tone, intent disputed
text: A team lead says your tone in chat was rude. You read the thread again and think your words were direct but not insulting.
explanation: You want to challenge their interpretation respectfully. "Disagreeing with Feedback Professionally" is for when you disagree with criticism, not for first hearing it.

title: New role, no regular sync
text: You have been in a new role for six weeks and are unsure whether your work matches what your supervisor expects. They have not scheduled any regular time to talk.
explanation: You want a standing short meeting for alignment, not a one-off question about a single task. "Asking Your Manager for Regular Check-Ins" helps you request brief weekly time.

title: Post-deliverable uncertainty, calendar gap
text: After finishing a big deliverable, you still feel uncertain about priorities for next month. Your manager's calendar is open but no review is booked.
explanation: You are asking to build ongoing feedback rhythm, not responding to criticism you just received. "Asking Your Manager for Regular Check-Ins" frames the request as helping you stay on track.

title: Remote week, ten-minute rhythm
text: You work mostly from home and rarely see your supervisor in person. You want a predictable ten-minute slot each week to confirm you are focusing on the right tasks.
explanation: This is about managing an existing job, not chasing a hiring outcome. "Asking Your Manager for Regular Check-Ins" suggests wording that shows initiative.

title: Video pause, point note ready
text: You are in a team video call and the discussion has paused. You have one point written down that fits the topic on screen.
explanation: You are ready to add an idea, not to ask for missing information. "Contributing to a Meeting" covers waiting for a pause and stating your point briefly.

title: Budget debate lull, suggestion ready
text: Around a conference table, two people have been debating budget numbers. There is a brief silence and you have a constructive suggestion.
explanation: Sharing your view in the group discussion is different from pushing back on private criticism. "Contributing to a Meeting" helps you offer input without over-talking.

title: Hybrid call, timeline risk noted
text: You are on a hybrid call; the chair asked for thoughts on the timeline. Your hand is not raised yet, but your note says one risk they have not mentioned.
explanation: You want to speak up with a prepared point, not clarify a private instruction afterward. "Contributing to a Meeting" is built for adding value in group settings.

title: Budget slide acronym, nodding room
text: You are listening to a budget presentation and realise you do not understand one acronym on the slide. Others are nodding.
explanation: You need a short clarification from the presenter, not to offer your own idea. "Asking a Question in a Meeting" shows how to raise your hand and ask concisely.

title: Shared chart, column meaning unclear
text: On a video call, the host shares a dense chart and moves on quickly. You wrote down a question about what one column means.
explanation: Classrooms and work calls both allow questions, but this is a live work session with colleagues. "Asking a Question in a Meeting" fits when you need a fact before the topic changes.

title: Group call, date still unclear
text: A client visit is being planned on a group call. You are unsure which date they confirmed, and the facilitator asks if anyone needs anything cleared up.
explanation: You are seeking information the group owns, not debating feedback one-to-one. "Asking a Question in a Meeting" keeps the ask brief and thanks them afterward.

title: Open office siren, exits filling
text: You are in an open-plan office when a loud siren starts and a flashing sign points toward the stairs. People around you stand up and head for the doors.
explanation: The building is signalling everyone to leave in an orderly way. "Handling a Fire Drill or Unexpected Alarm" tells you to follow others, use the stairs, and wait at the assembly point.

title: Assembly alarm, side door open
text: During a school assembly in the hall, an intermittent alarm sounds. A staff member opens the side door while pointing outside.
explanation: This is a safety evacuation cue, not a moment to share your opinion with the group. "Handling a Fire Drill or Unexpected Alarm" focuses on staying calm and following the route.

title: Third-floor panel, recorded exit notice
text: You are on the third floor of a library when the fire panel beeps and a recorded voice repeats that everyone should exit. The lift doors stay closed.
explanation: You need the evacuation steps, not sensory coping because the room is noisy. "Handling a Fire Drill or Unexpected Alarm" covers using the nearest exit and waiting for the all-clear.

title: Maths board step, notes mismatch
text: You are sitting in a maths lesson and the teacher writes a step on the board that does not match your notes. Several students are copying it down.
explanation: You need to speak up in a lesson with a teacher present. "Asking a Question in Class" uses raising your hand and keeping the ask short.

title: Science lab setup, diagram mismatch
text: During a science lab, your group is on step four of the worksheet but the equipment setup looks different from the diagram. The teacher is circulating nearby.
explanation: You want a spoken answer in the moment, not only a printed copy later. "Asking a Question in Class" fits when something in the lesson is unclear right now.

title: English read-aloud, homework confusion
text: In English class the teacher finishes reading a passage and asks if anyone is confused about the homework task. You still are.
explanation: The teacher invited questions to the whole room. "Asking a Question in Class" helps you raise your hand and ask one clear thing.

title: History table task, roles unset
text: Your teacher assigned a history project to a table of four students. Everyone has opened their laptops, but no one has suggested who does which part.
explanation: The group needs roles and a plan, not a debate about one fact. "Working in a Group" starts with finding out what each person will handle.

title: Poster build, workload uneven
text: You are in a design studio session with classmates building a poster. One person is doing all the cutting while the others watch.
explanation: Shared school work needs fair tasks and updates, not a formal workplace meeting contribution. "Working in a Group" helps you offer a specific job you can take on.

title: Lab pair, method changed silently
text: During a lab partners session, your teammate says the results look wrong. They keep changing the method without telling you why.
explanation: You need coordination inside the pair, not a hand-up question to the teacher yet. "Working in a Group" includes checking in when someone hits a problem.

title: Essay due now, paragraphs missing
text: An essay was due at the start of today's lesson and you still have two paragraphs left. The teacher is collecting folders from the front row.
explanation: You missed the deadline and need to speak up honestly before collection finishes. "When You Don't Finish Schoolwork on Time" suggests asking for more time early and calmly.

title: Registration ending, worksheet incomplete
text: You realised last night that the maths sheet is incomplete. Registration is ending and the teacher will ask for it in five minutes.
explanation: This is about unfinished assigned work, not needing the instructions repeated in writing. "When You Don't Finish Schoolwork on Time" covers apologising briefly and requesting an extension.

title: Rehearsal ahead, slides half built
text: Your group presentation is tomorrow but your section of slides is only half done. You need to tell the teacher before the after-school rehearsal.
explanation: You are accountable for school work timing, not calling an employer about absence. "When You Don't Finish Schoolwork on Time" helps you notify them before the deadline passes.

title: Novel discussion, plot detail disputed
text: In a class discussion about a novel, the student beside you states a plot detail you are sure is incorrect. The teacher is listening to both of you.
explanation: You want to offer a different view to a peer, not push back on a manager's review. "Disagreeing with a Classmate Respectfully" uses calm "I think" language.

title: Lab result blame, step skipped
text: Your lab partner insists the experiment failed because of the equipment. You believe the measurement step was skipped.
explanation: This is a respectful difference between students working together. "Disagreeing with a Classmate Respectfully" lets you explain your reasoning without attacking them.

title: Debate warm-up, old example challenged
text: During a debate warm-up, a classmate says your example does not count because it is too old. You believe it still supports the point.
explanation: Peer disagreement in class needs a lighter tone than speaking up in a staff meeting. "Disagreeing with a Classmate Respectfully" keeps both views allowed to exist.

title: Art demo steps, order uncertain
text: Your teacher explained a multi-step art project aloud while demonstrating. You took some notes but worry you missed the order of stages.
explanation: You want the steps captured in writing so you can follow them accurately. "Asking for Written Instructions" is a reasonable request to a teacher or manager.

title: Night close routine, details unheard
text: At your weekend job, the supervisor described how to close the till quickly at the end of the night. Customers are still nearby and you could not hear every detail.
explanation: You need a reference you can read later, not a debate about one vague phrase. "Asking for Written Instructions" includes asking for an email or checklist.

title: Placement training, safety sequence blurring
text: During training at a new placement, a mentor walked you through safety checks verbally. Back at your desk, the sequence is already blurring.
explanation: Remembering spoken steps is hard for many people; written backup is normal. "Asking for Written Instructions" helps you ask politely without sounding difficult.

title: Flood chapter, documentary memory link
text: You are reading a chapter about a flood in a geography textbook. A paragraph describes families leaving their homes, and it reminds you of a documentary you watched last year.
explanation: You are linking the text to something you already know, not guessing what happens next. "Making Connections While Reading" helps you name that link and why it fits.

title: Novel siblings clash, home parallel
text: In silent reading time, a character in your novel argues with a sibling about chores. The scene feels very similar to something that happened at your house.
explanation: A personal connection deepens understanding of the page you are on. "Making Connections While Reading" is for when the text echoes your life, another book, or the wider world.

title: Energy article, coastal wind memory
text: Your teacher asks you to jot margin notes while reading an article on renewable energy. One sentence mentions wind farms near the coast where you went on holiday.
explanation: You are noting how the article relates to something real you have seen, not raising your hand to ask the teacher a question. "Making Connections While Reading" guides that margin note.

title: Mystery opening, gate and footsteps
text: You opened a mystery story and the cover shows a locked gate at night. You have only read the first page describing footsteps in the rain.
explanation: You are guessing what might happen next from clues so far. "Making Predictions While Reading" encourages writing the guess and checking it as you continue.

title: Plant case study, cold-snap heading
text: In science class you are reading a case study about plant growth. The heading mentions a sudden cold snap, but the results section is still ahead.
explanation: You are thinking ahead about the outcome before you see the data, not asking the teacher to repeat themselves. "Making Predictions While Reading" fits pausing to wonder what the results will show.

title: Torn map reveal, class waiting
text: Your teacher paused the class read-aloud right after the hero finds a torn map. Everyone is waiting for the next page.
explanation: The story stopped at a cliffhanger moment meant for guessing. "Making Predictions While Reading" is about what you think will happen next, whether you turn out right or not.

title: History source, date mismatch noted
text: You are reading a history source and one date in the margin does not match the timeline on the board. You keep re-reading the sentence.
explanation: Something on the page puzzles you and you want to track that wonder. "Asking Questions While Reading" uses "I wonder" notes before you look it up or ask the teacher.

title: Character departure, reason still hidden
text: During independent reading, a character suddenly leaves town with no explanation. You have half a chapter left and feel confused.
explanation: Your question is about the text itself while you read, not speaking up in a whole-class lesson yet. "Asking Questions While Reading" helps you write the question and see if later pages answer it.

title: Tech article, unknown part listed
text: You are studying a how-to article for technology class. Step three mentions a part you have never heard of, and the glossary does not list it.
explanation: You need to flag confusion as you go, then decide whether to search or ask. "Asking Questions While Reading" is for active wondering, not only requesting written instructions afterward.

title: Quiet cafe, hobby friend asks
text: You are at a quiet café with someone you have met a few times through a hobby group. They ask if there is anything they should know to make hanging out easier for you.
explanation: They opened space for you to share something personal in a calm, private moment. "Disclosing Autism to a New Friend" walks through choosing trust, how to start, and what to say.

title: Walk home, pace slows kindly
text: You are walking home together after a board-game night at a mutual acquaintance's house. The other person says they want to understand you better and slows their pace so you can talk.
explanation: This is about sharing your neurotype with someone you are getting to know, not pausing a heavy conversation mid-argument. "Disclosing Autism to a New Friend" fits that gradual trust-building moment.

title: Text thread, quiet needs curiosity
text: You are texting with someone you have started seeing outside of class. They send a message saying they noticed you sometimes need quiet and they are curious what helps.
explanation: They invited a personal explanation, not a request to dim lights in a shared room right now. "Disclosing Autism to a New Friend" covers how to name your neurotype and what you need in relationships.

title: Closed-door one-to-one, support question
