text: You are in a one-to-one meeting with your manager in a small office with the door closed. They ask whether there is anything about how you work that would help them support you better.
explanation: They are asking about who you are and how you work, before listing specific desk changes. "Disclosing Autism at Work" covers choosing when to share and framing it professionally.

title: HR form, neurodiversity field open
text: HR sent you a form before your annual review. One question asks whether you want to mention any neurodiversity or access needs on file.
explanation: The form is about identity and workplace support, not stepping away for five minutes today. "Disclosing Autism at Work" helps you decide what to write and how to phrase it.

title: Onboarding chat, network intro offered
text: You are onboarding at a new company and your buddy mentions an employee network for neurodivergent staff. They ask if you would like an introduction to someone who can explain options.
explanation: This is a formal workplace moment about sharing your neurotype, not explaining your texting style to a neighbour. "Disclosing Autism at Work" is the right script for that conversation with HR or a manager.

title: Exam room wait, clipboard questions
text: You are in an exam room waiting for a clinician you have not met before. A nurse has just taken your blood pressure and left you with a clipboard of intake questions.
explanation: Early in the visit is the right time to mention how you communicate and process information. "Disclosing Autism to a Doctor" covers saying it plainly at the start of the appointment.

title: Telehealth intro, pre-symptom prompt
text: You booked a telehealth slot for a medication review. The clinician joins the call, confirms your name, and asks what you would like them to know before discussing symptoms.
explanation: You need the clinician to understand your communication preferences, not only to buy time before answering a personal question. "Disclosing Autism to a Doctor" fits this opening moment.

title: Dental check-up, rapid speech pace
text: You are at a dental clinic for a routine check-up. The hygienist is friendly but speaks quickly while adjusting the light above the chair.
explanation: Letting the clinician know how you communicate best helps the whole visit go smoothly. "Disclosing Autism to a Doctor" applies in medical settings, including when you need clearer, slower speech.

title: Park bench talk, group outings topic
text: You are sitting on a park bench with someone you have been messaging for a month. They say they have been wondering why group outings tire you out so much.
explanation: They asked about you personally, and you are ready to name your neurotype in plain language. "Telling a New Friend You Are Autistic" covers choosing the moment and what to say next.

title: Film night, dim lights noticed
text: You invited someone over to watch a film and they notice you keep the lights low and the volume moderate. They ask, without judgment, what that is about for you.
explanation: Their question is an opening to explain who you are, not only to negotiate the lamp in this room. "Telling a New Friend You Are Autistic" helps you answer honestly and calmly.

title: Long bus ride, party topic
text: You are on a long bus ride with someone from your evening class. Conversation turns to how you experience parties, and they lean in as if ready to listen.
explanation: This is a trust moment for sharing your identity, not leaving an event that has already become too much. "Telling a New Friend You Are Autistic" is built for that disclosure choice.

title: Library study, rocking noticed nearby
text: You are studying together at the library and you start rocking slightly in your chair without noticing. The person beside you glances over and asks what you are doing.
explanation: They noticed a repetitive movement and want a simple explanation, not a change to the room lighting. "Explaining Stimming to Someone" gives you calm language for what it is and why it helps.

title: Family dinner, bracelet comment raised
text: During a family dinner your cousin comments that you always fiddle with your bracelet when conversations get lively. Other relatives are listening.
explanation: The focus is on a specific soothing movement, not your overall texting preferences. "Explaining Stimming to Someone" helps you describe it as normal and helpful.

title: Project call, hand movement question
text: You are on a video call with a project partner. They message privately asking if your hand movements on camera mean you are stressed.
explanation: They misread your movement as mood, and you want to clarify what it actually does for you. "Explaining Stimming to Someone" covers a short, factual reply.

title: Class noise spill, slide focus fading
text: You are in a classroom lesson and the noise from group work at the next table is making it hard to focus. Your shoulders feel tight and you cannot follow the slide on the board.
explanation: You need a short pause with staff permission during class, not a vague step-out line in any setting. "Asking for a Break at School" covers raising your hand or using a break card.

title: Timed test, shaky hands rising
text: You are in the middle of a timed test and your pen keeps slipping because your hands feel shaky. The invigilator is walking the rows.
explanation: You need a regulated pause in a school setting, not a formal accommodation form for a future exam. "Asking for a Break at School" fits speaking quietly to the teacher or invigilator now.

title: Assembly bench, echoing speaker strain
text: You are in a school assembly sitting on a hard bench under bright lights. The speaker's voice echoes and you feel yourself shutting down.
explanation: You are still on campus and need staff-approved time away, not finding a corridor on your own in a shopping centre. "Asking for a Break at School" is for this structured environment.

title: Desk alerts, foggy focus moment
text: You are at your desk and a long string of notifications has left your head foggy. Your manager walks past on the way to the kitchen.
explanation: You need to tell a colleague or manager you are stepping away briefly in a workplace, not raise your hand in class. "Asking for a Break at Work" gives the short phrase and return plan.

title: Open office overlap, sentence reread
text: You are in an open-plan office during a busy afternoon. The printer, phone calls, and chat overlap and you realise you are staring at the same sentence.
explanation: This is about stepping away for a few minutes with colleagues informed, not asking permission to wear headphones all day. "Asking for a Break at Work" fits a quick reset at your job.

title: Team call tension, camera on
text: You are on a video call with your team and your camera is on. Your chest feels tight and you need air before you miss what people are saying.
explanation: You are in a work meeting and need a brief pause, not a general "I need to step out" line at a party. "Asking for a Break at Work" covers saying it clearly and coming back.

title: Shopping centre mix, ears sore
text: You are in a busy shopping centre and the music from different stores blends together. Your ears feel sore and you need somewhere quieter before you continue.
explanation: You are in public on your own and need to find a calm spot early, not ask a host to change the lighting at home. "Taking a Sensory Break in a Public Space" walks through leaving the floor and resetting.

title: Rush platform, shoulder brushes constant
text: You are waiting for a train on a crowded platform during rush hour. Announcements overlap and people brush past your shoulders.
explanation: No manager is here to notify; you choose where to stand or step away on your own. "Taking a Sensory Break in a Public Space" is for self-directed pauses in busy places.

title: Street festival drums, limit approaching
text: You are at a street festival with food stalls and drumming from a stage nearby. You feel your limit approaching and want to act before it gets worse.
explanation: You are not leaving a hosted gathering for the whole evening, you are finding a quieter corner while you stay in the area. "Taking a Sensory Break in a Public Space" covers acting early in public.

title: Morning report, five oclock target
text: You are working on a report due at five o'clock and realise the research is taking longer than you expected. It is only mid-morning.
explanation: You need a new deadline for this assignment, not a list of permanent desk adjustments. "Asking for Extra Time to Complete a Task" covers asking early and proposing a realistic date.

title: Coursework brief, deadline pressure seen
text: Your tutor emailed a coursework brief with a fixed hand-in date. After reading it, you can see you will need more days to do it properly.
explanation: This is one task with a movable deadline, not applying for exam accommodations through the disability office. "Asking for Extra Time to Complete a Task" fits emailing or speaking to your tutor ahead of time.

title: Guest prep list, timeline slipping
text: You are cleaning the house before guests arrive tonight and the list keeps growing. You look at the clock and know you cannot finish everything on the original schedule.
explanation: You need to renegotiate when the work will be done, not step away for five minutes from your desk. "Asking for Extra Time to Complete a Task" helps you ask household members or yourself for a revised plan.

title: New role, open-plan concentration strain
text: You have started a new role and the open-plan layout makes it hard to concentrate on detailed tasks. You have a list of changes that would help you do your job well.
explanation: You are ready to request ongoing workplace supports, not only share your neurotype in a first conversation. "Asking for Adjustments at Work" covers booking a meeting and naming specific accommodations.

title: Weekly hot-desk moves, energy drain
text: Your team hot-desks every week and you find the constant moves draining. You want to ask whether one quieter spot could be reserved on certain days.
explanation: A standing arrangement is different from stepping out once this afternoon. "Asking for Adjustments at Work" is for formal, lasting changes agreed with management or HR.

title: Feedback note, participation support plan
text: You received written feedback that your written updates are strong but meetings are hard to follow. You want to propose how you could participate more effectively.
explanation: You are negotiating workplace supports, not explaining your style to someone you just met socially. "Asking for Adjustments at Work" helps you link requests to how you work best.

title: Exam season form, deadline approaching
text: Exam season is listed on the university website and you have paperwork from your diagnosis. You need to register for a longer sitting before the deadline passes.
explanation: This is an official exam accommodation through the access office, not emailing a tutor about one essay. "Asking for Extra Time on a Test" covers contacting disability services and what to say.

title: Adviser form, extended-time checkbox
text: Your college disability adviser sent a form to confirm which supports you want this year. One checkbox mentions extended time in exam rooms.
explanation: You are applying for a standard testing adjustment at school, not asking HR for desk equipment at a job. "Asking for Extra Time on a Test" fits that formal process.

title: Parent meeting, mock papers ahead
text: You are in secondary school and your parent meeting is next week. Your teachers mention upcoming mock exams and you know timed papers are difficult for you.
explanation: You need a planned exam accommodation, not a break card during today's lesson. "Asking for Extra Time on a Test" guides talking to the school access team or SENCO.

title: Computer lab hum, headset in bag
text: You are in a computer lab and the hum of machines plus whispering makes it hard to finish an exercise. You have noise-cancelling headphones in your bag.
explanation: You want permission to wear headphones while you stay in the room, not leave for a corridor break. "Asking to Use Headphones in Class or Work" covers asking the teacher or manager calmly.

title: Office music, personal headset request
text: You started an office job last month and everyone works with low background music playing. You would focus better if you could listen to nothing through your own headset.
explanation: This is a specific daily tool request, not a full accommodation meeting with a written list. "Asking to Use Headphones in Class or Work" is the right short ask.

title: Workshop stations, rising table noise
text: You are in a workshop classroom where students move between stations. The teacher has asked everyone to stay at their table, but the noise level keeps rising.
explanation: You need approval to block sound while you remain in class, not ask someone to dim the lights at home. "Asking to Use Headphones in Class or Work" fits this focused request.

title: New volunteer team, update preferences
text: You joined a new volunteer team and the coordinator asks how you prefer updates: calls, texts, or written notes. They want to set you up well before your first shift.
explanation: They want practical preferences for how you communicate day to day, not a full personal disclosure yet. "Explaining Your Communication Style to Someone New" covers direct language and examples.

title: New lab partner, style check-in
text: You are paired with a lab partner who keeps making jokes you do not catch. They say they want to work well together and ask what helps you understand them.
explanation: This is proactive style-setting, not clearing up one confusing message after the fact. "Explaining Your Communication Style to Someone New" helps you describe literal speech, pauses, and written follow-ups.

title: Neighbor tea, plan wording preferences
text: A new neighbour invited you for tea and mentioned they talk quickly when nervous. They ask how you like people to phrase plans so nothing gets lost.
explanation: You are explaining your general preferences to someone new, not asking them to slow down in this one moment only. "Explaining Your Communication Style to Someone New" fits that broader conversation.

title: Service desk queue, rapid instructions
text: You are at a service desk and the staff member is reading instructions fast while people queue behind you. You are trying to follow which forms you need.
explanation: You need this person's speech pace changed right now, not permission to wear headphones later. "Asking Someone to Speak More Slowly or Clearly" gives a polite, direct line.

title: Group call, audio drops words
text: You are on a group video call and one speaker's connection keeps cutting their words. You realise you have missed the last two instructions.
explanation: You need clearer speech in the moment, not time to think about your feelings before replying. "Asking Someone to Speak More Slowly or Clearly" covers checking understanding out loud.

title: Training room, accent hard parsing
text: You are in a training session and the trainer has switched to a thick regional accent you find hard to parse. They pause for questions.
explanation: This is an immediate comprehension request, not a full overview of how you communicate in general. "Asking Someone to Speak More Slowly or Clearly" fits raising your hand and asking them to repeat.

title: Family living room, overlap headache
text: You are at a family gathering in a crowded living room and conversations overlap from every direction. Your head starts to pound and you need air soon.
explanation: You need a short, general step-out line in a social setting, not a workplace procedure with your manager. "Asking for a Break" covers noticing early and saying you need a moment.

title: Board-game night, brightness building
text: You are at a friend's flat for a board-game night and the room has become loud and bright. You feel yourself getting overloaded but want to stay if you can reset.
explanation: You may only need a brief pause, not to leave the whole evening yet. "Asking for a Break" is for saying you need to step out briefly before deciding to go home.

title: Community fair loudspeaker, shift ongoing
text: You are volunteering at a community fair and the stall next to yours starts using a loudspeaker. You are still committed to your shift but need a minute away.
explanation: This is a flexible social or community setting, not a classroom with a teacher to ask. "Asking for a Break" gives a simple phrase anyone can use.

title: Birthday flat, stacked input overload
text: You are at a birthday party in a small flat and the music, cooking smells, and chatter have stacked up for an hour. You know staying longer will make recovery harder.
explanation: You have reached your limit and need to end the visit, not only pause in another room for five minutes. "Leaving a Situation That's Too Much" covers telling the host and leaving politely.

title: Work social, plans keep changing
text: You are at a work social after a long day and people keep adding plans you did not expect. Your body feels wired and you want to go home.
explanation: Leaving the event is the step now, not telling your manager you will return to your desk. "Leaving a Situation That's Too Much" helps you say you are heading off.

title: Cinema lobby previews, panic rising
text: You are at a crowded cinema lobby waiting for friends who are still buying snacks. The previews noise from inside leaks through the doors and you feel panicky.
explanation: You need to exit the outing, not just find a quieter corner in the building while you wait. "Leaving a Situation That's Too Much" is for when staying is no longer workable.

title: House dinner, overhead glare rising
text: You are at a house gathering and someone turns on harsh overhead lights while people eat. You feel glare on your eyes and want to ask for a change.
explanation: You need to name what is bothering you and suggest a small adjustment, not slip away to a public corridor alone. "Communicating Sensory Needs" covers identifying the sense and asking politely.

title: Long car ride, wind noise pain
text: You are sharing a car with two others on a long drive. They want the windows down and the radio up, and the wind noise is becoming painful.
explanation: You are negotiating sound and airflow with people beside you, not asking a teacher to wear headphones in class. "Communicating Sensory Needs" fits this specific adjustment request.

title: Overnight stay, ticking clock all night
text: You are staying overnight at a relative's home and their kitchen clock ticks loudly through the night. You want to mention it before another evening passes.
explanation: You are asking for an environmental change, not explaining repetitive movement to curious relatives. "Communicating Sensory Needs" helps you describe the sound and a workable fix.

title: Quiet evening plan, sudden house guests
text: You planned a quiet evening at home and your housemate announces last minute that friends are coming over for dinner. You feel your chest tighten.
explanation: The challenge is an unexpected change to your evening, not needing silence before you answer a personal question. "Coping When Your Plans Change Unexpectedly" covers breathing first and deciding your next step.

title: Train station board, service cancelled
text: You arrived at the train station for a trip you mapped out carefully. A display board shows your service cancelled with no clear replacement yet.
explanation: Your schedule shifted suddenly; you are coping with change, not leaving a party because sensory input is too high. "Coping When Your Plans Change Unexpectedly" helps you pause before reacting.

title: Lunch break, presentation moved earlier
text: Your manager moves tomorrow's presentation to this afternoon while you are at lunch. You return to an inbox saying the meeting starts in twenty minutes.
explanation: The trigger is a sudden schedule change, not a request for a later deadline on one task. "Coping When Your Plans Change Unexpectedly" fits regrouping when plans shift without warning.

title: Morning kitchen, sibling tension lingering
text: Something your sibling said yesterday is still sitting heavily with you. You are alone with them in the kitchen this morning and the house is quiet.
explanation: You want to name that you have been hurt, not yet debate who was right about one comment. "Telling Someone You're Upset" covers choosing calm timing and stating your feeling.

title: Cancelled plan call, trust shaken
text: A close person cancelled plans you were looking forward to without much explanation. They call later and ask if everything is okay between you.
explanation: They opened the door to share how you feel, not to postpone your answer for later. "Telling Someone You're Upset" helps you say you felt hurt or disappointed clearly.

title: Sofa silence after harsh feedback
text: You received harsh feedback on something you cared about and have been quiet all evening. Your parent sits beside you on the sofa and waits.
explanation: You are naming an emotional state, not checking whether they meant their words literally. "Telling Someone You're Upset" is for saying you feel upset and why.

title: Serious walk topic, words stuck
text: Someone you care about raises a serious topic during a walk and waits for your reply. Your mind feels full and you cannot find words yet.
explanation: You are not ready to share a feeling fully formed; you need space before you respond. "Saying You Need Time to Process" gives a short line and a suggested follow-up time.

title: Family video chat, loaded question
text: You are in a video chat and a relative asks whether you are angry about a family decision. The question arrives while you are still sorting your thoughts.
explanation: You need processing time, not to walk away from a heated argument mid-sentence. "Saying You Need Time to Process" fits asking to continue the talk later.

title: Long text thread, reply uncertainty
text: Your partner texts a long message about weekend plans changing. You read it twice and still feel unsure what you want to say back.
explanation: You need time to think before replying, not a full coping plan for a cancelled train. "Saying You Need Time to Process" covers delaying your answer without shutting the person out.

title: Project success table, eyes on you
text: You just heard that a project you cared about went well, and a teammate grins at you across the table. They seem to expect some reaction.
explanation: You want to share positive news in words, not ask for delay before you speak. "Telling Someone You're Happy" covers saying it plainly even if your face stays neutral.

title: Living room unwrap, perfect book inside
text: You open a gift from a relative and it is exactly the book you wanted. They watch your face closely in the living room.
explanation: This is a joyful moment to name out loud, not a hurt you are carrying from yesterday. "Telling Someone You're Happy" helps you put the feeling into words they can hear.

title: Corridor bump-in after exam result
text: You pass an exam you studied hard for and bump into a coursemate in the corridor. They ask how it went.
explanation: You want to express good news, not recover from an awkward comment you made earlier. "Telling Someone You're Happy" is for sharing positive feelings directly.

title: Reception crowd, timing feels unfamiliar
text: You are at a wedding reception and everyone seems to know when to stand, toast, and laugh together. You are scanning the room trying to copy the timing.
explanation: The strain is from unwritten social rules piling up, not only sensory volume that means you must leave now. "When You're Overwhelmed by Social Expectations" helps you pause, step back, or use a script line.

title: Work lunch table, cues feel unclear
text: You are at a work lunch and colleagues keep making small talk you cannot follow while also eating. You feel pressure to smile and nod correctly.
explanation: Hidden rules about how to act are the load, not a single request for a five-minute pause. "When You're Overwhelmed by Social Expectations" fits when performing expected behaviour feels exhausting.

title: Awards audience, applause timing unclear
text: You are at a school awards evening and families cheer at moments you did not expect. You feel exposed sitting in the audience unsure when to clap.
explanation: You are overloaded by social performance demands in the room, not asking for time before answering one direct question. "When You're Overwhelmed by Social Expectations" addresses that pressure.

title: Class remark replay, intent unclear
text: A classmate repeats something you said earlier in a way that sounds unkind. You are not sure they meant it badly, but the wording bothers you.
explanation: You want to check what they meant before you react, not launch into how hurt you feel. "Addressing a Misunderstanding" covers asking whether they meant it literally.

title: Manager email, interest misread
text: Your manager emails that you seemed "uninterested" in a meeting. You thought you were listening carefully and want to clear it up.
explanation: This is about mismatched interpretations, not settling yourself after a small slip you made earlier. "Addressing a Misunderstanding" helps you ask what they observed and share your view.

title: Ambiguous joke text, meaning unclear
text: A friend texts a joke that could be teasing or serious. You read it three times and still are not sure how to take it.
explanation: You need clarity on meaning first, not to tell them you feel upset before you know their intent. "Addressing a Misunderstanding" fits checking what they meant by the message.

title: Public comment sting, private follow-up
text: Someone you trust made a comment about how you dress in front of others. Hours later you still feel stung and want to talk privately.
explanation: You are naming specific behaviour and its impact, not only saying you feel bad in general. "Telling Someone Their Behaviour Hurt You" covers asking if now is a good time and using "I" statements.

title: Team table interruptions, patience thinning
text: A colleague keeps finishing your sentences in meetings even after you pulled away. You want it to stop without escalating to HR yet.
explanation: You are addressing repeated behaviour that affects you, not checking one ambiguous phrase they used once. "Telling Someone Their Behaviour Hurt You" fits a direct, calm conversation.

title: Shared kitchen, borrowed items again
text: Your roommate borrowed your things without asking again. You feel disrespected and they are in the kitchen making tea.
explanation: This is about their actions and how they landed on you, not requesting workplace accommodations. "Telling Someone Their Behaviour Hurt You" walks through timing and clear wording.

title: Hallway chores argument, pulse rising
text: You and someone you live with are raising voices in the hallway about chores. Your heart is racing and you feel words getting sharper.
explanation: The exchange is heated right now and you need to pause before saying more, not plan a polite goodbye to a party. "Walking Away from a Heated Argument" covers stating you need a break and leaving the room.

title: Group thread spiral, hands shaking
text: A group chat thread turned argumentative and people are pinging you to take sides. Your hands shake as you type and delete replies.
explanation: You need to step back from an escalating conflict, not ask for a day to process a single calm question. "Walking Away from a Heated Argument" fits logging off or pausing the chat.

title: Team table dispute, pressure building
text: You are in a meeting and two teammates disagree loudly across the table while others watch. You feel caught in the middle and close to snapping.
explanation: Tension is rising in the room and you need to remove yourself before you react, not announce a routine five-minute desk break. "Walking Away from a Heated Argument" is for heated conflict moments.

title: Desk replay after room silence
text: You realise you interrupted someone during a team story and the room went quiet. The meeting has ended and you are back at your desk replaying it.
explanation: You are managing your own thoughts after a slip, not asking them to clarify one phrase from the story. "Recovering After a Social Mistake" covers letting the thought pass and deciding if a brief apology helps.

title: Street wave mix-up, embarrassment lingering
text: You waved at someone in the street who was actually waving to the person behind you. You are walking home alone feeling embarrassed.
explanation: Nothing requires a long repair conversation; you are settling yourself after a small public slip. "Recovering After a Social Mistake" helps you move on without spiralling.

title: Wrong group post, phone face-down
text: You sent a message to the wrong group chat and only noticed after several people reacted. You put your phone face down and feel hot.
explanation: Your first step is grounding yourself after the error, not telling someone their behaviour hurt you. "Recovering After a Social Mistake" addresses the replay and what to do next.

title: School walk home, forgotten birthday
text: You are walking home from school with someone you care about. They have been quiet since lunch and finally say you forgot their birthday was yesterday.
explanation: They are hurt because of something you did, and you need to own it clearly with a close friend. "How to Say Sorry to a Friend" walks through naming what happened and listening to them.

title: Board-game table, sharp comment lands
text: You are at a board-game night and your comment about the rules came out sharper than you meant. Your friend puts the pieces down and their shoulders slump.
explanation: This is repair with someone you know well after you upset them, not managing your own anger in private. "How to Say Sorry to a Friend" fits a calm, direct conversation with them.

title: Private detail spread, trust cracked
text: You shared something private that a classmate told you in confidence. They found out from someone else and sent you a short message asking why you did that.
explanation: You need to address harm you caused in the friendship, not rebalance who texts first. "How to Say Sorry to a Friend" covers taking responsibility and checking if they are okay.

title: Busy hallway turn, books dropped
text: You are in a busy hallway between classes and turn quickly with your backpack on. Someone behind you stumbles and drops their books.
explanation: You caused a physical bump by accident and should check on them right away. "Apologizing When You Hurt Someone by Accident" covers saying you did not mean to and offering help.

title: Cafe table bump, sleeve splashed
text: You are carrying drinks to a table at a café and bump the tray against someone's arm. Hot liquid splashes onto their sleeve and they wince.
explanation: This was unintentional harm in the moment, not breaking something they lent you earlier. "Apologizing When You Hurt Someone by Accident" is for quick, honest check-ins after accidents.

title: Park catch wide, passerby hit
text: You are playing catch in the park and the ball goes wide. It hits a stranger on the leg and they stop walking to rub the spot.
explanation: You did not mean to hit them and should speak up immediately. "Apologizing When You Hurt Someone by Accident" fits when your action surprised or stung someone without planning to.

title: Sent draft mismatch, inbox dread
text: You realise you attached the wrong file to an email your teacher already opened. The subject line clearly says it was your final draft.
explanation: You need to name the error and fix it, not only sit with disappointment about a grade. "What to Do When You Make a Mistake" covers admitting it and taking the next step to put it right.

title: Porch light on, feeding missed
text: You promised to feed your neighbour's cat while they were away. You remembered too late tonight and see their porch light on as they pull into the driveway.
explanation: You forgot a responsibility and need to own it and repair what you can. "What to Do When You Make a Mistake" is about honest repair, not host etiquette at a dinner party.

title: Missed study call, fifteen-minute wait
text: You double-booked yourself and missed a video call with a study partner who waited fifteen minutes. They message asking if you are still coming.
explanation: You need to acknowledge your scheduling error and make a plan, not invite them to a new activity from scratch. "What to Do When You Make a Mistake" fits owning what happened and fixing it.

title: Bus ride loan, headphones cracked
text: You borrowed a friend's headphones for one bus ride. When you take them out of your bag, one ear cup has cracked off the band.
explanation: Something of theirs is damaged while in your care and they need to hear about it soon. "When You Break or Lose Someone's Belonging" covers telling them honestly and offering to replace or repair it.

title: Puddle-soaked loaned library copy
text: You were carrying a library book a classmate lent you and it slipped into a puddle. The cover is soaked and the pages are wavy.
explanation: Their item is harmed and you must tell them what happened, not only respond to a brief bump in the hall. "When You Break or Lose Someone's Belonging" is for damage to something they trusted you with.

title: Desk discovery, missing USB stick
text: You thought you put their USB stick back in their bag after copying photos. At home you find it still on your desk and they message asking if you have seen it.
explanation: You misplaced something of theirs and need to return it and be upfront. "When You Break or Lose Someone's Belonging" applies when their property is missing or harmed in your hands.

title: After class approach, eyes lowered
text: A classmate who argued with you at lunch approaches after last period. They look at their shoes and say they should not have spoken to you that way.
explanation: They are offering repair and you choose how to respond, not venting your own anger first. "Accepting an Apology from Someone Else" covers listening and deciding if you are ready to move on.

title: Bedroom doorway, journal boundary crossed
text: Your sibling comes into your room after dinner. They say they are sorry for reading your journal and will not do it again.
explanation: Someone else is asking for forgiveness; you are not the one initiating repair. "Accepting an Apology from Someone Else" fits when you decide whether to accept it or need more time.

title: Desk-side check-in before logoff
text: A coworker stops by your desk before you log off. They say they are sorry their email yesterday sounded harsh and they did not mean it personally.
explanation: They are apologizing to you, not the other way around. "Accepting an Apology from Someone Else" helps you respond without pretending the hurt never happened.

title: Classroom door wait, presentation misstep
text: You spoke over your project partner during a presentation and the teacher frowned. After class they wait by the door with a tired expression.
explanation: You need a brief, professional repair at school, not a long emotional support chat. "Apologizing at School or Work" covers a specific, calm apology in that setting.

title: Office summons after dated report
text: You sent a report to your manager with a wrong date on the cover page. They reply asking you to come by their office when you have a minute.
explanation: This calls for a respectful workplace conversation, not only fixing the file in silence. "Apologizing at School or Work" is built for teachers, managers, or colleagues in formal roles.

title: Late arrival, clock glance moment
text: You arrived twenty minutes late to a team meeting and everyone had already started without you. The facilitator glances at the clock as you sit down.
explanation: You owe a brief, professional acknowledgment in a work or school meeting context. "Apologizing at School or Work" fits lateness or disruption in those settings.

title: Shop queue bump, topic returning
text: You already said you were sorry for bumping someone in the shop queue. They smiled and said it was fine, but you keep bringing it up as you wait.
explanation: They have moved on and repeating it shifts focus onto you. "Saying Sorry Without Over-Apologising" is for one clear apology, then letting it go.

title: Resolved mix-up, guilt loop continues
text: Your friend texted that they are not upset about the mix-up anymore. In person you start explaining again how bad you feel for the third time.
explanation: You already repaired things; now you need to stop re-opening the wound. "Saying Sorry Without Over-Apologising" helps you apologise once clearly and move forward.

title: Team call fix, self-critique spiral
text: You made a small error on a shared document and your teammate fixed it during the call. They said "all good" but you keep saying how terrible you are at your job.
explanation: One sincere acknowledgment was enough; piling on makes others uncomfortable. "Saying Sorry Without Over-Apologising" covers saying it once and showing change through actions.

title: Kitchen meal, serving bowl arrives
text: Everyone in your family is sitting at the kitchen table and food is being passed around. Your parent sets a bowl in front of you and others are still serving themselves.
explanation: This is everyday eating with people you live with, including waiting and basic courtesy at home. "Table Manners at Home" covers those familiar mealtime habits.

title: Holiday dinner, last dish arriving
text: It is a holiday evening and relatives are gathered in the dining room. Plates are full and conversation has paused while the last dish is carried in.
explanation: The setting is your home or family table, not a public dining room with staff. "Table Manners at Home" fits relaxed rules with people you eat with often.

title: School morning breakfast, milk request
text: You are eating breakfast before school while your sibling pours cereal. Your guardian asks you to pass the milk and others are still getting settled.
explanation: This is a routine family meal at home, not choosing a seat in a cafeteria with classmates. "Table Manners at Home" is for mealtimes where you live.

title: Celebration dinner, quieter room tone
text: You are at a sit-down restaurant for a relative's celebration. Servers move between tables and voices stay lower than at home.
explanation: Shared public dining with wait staff calls for quieter voices and patience until everyone is served. "Table Manners at a Restaurant" covers that setting.

title: Small bistro lunch, plate delay
text: You are out for lunch at a small bistro with two friends. The waiter sets down plates and one friend is still waiting for their order.
explanation: You are paying to eat in a shared space with staff, not at your kitchen table. "Table Manners at a Restaurant" includes how to get attention politely and wait for others.

title: After-hours team meal, menus open
text: Your team booked a table at a chain restaurant after work. Menus are on the table and people around you are speaking in calm voices.
explanation: This is dining out in public, not visiting someone's house as a guest. "Table Manners at a Restaurant" fits meals where staff and other diners share the room.

title: Quiet library line, throat tickle
text: You feel a tickle in your throat while waiting in a quiet library queue. People nearby are reading and the room is very still.
explanation: Your body is about to react and you need to cover up and minimise spread. "Sneezing or Coughing in Public" covers elbow, tissue, and a brief excuse me.

title: Crowded bus ride, cough building
text: You are on a bus holding the pole when a cough builds. Passengers are packed close and someone shifts away slightly.
explanation: You need to manage a cough or sneeze safely around strangers, not ask them to step back for conversation space. "Sneezing or Coughing in Public" fits that moment.

title: Exam room hush, nose running
text: You are in a classroom test and your nose starts running. The invigilator looks up when you shift in your chair.
explanation: A sneeze or cough in a quiet shared room needs covering and quick hygiene. "Sneezing or Coughing in Public" is for health manners around others, not stomach noises.

title: Silent study hall, stomach rumble
text: You are in a silent study hall and your stomach makes a loud rumble. A few heads turn toward your desk.
explanation: An involuntary body sound in a quiet room calls for a brief excuse me and moving on, not covering your mouth for a cough. "When Your Body Makes an Embarrassing Noise" fits that awkward moment.

title: Lift pause, sudden sound moment
text: You are in a lift with two strangers when a sudden noise comes from your direction. The doors have not opened yet.
explanation: Bodies sometimes make sounds; a quiet acknowledgment is enough without a long conversation. "When Your Body Makes an Embarrassing Noise" helps you handle it calmly.

title: Front row seat, chair creak
text: You are sitting in the front row of a small meeting and your chair creaks loudly during a pause. The presenter waits a beat before continuing.
explanation: An unexpected noise in a formal quiet moment is different from waiting in a line. "When Your Body Makes an Embarrassing Noise" covers low-key responses without drawing more attention.

title: Post office line, parcel behind
text: You arrive at the post office and several people are already standing in a line marked on the floor. Someone joins behind you with a parcel.
explanation: You need to find the back of the line and wait your turn. "Waiting Your Turn in a Queue" covers spacing and patience until it is your turn.

title: Coffee counter line, side cutter
text: You are at a coffee shop counter and a barista is serving the person ahead of you. Another customer walks up and stands beside you instead of behind.
explanation: Order matters here; you may need to note you were next without holding a door. "Waiting Your Turn in a Queue" is for line fairness in public.

title: Ticket window line, showtime delay
text: You are buying cinema tickets and a rope guides people toward one window. The person in front is still choosing showtimes on the screen.
explanation: Everyone is waiting for the same service point; cutting in is not the issue. "Waiting Your Turn in a Queue" fits ticket or checkout lines.

title: Office exit, footsteps close behind
text: You are leaving your office building and hear footsteps close behind you on the way to the door. Someone is carrying a box with both hands.
explanation: A quick hold on the door helps them pass without juggling the box. "Holding a Door Open for Someone" is a brief courtesy, not a talk about personal distance.

title: Shop entrance, frame walker behind
text: You push open the shop entrance and an older person with a walking frame is a few steps behind you. A gust would pull the door closed quickly.
explanation: They need the door held briefly; you are not checking in on their emotions. "Holding a Door Open for Someone" covers that small helpful pause.

title: Apartment entry, bags and heavy door
text: You are entering your apartment block and someone from upstairs is right behind you with grocery bags. The heavy door swings back fast on its own.
explanation: Holding the door for a moment is enough; you are not hosting them inside your home. "Holding a Door Open for Someone" fits that short transition through an entrance.

title: Sleepover arrival, shoes by mat
text: You arrive for a sleepover and your friend opens the front door in socks. Their parent points to a pile of shoes by the mat.
explanation: You are visiting their home and follow their house rules. "Good Manners as a Guest at Someone's Home" covers shoes, thanks, and asking before using things.

title: Dinner visit, unknown bathroom door
text: You are at a friend's house for dinner and they show you where to put your coat. You notice a closed door and are not sure which room is the bathroom.
explanation: As a guest you ask before wandering and thank them for having you. "Good Manners as a Guest at Someone's Home" fits private visits, not restaurant dining.

title: Rare relative visit, teacups pending
text: You are visiting a relative you do not see often. They offer tea in the living room and you are unsure whether you should help clear cups.
explanation: Being thoughtful in someone else's home includes thanks and offering to help tidy. "Good Manners as a Guest at Someone's Home" is for that visit, not unwrapping a present.

title: Crowded train, shoulder pressure constant
text: You are on a crowded train and the person next to you keeps leaning into your shoulder. There is nowhere else to stand.
explanation: You may need to step back or ask for more room; holding a door is a different moment. "Respecting Personal Space" covers comfortable distance in shared spaces.

title: Locker chat, standing far too close
text: A classmate stands very close while explaining a homework question. You can smell their lunch and feel boxed in at your locker.
explanation: They are too close for comfort in a one-to-one chat. "Respecting Personal Space" includes stepping back or asking for a little more room politely.

title: Library huddle, laptop shoulder crowd
text: Your group project huddles around one laptop in the library. One person keeps leaning over your shoulder to point at the screen.
explanation: Physical closeness during work can feel overwhelming even when they mean well. "Respecting Personal Space" helps you set a comfortable distance while staying cooperative.

title: Art class seat, comic connection
text: You have chatted with someone in art class a few times about the same comic series. Today they smile when you walk in and save the seat beside them.
explanation: You want to move from occasional chats toward spending time together. "Asking Someone to Be Your Friend" covers suggesting a hangout when you already have something in common.

title: Lunch table chat, club mention
text: You started a new job and eat lunch at the same small table as a colleague who mentions a board-game club. They ask what you play at home.
explanation: You are building a friendship, not locking in one Saturday plan yet. "Asking Someone to Be Your Friend" fits when you want to connect beyond work small talk.

title: Youth club snack table, easy laugh
text: You see the same person at youth club every week and you both volunteer on the snack table. Tonight they laugh at your joke and the room feels less stiff.
explanation: You are ready to suggest spending time together outside the club routine. "Asking Someone to Be Your Friend" is for that step from familiar face to friend.

title: Corridor run-in, local show announcement
text: A band you both like announced a small local show on Saturday. You run into them in the corridor and think they might want to go.
explanation: You have a specific activity and time in mind to propose. "Inviting Someone to Do Something Together" covers naming the plan and accepting their answer calmly.

title: Early finish, study idea window
text: You and a classmate finished a group task early. You would like to study together for next week's test and they seem free after school.
explanation: This is one planned activity with a date, not joining a game already running. "Inviting Someone to Do Something Together" fits suggesting study or hangout plans.

title: Fence chat, fair suggestion forming
text: Your cousin is visiting for the weekend and you thought your neighbour might enjoy the community fair. You see them watering plants over the fence.
explanation: You are inviting them to a particular outing, not learning how to be neighbours. "Inviting Someone to Do Something Together" covers a clear invite with time and place.

title: Lunch table nickname loop, watching faces
text: At lunch a few students keep repeating a nickname you do not like. They laugh each time and look at you to see your reaction.
explanation: Repeated comments aimed at you need a calm boundary or walking away. "When Someone Is Teasing You" helps you tell them to stop and get support if it continues.

title: Locker room mimicry, silence around
text: In the locker room someone keeps mimicking how you walk. Others watch and nobody speaks up.
explanation: You are the target, not a bystander watching someone else. "When Someone Is Teasing You" is for when the comments are aimed at you and feel mean, not playful.

title: Practice miss joke, chest tight
text: A teammate jokes about your miss every time the ball goes wide. It is the third practice in a row and your chest feels tight.
explanation: Ongoing jokes at your expense are different from frustration with the game itself. "When Someone Is Teasing You" covers saying you do not like it and leaving if needed.

title: Bathroom corner scene, younger voice shaking
text: You walk into the school bathroom and hear two older students cornering a younger student by the sinks. The younger student's voice shakes.
explanation: Someone else is being targeted and you can stand with them or get help. "When You See Someone Being Bullied" covers safe ways to intervene and tell an adult.

title: Playground blockage at climbing frame
text: You are on the playground and see a group blocking another child from the climbing frame. The child tries to go around and the group steps in front again.
explanation: Another person is being excluded on purpose; this is not about game rules. "When You See Someone Being Bullied" fits when you witness harm to someone else.

title: Group thread pile-on, no reply
text: You open a group chat and see several people piling on one member with cruel memes. That person has not replied in hours.
explanation: You are witnessing others target someone, not receiving mean messages yourself. "When You See Someone Being Bullied" includes standing with them and reporting what you saw.

title: After-school meet-up, red eyes downcast
text: Your friend meets you after school with red eyes and will not say what is wrong at first. They walk slowly and keep looking at the ground.
explanation: They seem sad and you want to support them gently, not answer a casual "are you okay?" from a stranger. "Helping a Friend Who Is Upset" covers listening and offering to help.

title: Lunch tray untouched, face wiped
text: Someone you sit with at lunch has been quiet all week. Today they push food around the tray and wipe their face quickly when you look over.
explanation: They may need emotional support, not just a seat. "Helping a Friend Who Is Upset" fits when you notice a friend struggling and want to check in kindly.

title: Brief call request after home shock
text: Your friend texts that something bad happened at home but does not give details. They ask if you can call for a few minutes.
explanation: They are reaching out while distressed; your role is to listen and stay steady. "Helping a Friend Who Is Upset" is for supporting someone you care about.

title: Meetup planning always starts with you
text: You always send the first message to plan meetups. The last three times they cancelled without suggesting another day.
explanation: The pattern is about balance in the friendship, not one specific hurt you caused. "When a Friendship Feels One-Sided" covers talking about who reaches out and how it feels.

title: Weekend drives one way only
text: You drive to their house each weekend but they have not visited yours in months. When you mention it they change the subject.
explanation: You want to address fairness over time, not invite them to one new event. "When a Friendship Feels One-Sided" helps you name the pattern calmly.

title: Class seat shared, backup feeling
text: In class they sit with you but never include you when their other friends are around. You feel like a backup option.
explanation: You need a conversation about reciprocity, not only coping with feeling left out in the moment. "When a Friendship Feels One-Sided" is for when effort does not go both ways.

title: Bus stop crowd, risky dare push
text: Older students at the bus stop say you are boring unless you try something you do not want to do. They keep nudging your shoulder and laughing.
explanation: They are pushing you to go along with something uncomfortable. "Handling Peer Pressure" covers a clear no and walking away if they keep pushing.

title: Sleepover circle, prank dare spotlight
text: Friends at a sleepover keep daring you to prank a neighbour. Everyone is watching to see what you will do.
explanation: The group wants you to act against your comfort, not follow host manners. "Handling Peer Pressure" is for staying firm when others urge you to join in.

title: Pre-game stunt challenge, camera out
text: A teammate says everyone will think you are scared if you skip a risky stunt before the game. They hold out a phone to film you.
explanation: You need to refuse something unsafe or uncomfortable because of group push, not intervene as a bystander. "Handling Peer Pressure" fits direct pressure to conform.

title: Morning notifications, harsh photo comments
text: You wake up to several harsh comments on a photo you posted. The same person has replied on older posts too.
explanation: Unkindness directed at you online needs pausing, saving evidence, and telling someone trusted. "When Someone Is Mean to You Online" covers those steps.

title: Game team chat, insults scrolling
text: During an online game someone types insults about you in the team chat. Other players stay silent.
explanation: Targeted cruelty in a digital space is different from arguing about game rules. "When Someone Is Mean to You Online" helps you protect yourself and report it.

title: Private text shared, emoji pile-on
text: A classmate shares a private message you sent them in a group chat with rude captions. People you know are reacting with emojis.
explanation: Your trust was broken online and you need support, not only a face-to-face repair for a careless phrase. "When Someone Is Mean to You Online" fits digital harm aimed at you.

title: First-week cafeteria, lone table seat
text: It is your first week at a new school. The cafeteria is loud and you see an empty chair at a table where one person is eating alone.
explanation: You want to join someone at a meal without a long friendship talk first. "Asking to Sit with Someone at Lunch" covers asking if the seat is free.

title: Break room, empty chair beside colleague
text: You are at work on a break and the staff room has two tables. A colleague you have spoken to once is sitting alone with space beside them.
explanation: A low-pressure seat at lunch is the goal, not planning a hangout outside work yet. "Asking to Sit with Someone at Lunch" fits that simple approach.

title: Camp dining table, open spot across
text: You are at summer camp and do not know anyone at your table yet. One camper is reading and there is an open spot across from them.
explanation: You need a place to eat near someone, not invite them to an activity later. "Asking to Sit with Someone at Lunch" is for mealtime seating questions.

title: Haircut joke lands, table quiet
text: You made a joke about someone's new haircut and their smile disappeared. The table went quiet and they stared at their plate.
explanation: Your words hurt them and you need to check in and clarify what you meant. "Saying Something Accidentally Hurtful" covers apologising and listening without getting defensive.

title: Sketchbook packed, wording taken wrong
text: You told a friend their drawing looked "simple" meaning you liked how clear it was. They packed up their sketchbook and stopped talking.
explanation: They heard hurt in what you said even though you meant something kind. "Saying Something Accidentally Hurtful" helps you repair when your intent and their reaction do not match.

title: Fast text reply, outfit misunderstanding
text: You replied to a text too quickly and they read it as criticism of their outfit. They send a message asking if you were being serious.
explanation: Tone got lost in writing and they are hurt by how it read. "Saying Something Accidentally Hurtful" fits clarifying your meaning and hearing how they took it.

title: Family board night, final score posted
text: You are at a family board-game night and the final score is on the table. Your cousin grins and starts putting the pieces back in the box.
explanation: The round is over and you came out behind; a calm, brief response keeps things friendly. "Losing a Game Gracefully" covers breathing first and acknowledging the other player without replaying every mistake.

title: Club match end, results screen set
text: You are in an after-school video-game club and the match timer hits zero. The screen shows the other player's name at the top of the results list.
explanation: You did not win this round and others are watching how you react. "Losing a Game Gracefully" is for staying steady and ending on a respectful note instead of arguing about the score.

title: Chess board reset after checkmate
text: You are at chess club and your opponent calls checkmate. They slide their chair back and wait for you to reset the board.
explanation: They won fairly and the match is finished. "Losing a Game Gracefully" fits when you need to accept the outcome and decide calmly whether to play again.

title: Kitchen card round, empty hand first
text: You and two friends just finished a card round at the kitchen table. Your hand was the last one empty and the others are looking at their cards.
explanation: You came out ahead and the moment is about how you act toward the others, not celebrating loudly. "Winning Without Gloating" covers a brief, friendly close and an optional rematch.

title: Pickup point ends, bench walk-back
text: Your team scores the final point in a lunchtime pickup match. The other side walks toward the bench and a few people clap.
explanation: Your side finished ahead; the focus is staying respectful so people want to play again. "Winning Without Gloating" helps you acknowledge others without replaying every highlight.

title: Trivia finale, only correct sheet
text: The trivia host reads the last answer and your team's sheet has the only correct response. The room goes quiet while points are added.
explanation: You did well in a group activity and others are watching your reaction. "Winning Without Gloating" is for keeping praise brief and inviting another round if people want one.

title: Neighborhood park, swings already moving
text: You arrive at a neighbourhood park after school. Several children are on the climbing frame and the swings are moving.
explanation: You are in a shared outdoor play space with others already using equipment. "Playing at the Playground" covers looking around, waiting your turn, and asking politely before joining in.

title: Recess yard spread, slide queue
text: Recess just started and your class is spread across the school yard. A group is lining up for the slide while you stand near the fence.
explanation: This is unstructured outdoor time with classmates and shared structures. "Playing at the Playground" fits watching what others do and moving in safely without pushing.

title: Sand pit tools, space beside pair
text: You are at a community sand pit with buckets and shovels. Two younger children are building together and there is space beside them.
explanation: You want to use the same area without taking over their space. "Playing at the Playground" includes gentle approaches and telling an adult if someone is unkind.

title: Park circle activity, laughter continues
text: You are at the park and a group is running a tag-style activity in a circle. They laugh every time someone is caught and start again.
explanation: Others are already playing and you want to be included. "Asking to Join a Game Already in Progress" covers watching briefly, waiting for a pause, and asking if you can take part.

title: Half-court keep-away, sideline glance
text: On the basketball half-court three students are playing keep-away. The ball slows down near the sideline and they glance around.
explanation: You want to enter an activity that started without you, not build a whole new friendship from scratch. "Asking to Join a Game Already in Progress" fits that short, direct request at a natural break.

title: Teen corner cards, pattern observed
text: In the library teen corner two people are dealing cards into piles. You have watched two hands and think you understand the pattern.
explanation: They are mid-activity and you need a polite way to ask in. "Asking to Join a Game Already in Progress" includes accepting a no calmly and trying again another time.

title: Living-room blocks, same piece reached
text: You and a sibling are building with blocks on the living-room floor. You both reach for the same long piece at the same time.
explanation: Only one person can use that piece right now and you need a fair order. "Taking Turns While Playing" covers waiting, naming whose go it is, and asking calmly if you forget.

title: Dice still rolling, board scrambled
text: During a board game at a friend's house both of you move pieces before the dice have stopped rolling. The board is suddenly mixed up.
explanation: The order of play got confused and you need to reset fairly. "Taking Turns While Playing" is for tracking turns out loud and cheering the other person sometimes.

title: Shared controller, couch wait stretching
text: You are sharing one controller on a console with a cousin. They have held it through two levels and you are waiting on the couch.
explanation: You are already playing together and need a clear swap, not permission to enter from outside. "Taking Turns While Playing" fits when both people need equal time with the same item.

title: Puzzle level repeat, fail tone again
text: You have tried the same puzzle level six times on your tablet and your hands feel tight on the case. The fail sound plays again.
explanation: The activity itself is raising your stress and you may need a short pause. "When a Game Gets Frustrating" covers noticing your body, breathing, and saying you want a break from this round.

title: Co-op board timer, goal card missed
text: You are playing a cooperative board game and the group keeps missing the goal card. Someone sighs loudly and the timer on the table is almost empty.
explanation: Tension is building during play, not because someone cheated. "When a Game Gets Frustrating" helps you step back before reactions spill onto others.

title: Club table, cold dice streak
text: At game club your dice rolls have been low for twenty minutes. You stare at the board and feel your face getting hot.
explanation: Bad luck in the moment is making it hard to stay calm, even if no one is being mean. "When a Game Gets Frustrating" is for pausing or stopping before you snap.

title: Board round, double move shrugged off
text: You are playing a board game with friends and one person moves twice before anyone else has gone. They shrug when you point at the rule sheet.
explanation: Someone is bending agreed rules and it is affecting fairness. "When Someone Doesn't Follow the Rules" covers calm clarification and choosing whether to keep playing.

title: Lunchtime pitch, handball dispute stalls
text: During a lunchtime soccer game a teammate keeps picking up the ball with their hands. Others on both teams stop and look at the ref who is not there.
explanation: The issue is rule-breaking in play, not personal teasing aimed at you. "When Someone Doesn't Follow the Rules" fits naming the rule and suggesting you check together.

title: Camp card points claim dispute
text: In a card game at camp someone claims extra points that the printed instructions do not mention. They insist that is how their family always plays.
explanation: You need to address whether the agreed rules are being followed, not how to act after a clear win. "When Someone Doesn't Follow the Rules" helps you stay calm and decide if you still want to play.

title: Sofa handheld, cousin reaches over
text: Your cousin visits and reaches for the handheld you are using on the sofa. They ask if they can try it while you are mid-level.
explanation: Something you are using belongs to you and another person wants a turn. "Sharing Toys or Equipment" covers asking before taking and offering a turn when you are done.

title: Art desk, lone fineliner request
text: At art class a classmate taps your pencil case and asks to borrow your only fine-liner. You are still shading your own page.
explanation: This is about lending something for a short time, not handing over a wrapped present. "Sharing Toys or Equipment" fits saying you are using it now and when they can have a go.

title: PE court, one ball waiting
text: In PE there is one basketball left and three people are waiting. You have had it for several minutes while others practice shots nearby.
explanation: Shared school equipment needs fair use, not joining a new outdoor activity. "Sharing Toys or Equipment" is for taking turns and returning items in good condition.

title: Holiday dinner, wrapped box mismatch
text: At a holiday dinner your aunt places a wrapped box in front of you while relatives watch. You open it and the item inside is not something you would choose.
explanation: Someone cared enough to choose something for you and is waiting for your reaction. "Receiving a Gift You Don't Like" covers a brief, honest thank-you without saying you dislike it.

title: Secret Santa table, bright sweater reveal
text: Your workplace Secret Santa exchange ends and you unwrap a bright sweater that does not match anything you wear. The giver smiles from across the room.
explanation: You are on the receiving end and need a polite response, not tips for handing something over. "Receiving a Gift You Don't Like" helps you find something true to say and move on.

title: Cafe scarf reveal, color overload
text: A friend gives you a handmade scarf in a cafe. The colours are loud for you, but they lean forward, eager to see your face.
explanation: Your job is to respond kindly to their effort, not to explain a general dislike of a hobby. "Receiving a Gift You Don't Like" fits keeping thanks brief and sincere.

title: Birthday morning box, long-wanted series
text: Your parent hands you a small box on your birthday morning. Inside is the book series you have mentioned for months.
explanation: You genuinely want this item and can show real enthusiasm. "Receiving a Gift You Love" covers thanking them and saying what you like about it.

title: Graduation party unwrap, chosen headphones
text: At your graduation party a relative gives you headphones you picked out online together. They watch while you lift them out of the tissue paper.
explanation: You are delighted and they can see it; the moment calls for warm thanks, not instructions for giving. "Receiving a Gift You Love" fits showing honest excitement in your own way.

title: Lunch table case, rare expansion
text: Your friend slides a game case across the table at lunch. It is the expansion you have been saving up for but could not find in shops.
explanation: This is a welcome surprise you want to acknowledge clearly. "Receiving a Gift You Love" helps you thank them and name why it matters to you.

title: School gate meet-up, wrapped notebook ready
text: You bought a notebook for a classmate's birthday and wrapped it at home. You meet them at the gate and they have not seen it yet.
explanation: You are the one offering something, not opening a package yourself. "Giving Someone a Gift" covers handing it over, saying who it is for, and waiting while they open it.

title: After-school doorway, collage behind back
text: You made a photo collage for your sibling's room and it is in a folder behind your back. They walk in after school and you want to surprise them.
explanation: You are presenting something you prepared, not reacting to what someone gave you. "Giving Someone a Gift" fits a simple line like this is for you and letting them respond.

title: Desk move day, plant in hands
text: At work you picked up a plant for a colleague who is moving desks. You stop by their cubicle with the pot in both hands before the team meeting.
explanation: This is a one-to-one handoff, not navigating a whole party schedule. "Giving Someone a Gift" covers offering the item and responding if they thank you.

title: Costume street walk, porch lights on
text: You are walking with a parent along a lit street in costume. The porch light is on at the next house and other children are ahead on the path.
explanation: You are going door to door for sweets in a planned neighbourhood route. "Trick-or-Treating" covers knocking, waiting, and thanking the person who answers.

title: Doorstep bowl sign, one-piece note
text: Your group stops at a house where a bowl sits on a small table by the door. A sign asks visitors to take one piece each.
explanation: This is the seasonal door-to-door routine, not a shop checkout line. "Trick-or-Treating" includes taking one treat, saying thanks, and moving to the next house.

title: Doorbell moment, bag held open
text: You ring a doorbell and hear footsteps inside. The porch light is on and your bag is open in your hands.
explanation: Someone is about to open the door for the Halloween visit script. "Trick-or-Treating" fits the short greeting and thank-you before you continue down the street.

title: Community hall balloons, music inside
text: You arrive at a community hall where balloons hang by the door. Inside, music plays and children are gathered around a table with cake plates.
explanation: You were invited to celebrate one person's special day in a group setting. "Going to a Birthday Party" covers greeting the host, joining activities, and thanking them before you leave.

title: Front door drop-off, present in hand
text: You are dropped off at a friend's house with a bag and a wrapped present. Their parent opens the door and you hear voices in the living room.
explanation: This is a birthday visit with games and cake, not a regular sleepover with house rules only. "Going to a Birthday Party" helps you greet the birthday person and pace yourself if it gets busy.

title: Bowling lanes, sash and shoe rack
text: You are at a bowling alley party and shoes are being handed out. The birthday person is wearing a sash and people are picking lanes.
explanation: You are there for someone's birthday outing with structured activities. "Going to a Birthday Party" fits arriving, taking part briefly if you can, and saying thanks at the end.

title: Family gathering, overlapping voices and doors
text: You are at a large family gathering and conversations overlap in every corner. The kitchen door keeps swinging open and your ears are starting to ache.
explanation: The crowd and noise are building faster than you can process. "When a Holiday Celebration Feels Overwhelming" covers finding a quieter spot, a brief break outside, or a signal to leave early.

title: Festival tent lights, band too close
text: At a winter festival tent, lights flash and a band plays close to the seats. Your chest feels tight and you cannot follow what your cousin is saying.
explanation: A seasonal event is too intense right now, not a brand-new place you will visit often. "When a Holiday Celebration Feels Overwhelming" helps you step away without staying until the very end.

title: New year flat, countdown noise swell
text: You are at a New Year's party in a small flat. People shout over the countdown rehearsal and someone keeps bumping your chair from behind.
explanation: The holiday setting itself is the overload, not one friend's birthday schedule. "When a Holiday Celebration Feels Overwhelming" is for planning breaks and leaving when you need to.

title: Model rebuild loop, hands clenching
text: You have rebuilt the same model three times and a piece keeps snapping off. Your jaw is clenched and you want to throw the parts across the room.
explanation: Strong body signals mean you need to cool down before you act. "When You Feel Frustrated or Angry" covers breathing, stepping away, and choosing what to do once you are calmer.

title: Lunch line cut, fists tightening
text: Someone cut in front of you in the lunch line after you waited ten minutes. Your face feels hot and your hands are in tight fists.
explanation: You are upset and need to manage your reaction, not only address line order with a stranger. "When You Feel Frustrated or Angry" fits noticing the feeling and pausing before you speak.

title: Hallway grade shock, paper crumpling urge
text: You studied for a test and still got a low mark back. In the hallway you stare at the paper and want to rip it up.
explanation: The sting is intense right now; you need regulation before problem-solving. "When You Feel Frustrated or Angry" is for physical release and reflection after you settle.

title: New-school eve, bus route nerves
text: Tomorrow you start at a new school and your bag is packed by the door. Tonight your stomach flutters every time you think about the bus route.
explanation: Something upcoming is on your mind and your body is reacting ahead of time. "When You Feel Nervous or Anxious Before an Event" covers slow breathing and naming one small thing you look forward to.

title: Backstage lineup, two names away
text: You are backstage at a recital and can hear the audience settling. Your name is two performers away on the list taped to the wall.
explanation: A scheduled performance is about to start, not an open-ended overload in the moment. "When You Feel Nervous or Anxious Before an Event" helps you prepare right before you go on.

title: Pre-appointment hour, clock-check loop
text: You have a dentist appointment in an hour and keep checking the clock. Your legs bounce and you keep re-reading the reminder text.
explanation: You are anticipating a specific appointment, not answering someone who asked about your mood. "When You Feel Nervous or Anxious Before an Event" fits the lead-up hours, not the chair itself.

title: Family lounge, laughter too loud
text: Your family is watching a comedy show that uses loud sound effects. Everyone is laughing but you want to leave the room.
explanation: You can dislike the show without a fight; you may stay quiet or step out politely. "When You Don't Like Something" covers honest but calm responses if someone asks your opinion.

title: Tasting table, strong cheese pass
text: At a group tasting everyone is trying a strong cheese and nodding. Someone passes the plate to you and waits for you to take a piece.
explanation: You are not required to pretend enthusiasm for food you do not want. "When You Don't Like Something" helps you decline or say it is not your thing without insulting others.

title: Weekend drill sign-up, low interest
text: A club you joined mostly plays a sport you find boring. The coach asks who wants extra practice on Saturday.
explanation: Your preference matters and you may need to speak up if it affects you directly. "When You Don't Like Something" is for polite honesty, not coping with a letdown after hopes were high.

title: Corridor chat, favorite book finished
text: You just finished a book you adored and run into a classmate in the corridor. They ask what you have been reading lately.
explanation: You want to tell someone about something you care about without overwhelming them. "Sharing Excitement About Something You Love" covers starting with the best part and watching if they are engaged.

title: Coffee machine chat, album release excitement
text: Your favourite band released a new album and you meet a coworker by the coffee machine. They smile and say they have not heard it yet.
explanation: You are enthusiastic about a hobby, not announcing a competitive result. "Sharing Excitement About Something You Love" fits sharing a highlight and inviting them to ask a question.

title: Model photo share, cousin curious
text: You built a detailed model over the weekend and bring a photo to show your cousin. They lean in and say they do not know much about that hobby.
explanation: You want to connect through something you enjoy without lecturing. "Sharing Excitement About Something You Love" helps you pick one interesting detail and notice their reactions.

title: Monday phone photos, missing invite sting
text: You see photos from a weekend outing on your phone. Several classmates were there and no one mentioned it when you sat with them on Monday.
explanation: You are hurt because you were not included and want to understand why. "When You Feel Left Out" covers pausing before you assume intent and asking calmly if there was a reason.

title: Lunch table whispers, subject shift
text: At lunch your usual group is whispering and laughing across the table. When you ask what is funny they change the subject quickly.
explanation: Feeling on the outside of a group moment is different from being teased directly. "When You Feel Left Out" helps you name the feeling and decide whether to talk to someone you trust.

title: Group chat replay, movie night missed
text: Your team chat shows plans for a movie night that happened last night. You were online earlier that day but got no message.
explanation: Missing an invite hurts; this is not the same as cruel messages aimed at you online. "When You Feel Left Out" fits when you need to address exclusion with friends or an adult.

title: Gym door list, alternate column
text: You trained for weeks and did not make the team list posted on the gym door. You read your name on the alternate sheet instead.
explanation: Something you cared about did not turn out how you hoped. "When You Feel Disappointed" covers naming the feeling and waiting before big decisions while it is still sharp.

title: Refund email morning, Saturday plans gone
text: A concert you booked months ago was cancelled this morning. The refund email arrived but you had already planned your whole Saturday around it.
explanation: Plans fell through and you need space to process that loss. "When You Feel Disappointed" is for talking it through when you are ready, not emergency grounding in the moment.

title: Prepared living room, last-minute cancel
text: Your friend said they would come over and texted an hour ago to cancel. You had set up snacks and a film on the TV.
explanation: You are let down by changed plans; you are not the one who needs to repair harm you caused. "When You Feel Disappointed" fits when you need to sit with the feeling and reach out to someone you trust.

title: Bedside overload, task order frozen
text: Homework, messages, and chores piled up today and your head is buzzing. You sit on your bed and cannot pick which task to start.
explanation: Too many demands at once need a pause and one tiny next step. "When Everything Feels Like Too Much" covers stopping, grounding, and choosing just one thing when you are ready.

title: Bright mall aisles, list forgotten
text: The shopping centre is crowded and bright after school. Sounds blur together and you cannot remember what you came in to buy.
explanation: Right now everything is hitting at once in a public place. "When Everything Feels Like Too Much" helps you find quiet, breathe, and decide one small action instead of pushing through.

title: Phone buzzing nonstop, body trembling
