text: You have had three difficult conversations today and your phone will not stop buzzing. You feel shaky and need to sit down.
explanation: This is overload from many stressors, not anger at one person only. "When Everything Feels Like Too Much" is for a full reset before you tackle anything else.

title: Shared flat talk, meaning crossed
text: You explained why you needed quiet time and your roommate heard it as you being rude. They cross their arms and repeat what they think you meant.
explanation: They heard a different meaning from your words and you want another chance to clarify. "When You Feel Misunderstood" covers rephrasing calmly and checking if it makes more sense now.

title: Class discussion, point reframed publicly
text: In class discussion the teacher summarised your point differently than you intended. A few students nod at their version while you still have your hand half raised.
explanation: Your meaning did not land; you need to restate, not only say you dislike the topic. "When You Feel Misunderstood" fits asking to try again with different words or an example.

title: Weekend text, meaning flipped back
text: You sent a long message about your weekend and your friend replied as if you were complaining about them. Their answer does not match what you meant at all.
explanation: Written tone caused a mismatch and you want to repair understanding, not only repair a joke that landed badly. "When You Feel Misunderstood" helps you explain again or pause until later.

title: Youth club hallway, first-time jitters
text: You step into a youth club building for the first time and the hallway smells of paint and snacks. People you do not know are signing in at a desk.
explanation: The place itself is unfamiliar and your body is on alert. "When You Feel Anxious in a New Environment" covers finding one anchor, moving slowly, and knowing you can leave if you need to.

title: New job break room, sign confusion
text: You are on your first day at a new job and follow a printed map to the break room. The buzz of machines and voices makes it hard to read the signs.
explanation: You are already inside an unfamiliar building, not waiting for one event later. "When You Feel Anxious in a New Environment" fits exploring at your own pace on day one.

title: Unfamiliar flat layout, coat uncertainty
text: You arrive at a friend's new flat and the layout is nothing like their old place. They are in the kitchen and you stand in the doorway unsure where to put your coat.
explanation: A changed physical space can feel uncertain even with people you know. "When You Feel Anxious in a New Environment" helps you take it step by step and ask where things go.

title: Quiet desk check-in, teacher kneeling
text: Your teacher kneels beside your desk after you have been quiet all period. They say your name softly and ask how you are doing.
explanation: Someone noticed you are struggling and opened the door for an honest answer. "When Someone Asks "Are You Okay?" and You're Not" covers choices from a brief truth to asking for time to talk later.

title: Cubicle stop-by, hard-day check
text: A coworker stops by your cubicle at the end of a hard day. They tilt their head and ask if everything is all right.
explanation: They are checking on you directly; you can answer without pretending you are fine. "When Someone Asks "Are You Okay?" and You're Not" helps you decide how much to share in a workplace moment.

title: Back step sit, parent waiting
text: Your parent finds you sitting on the back step after an argument at school. They sit down and ask if you want to talk about what happened.
explanation: A trusted person is offering space to open up, not delivering a full coping plan for overload. "When Someone Asks "Are You Okay?" and You're Not" fits naming that you are not okay and choosing whether to explain now.

title: Quiet stacks entrance, desk glance
text: On a quiet Saturday you step inside a tall building full of labelled shelves and soft footsteps. A person at the front desk glances up as you pause near the entrance.
explanation: A calm shared indoor space with clear expectations about voice and handling items is what "Visiting the Library" is for, including borrowing when you are ready.

title: Novel search, shelf section unsure
text: Your class needs a specific novel and someone said this building keeps copies. You walk past rows of spines unsure which section to check first.
explanation: You are new to the building and need general orientation before a focused conversation with staff. "Visiting the Library" covers how the space works day to day.

title: Card wallet, paperbacks underarm arrival
text: You have a plastic card in your wallet and a stack of paperbacks under your arm from home. Automatic doors close behind you and wall signs ask for low voices.
explanation: You are entering with items to hand back, but the moment is still about using the building respectfully. "Visiting the Library" sets the baseline before you reach the returns point.

title: Science aisle repeat, lanyard nearby
text: You have checked the science aisle twice and still cannot spot the title on your phone screen. A person in a lanyard is re-shelving nearby and looks approachable.
explanation: You need a specific item located and staff are the right people to ask. "Asking a Librarian for Help" walks through a polite request and how to describe what you need.

title: Comic spine row, desk queue
text: You need the next volume in a comic series and every spine in the row looks similar. The main desk has a short queue and one person free.
explanation: This is a targeted question to trained staff, not a casual chat while browsing. "Asking a Librarian for Help" fits describing title, author, or topic clearly.

title: Busy kids corner, train book hunt
text: You are helping a younger relative find a picture book about trains. The children's corner is busy and you cannot see anyone working there yet.
explanation: You are stuck on locating material and need staff input, not setting up a timed session on a machine. "Asking a Librarian for Help" is the right script for that desk conversation.

title: Walk-home return, green slot light
text: The paperback in your bag is due tomorrow and you pass the building on your walk home. An outdoor slot has a green light and short instructions on a sticker.
explanation: Items you have finished with need to go back on time, using the slot or desk if needed. "Returning a Borrowed Book" covers due dates, drop-off, and any fees calmly.

title: Overdue notice screen, counter pause
text: You open your bag at the front counter and the home screen showed an overdue notice. The person behind the glass smiles and waits for you to step forward.
explanation: You are completing a return and may need to settle a fee, not starting a search for new material. "Returning a Borrowed Book" has the steps for desk handover and payment.

title: Return stack inside, outdoor box full
text: Three items need to go back before you can take out anything new. The outdoor box is full so you head inside with them stacked neatly.
explanation: The task is finishing loans, not logging onto a shared screen. "Returning a Borrowed Book" fits multiple items and asking for proof if you want it.

title: Essay deadline, screen row login prompts
text: You need to finish a short essay and the tables at home are too noisy today. A wall sign lists session limits and a row of screens shows login prompts.
explanation: You are using a booked or walk-in workstation in a quiet public building. "Using a Library Computer or Study Area" covers login, volume, and logging out when you leave.

title: Reserved terminal notice, staff passing desks
text: You enter your membership number but the screen says the machine is reserved for another hour. A staff member walks past the cluster of desks.
explanation: The issue is access to shared equipment, not finding a book on the shelves. "Using a Library Computer or Study Area" fits checking booking rules and asking staff if you are unsure.

title: Session timer minute left, card waiting
text: You finished your research and another person is waiting with their card ready. Your session timer shows one minute left.
explanation: You need to end your session cleanly and leave the desk tidy. "Using a Library Computer or Study Area" includes logging out and clearing the space for the next person.

title: Quiet room call, group booking prep
text: Six friends want to eat together next Friday and the place only takes bookings by phone. You are in a quiet room with the menu open on your laptop.
explanation: You are arranging a table before anyone travels to the venue. "Making a Restaurant Reservation" covers date, time, party size, and confirming details on the call.

title: Birthday seat count, call-only site
text: Your parent asks you to organise seats for a birthday and gives you the date and how many people. The website says to call rather than book online.
explanation: Planning ahead by phone is different from managing noise once you are seated. "Making a Restaurant Reservation" is for locking in the booking and noting dietary needs early.

title: Full-tonight page, redial for cancellations
text: The bistro shows tonight as full on the website but the recorded message says to try for cancellations. You press redial and hear it ringing again.
explanation: You are still securing a table by phone, not dressing for a ceremony or walking in unannounced. "Making a Restaurant Reservation" fits giving your name and repeating the agreed time.

title: Foyer arrival, apron host tablet
text: You push open the glass door and the foyer smells like bread and grilled food. A person in a black apron looks up from a tablet near the entrance.
explanation: You have arrived and need to be shown to a table, including saying if you already booked. "Arriving and Being Seated at a Restaurant" covers that first moment inside.

title: Seven oclock arrival, bench queue hallway
text: Your group agreed to meet at seven and you are first to arrive. The hallway is narrow and several parties are waiting on a bench.
explanation: You are at the door waiting to be seated, not yet negotiating sensory needs at the table. "Arriving and Being Seated at a Restaurant" fits giving your name or party size calmly.

title: Seating preference request, corner table gesture
text: You were told there might be a quieter spot away from the kitchen. The host gestures toward a corner table and waits for you to follow.
explanation: You are still in the arrival and seating phase, which can include asking to move if the first table is uncomfortable. "Arriving and Being Seated at a Restaurant" covers that request politely.

title: Menu icons unclear, notepad ready
text: The menu has small icons but you are not sure what they mean for your nut sensitivity. The server returns with a notepad and pen ready.
explanation: You need clear information about ingredients before you order, not a medical appointment. "Asking About Allergens or Dietary Needs" helps you state your needs and confirm them with staff.

title: Pasta place table, ingredient check needed
text: Your friend suggested this pasta place but you avoid gluten. Before anyone orders, the waiter is standing at the end of the table.
explanation: This moment is about safe food choices with the server present, not only choosing a quiet corner in advance. "Asking About Allergens or Dietary Needs" fits asking which dishes are suitable.

title: Soup and bread, ingredient confirmation pause
text: Your soup arrives with bread on the side that you did not request. You need to check ingredients before you touch the bowl.
explanation: A safety check with staff is needed, not waiting longer because the kitchen is slow. "Asking About Allergens or Dietary Needs" covers calm questions about preparation and cross-contact.

title: Empty dessert plates, server eye contact
text: Dessert plates are empty and your group has been chatting for twenty minutes. You catch the server's eye from across the room.
explanation: The meal is finished and you are ready to settle up. "Paying the Bill at a Restaurant" covers asking for the check, reviewing it, and paying by card or cash.

title: Bill folder down, total seems high
text: The leather folder arrives face down on the table and the total looks higher than you remember ordering. Your card is already in your hand.
explanation: You are at the payment stage and may need to question a line on the total. "Paying the Bill at a Restaurant" includes checking the amount matches what you ordered.

title: Solo lunch table, rush building noise
text: You ate alone and want to leave before the lunch rush builds. The room is getting louder and you shift in your chair.
explanation: You are done eating and need to close the visit with payment, not change tables on arrival. "Paying the Bill at a Restaurant" fits asking for the check and leaving when you are ready.

title: Main course delay, neighboring table ahead
text: Your mains were supposed to arrive twenty minutes ago and the table next to you is onto puddings. Steam still rises from your empty plates.
explanation: The issue is a long wait after ordering, not a mistaken delivery to your table. "When Your Food Takes Too Long" helps you check in politely with staff.

title: Work lunch clock, trays pass by
text: You ordered for a work lunch and your meeting starts in fifteen minutes. The server passes with trays for another section but not yours.
explanation: You are still waiting on food that was ordered, not ready to pay yet. "When Your Food Takes Too Long" fits a calm update request before you need to leave.

title: High chair wait, kitchen backlog growing
text: The kitchen seems backed up and your child is getting restless in the high chair. You raise a hand as the server walks toward the bar.
explanation: You need a status update on an order that has not arrived, not ingredient information before ordering. "When Your Food Takes Too Long" is for checking on delay without escalating.

title: Shared starters math, folder center table
text: Four of you shared starters and nobody wrote down who had what. The folder lands in the centre and phones come out with calculators.
explanation: The group needs to agree how to divide costs before anyone pays. "Splitting a Bill with Others" covers equal splits, paying for your own items, and tips.

title: Dessert turn memory, napkin math scribbles
text: Your cousin offered to cover dessert last time and now everyone assumes you will figure the maths. Numbers are scribbled on a napkin.
explanation: You are working out fair shares among diners, not asking the server for a single check by yourself. "Splitting a Bill with Others" fits deciding the split method with the group.

title: Salad-only share, combined receipt confusion
text: One person only had a salad but the receipt lists one combined total. You need to speak up before anyone taps their card.
explanation: This is about dividing payment fairly among people at the table. "Splitting a Bill with Others" helps you clarify who pays for what before cards go down.

title: Early table need, number dial outside
text: Reviews mention loud music after eight and you need an early table tonight. You dial the number from outside before your group walks in.
explanation: You are planning the visit for comfort, including quieter seating when possible. "Eating Out with Specific Sensory Needs" covers researching the venue and asking for adjustments.

title: Fluorescent buzz, booth request forming
text: The fluorescent lights buzz and plates clatter on every side. You brought something soft for your ears and want to ask about a booth in the back.
explanation: You are managing sensory load during the meal, not only paying at the end. "Eating Out with Specific Sensory Needs" fits bringing tools and requesting changes from staff.

title: Bright room mismatch, exit sign cue
text: You checked photos online but the actual room feels brighter than expected. Your support person nods toward the exit sign and waits for your cue.
explanation: A busy dining room with a clear exit plan matches preparing for overload while eating out. "Eating Out with Specific Sensory Needs" includes knowing where you can take a break.

title: Cash-only share, machine hovering nearby
text: The meal is over and your friend says to use one card, but you only brought cash for your portion. The server is hovering with the card machine.
explanation: You need to agree how costs are divided or ask for separate checks before payment. "Splitting a Bill at a Restaurant" covers saying how you want to pay your share.

title: Printed total arrives, drink-only meal
text: Two colleagues shared a pizza and a dessert; you had only a drink. They look at you expectantly when the printed total appears.
explanation: The moment is about fair division among diners, not checking whether the total matches your solo order. "Splitting a Bill at a Restaurant" helps you speak up about paying only for what you had.

title: Group chat plan, server uninformed yet
text: The group chat agreed everyone pays for their own items but nobody mentioned it to the server yet. You need to speak before they process payment.
explanation: You are clarifying split or separate checks at the end of the meal. "Splitting a Bill at a Restaurant" fits asking the server before one person pays for everyone.

title: Cross-town hospital route, map lines
text: You have never crossed town on the bus to the hospital and need to be there by nine. At home you open a maps app and stare at coloured lines.
explanation: You are preparing the route and timing before you travel. "Planning a Journey on Public Transport" covers apps, departure time, and a backup if plans change.

title: Rail closure notice, coat-on replanning
text: A storm closed one rail line and your usual route home is posted as unavailable online. You sit with your coat on checking alternative times.
explanation: You are replanning before you set off, not already waiting on a platform. "Planning a Journey on Public Transport" fits choosing another route and leaving early enough.

title: Unknown address prep, stop names noted
text: Your cousin invited you to their flat and the address is in an area you do not know. You charge your phone and write down stop names on paper.
explanation: Figuring out how to get there is the task, not settling into a new neighbourhood long term. "Planning a Journey on Public Transport" helps you map the trip and who to call if needed.

title: Shelter screen, contactless missing realization
text: You reach the stop and realize you do not have a contactless card loaded. A touchscreen glows under the shelter with several destination buttons.
explanation: You need a valid fare before boarding, using a machine or app. "Buying a Bus or Train Ticket" covers selecting the journey and keeping the ticket until you exit.

title: Machine queue deep, service due soon
text: The queue at the machine is three people deep and your service is due in eight minutes. Someone behind you shuffles impatiently.
explanation: You are purchasing travel at a machine or counter, not withdrawing cash from a bank. "Buying a Bus or Train Ticket" fits finishing the purchase or asking nearby staff if you are stuck.

title: Wrong fare zone, doors closing soon
text: You tapped a different fare zone on the app and staff might check tickets at the next stop. You need a valid paper slip before the doors close.
explanation: The immediate step is getting the right ticket in hand, not replanning the whole journey at home. "Buying a Bus or Train Ticket" is for fixing fare before you travel.

title: High hall screens, platform not visible
text: You step off the street into a high hall with departure screens flickering above. Your pocket buzzes with the time but you cannot see your platform yet.
explanation: You are inside the station finding where to go next. "Using a Train Station for the First Time" covers boards, platforms, and confirming the right service.

title: Platform-change call, itinerary in hand
text: A voice announces a platform change and people around you start walking quickly. You hold your printed itinerary and look for matching numbers.
explanation: You are navigating the station to reach the correct platform, not texting that you will be late. "Using a Train Station for the First Time" fits following signs and asking staff if unsure.

title: Open doors moment, carriage uncertainty
text: You are not sure whether to board the carriage in front of you. A uniformed worker stands by the open doors checking watches.
explanation: Confirming destination before boarding is part of using the station, not buying a ticket at the stop outside. "Using a Train Station for the First Time" includes asking if this is the right train.

title: Delay board update, showtime pressure rising
text: The display board flips your service to forty minutes late and the waiting room fills up. You have tickets for a show that starts in an hour.
explanation: Your service is running late and you need updates and a calm plan. "When Your Bus or Train Is Delayed" covers checking boards, waiting safely, and messaging anyone waiting for you.

title: Rainy curb crowd, engineering works notice
text: Buses are stacked at the curb and the driver says engineering work is the cause. Rain drips off your hood onto your phone screen.
explanation: You are already at the stop dealing with a late departure, not buying a ticket for the first time. "When Your Bus or Train Is Delayed" fits waiting and asking about alternatives if it is very long.

title: Cafe meet pending, revised time repeated
text: You were meeting a friend at a cafe near the station and they messaged asking where you are. The overhead speaker just repeated another revised time.
explanation: A delay while you are en route calls for an update and patience, not learning the station layout for the first time. "When Your Bus or Train Is Delayed" includes texting your new arrival time.

title: Security line hall, boarding groups listed
text: Your holiday bag is packed and you arrive at a huge building with long security lines. A screen lists boarding groups and your flight number.
explanation: Air travel has its own sequence from check-in through security to the gate. "Travelling on an Aeroplane" walks through arriving early, screens, and boarding when called.

title: Cabin row reached, crew aisle check
text: You find your row and buckle in while others stow bags overhead. A crew member walks the aisle with a checklist.
explanation: You are on board following crew instructions, not waiting for a delayed train at a platform. "Travelling on an Aeroplane" covers seating and asking for support if you need it.

title: Seatbelt sign flash, in-flight uncertainty
text: The seatbelt sign flashed after bumps and you are unsure what you are allowed to do. The person beside you has put on headphones.
explanation: In-flight rules and crew directions are the focus, not planning a bus route at home. "Travelling on an Aeroplane" fits staying seated when asked and speaking to crew if you need help.

title: App pin matched, curbside window down
text: You booked a car to the dentist and the app shows a pin and licence plate. A grey vehicle pulls up and the driver lowers the window.
explanation: A booked private car pickup is different from buying a fare at a public machine. "Using Ride-Share Apps (Uber, Lyft, etc.)" fits confirming the driver and getting in safely.

title: Similar street corners, arrival alert buzzing
text: The map says three minutes away but you are standing on a corner with two similar street names. Your phone vibrates with a driver-arriving alert.
explanation: You are coordinating an app pickup, not mapping a full public transport route. "Using Ride-Share Apps (Uber, Lyft, etc.)" covers the pickup point and matching the vehicle shown.

title: Late film exit, pickup point confirmation
text: You need to get home after a late film and public services have stopped. You select a vehicle size and confirm the pickup point on the app.
explanation: When buses and trains are not running, a booked car can be the option. "Using Ride-Share Apps (Uber, Lyft, etc.)" is for requesting and meeting the driver at the curb.

title: Sunny lawn blanket, off-lead pet nearby
text: It is a sunny afternoon and you spread a blanket on grass between families playing catch. Someone's pet trots close to your snacks without a lead.
explanation: A shared outdoor space with room for others and simple courtesy is what "Going to the Park" describes, including giving people space on paths and benches.

title: Shaded tree patch, benches all taken
text: You planned to read outside and every bench along the path is taken. You find a patch of shade under a tree away from the playground noise.
explanation: You are enjoying open green space at your own pace, not checking in at a swimming facility. "Going to the Park" fits picking a spot and being mindful of others nearby.

title: Familiar path fountain, jogger nod moment
text: You are walking a familiar loop and a jogger nods as they pass. You slow down near a shared drinking fountain.
explanation: A brief nod in open air is enough in a casual outdoor setting. "Going to the Park" covers low-key contact without needing a long conversation.

title: Studio mats set, instructor eye contact
text: The studio door shows mats laid out and music is already playing. You are in new trainers and the instructor makes eye contact.
explanation: A scheduled class with an instructor is different from using machines on your own. "Joining a Fitness Class for the First Time" covers arriving early and saying you are new.

title: Missing clipboard name, class starting soon
text: You signed up online but your name is not on the clipboard at reception. A session is due to start in two minutes and people are filing in.
explanation: Your first class needs a quick check-in with staff or the instructor, not choosing a cinema seat. "Joining a Fitness Class for the First Time" fits letting them know it is your first time.

title: Mid-routine strain, pace reduction needed
text: Midway through the routine your heart rate feels high and you need to slow down without leaving. The instructor sweeps the room.
explanation: You can modify moves in a class at your own pace. "Joining a Fitness Class for the First Time" reminds you that going slower is acceptable and you do not have to chat with others.

title: Turnstile beep green, weight-room hum
text: You scan your new membership card and the turnstile beeps green. Rows of machines hum and someone is wiping down a bench.
explanation: Independent equipment use with induction and wiping down gear is what "Using a Gym for the First Time" covers, not a led group session.

title: Warning-sticker machine, staff desk distance
text: You want to try a machine with a warning sticker but no one showed you it yet. A staff member in branded kit is at the desk twenty metres away.
explanation: Asking staff before using unfamiliar equipment is part of a first gym visit. "Using a Gym for the First Time" includes induction and not using machines you have not been shown.

title: Towel on bench, next person waiting
text: You finished your set and left a towel on the seat. Another person waits with their water bottle and looks at the equipment.
explanation: Shared equipment etiquette applies in the gym, including wiping and re-racking weights. "Using a Gym for the First Time" fits cleaning up after yourself so others can use the machine.

title: Dim foyer scents, numbered door ushers
text: You printed your seat code and the foyer is dim with concession smells. Ushers are directing people toward numbered doors.
explanation: A timed screening with assigned seats and quiet during the show is what "Going to the Cinema" is for. Arriving a few minutes early fits the usual flow.

title: Trailer fade, phone glow ahead
text: The trailers end and the room goes darker; someone's screen lights up two rows ahead. You adjust in your allocated seat.
explanation: You are inside a dark auditorium where phone silence and quiet eating matter. "Going to the Cinema" covers settling in for the feature, not planning a restaurant visit.

title: Queue rush past, facilities stop needed
text: You arrived as the queue was moving fast and now need the facilities before the feature. The hallway is crowded between screens.
explanation: You are at a cinema visit where timing and quiet matter when you return. "Going to the Cinema" is the overall outing; a quick break still fits staying mindful of others when you go back in.

title: Entrance map fold, roped sculpture hall
text: You pick up a folded map at the entrance and the hall echoes with footsteps. A volunteer stands near a roped-off sculpture.
explanation: Indoor culture venues share quiet voices and not touching displays unless allowed. "Visiting a Museum or Gallery" covers maps, pacing yourself, and taking breaks.

title: Tired legs, courtyard seating sign
text: After an hour your legs ache and every bench is occupied. A sign points to a courtyard with seats and a small cafe.
explanation: Long visits can include sitting down or stepping outside without ending the day entirely. "Visiting a Museum or Gallery" reminds you that breaks and leaving early are fine.

title: Egypt room crowd, doorway air break
text: The crowd in the Egypt room is dense and you feel pressed on all sides. You step toward a doorway marked exit to air.
explanation: When a gallery room feels too busy, you can step out and return another day. "Visiting a Museum or Gallery" includes knowing you can leave if it gets overwhelming.

title: Town-square weekend, short plan ready
text: Flyers promised live bands and food trucks this weekend in the town square. You arrive with sunglasses and a short plan written on your phone.
explanation: A large outdoor event needs advance thinking about noise, crowds, and exits. "Attending a Community Event or Festival" covers researching the event and bringing what helps your senses.

title: Main stage drums, side street search
text: Drums start on the main stage and the path to the facilities is packed. Your ear protection is in your bag and you look for a calmer side street.
explanation: Festivals can get loud and crowded; having a quiet spot and a way to step away matters. "Attending a Community Event or Festival" fits knowing where exits and calmer areas are.

title: Information tent meetup, view blocked
text: You agreed to meet your sibling at the information tent at noon. The clock on your phone shows 11:58 and banners block your view.
explanation: Busy public events work best with a meet-up plan and tools for overload. "Attending a Community Event or Festival" includes going with someone you trust when possible and leaving early if needed.

title: Mall corridor sign, cubicle latch issue
text: You are at a shopping centre and the stick-figure sign points down a corridor. The door on your chosen cubicle does not seem to latch fully.
explanation: Using a shared cubicle with privacy and basic hygiene steps is what "Using a Public Toilet" covers, including locking the door when you can.

title: Service station stop, sink queue pressure
text: After a long bus ride you follow signs to the facilities at the service station. The tap sputters and there is a queue behind you.
explanation: You are using a public cubicle and sink, not waiting for a delayed service. "Using a Public Toilet" includes washing hands and leaving the space tidy.

title: Sink finished, overflowing towel bin
text: You finished at the sink and the paper towel bin is overflowing. Someone is waiting outside the door with a stroller.
explanation: The routine is flush, wash, dry, and dispose of towels before you leave. "Using a Public Toilet" fits finishing up so the next person can use the space.

title: Bakery display queue, counter pause
text: You are at a small bakery with a glass display and a short line ahead of you. When the person in front steps away, the person behind the counter looks at you and waits.
explanation: You are at a counter choosing food and a drink to take away. "Ordering at a Café Counter" walks through reading the menu, speaking clearly, and collecting when your name is called.

title: Station kiosk line, gate clock running
text: Your train leaves in twelve minutes and the station kiosk sells hot drinks before the gates. You are next in line with your wallet ready.
explanation: You still need to purchase a drink and possibly a snack before you board, not buy travel fare. "Ordering at a Café Counter" fits saying what you want and moving aside to wait.

title: Market stall chalkboard, two-option pause
text: A weekend market stall has a chalkboard menu and a portable card reader on the table. The vendor smiles while you decide between two options.
explanation: This is a quick purchase at a counter, not being shown to a table for a full meal. "Ordering at a Café Counter" covers stating your choice, any extras, and paying before you step away.

title: Cake stand choice, nut safety check
text: You want a slice from the cake stand but nuts make you unwell. The person at the till is wiping the counter and a short queue has formed behind you.
explanation: Before you buy, you need clear information about ingredients, not a full symptom list for a doctor. "Asking About Allergens in a Café" covers asking staff to check and choosing something else if they cannot confirm.

title: Lunch spot counter, dairy question pending
text: A friend suggested this spot for lunch and you need to know whether the soup contains dairy. You approach the counter with a photo of the menu on your phone.
explanation: You are checking safety of a specific item before you commit, not weighing grams at a deli. "Asking About Allergens in a Café" fits naming your restriction and asking who can verify it.

title: Unlabeled pastry case, sesame concern
text: The pastry case has no ingredient labels and your skin reacts to sesame. You point at one item and the barista turns toward you.
explanation: You need ingredient confirmation before eating, not reporting that the wrong item was handed to you. "Asking About Allergens in a Café" is for that check at the counter.

title: Corner socket table, empty cup hour
text: You found a corner table with a plug socket and opened your laptop. An hour has passed, your cup is empty, and other tables are filling up.
explanation: You are using a paid seat for focused work in a busy public space, not booking a library session. "Staying to Work or Study in a Café" covers buying something, keeping volume low, and leaving tidy.

title: Revision table, nearby chatter rising
text: You are revising for an exam with earbuds in, but a group nearby is chatting loudly. The person clearing tables glances in your direction as they pass.
explanation: You chose this spot to concentrate for a while, not to tour quiet exhibits. "Staying to Work or Study in a Café" reminds you about headphones, voice level, and when to buy another drink or move on.

title: Busy-hour sign, seat search growing
text: You planned to stay until closing and a small sign mentions table limits during busy hours. New customers are scanning the room for somewhere to sit.
explanation: The moment is about sharing space fairly while you study, not placing a new food order. "Staying to Work or Study in a Café" fits not spreading across seats and tidying when you leave.

title: Name-tag mismatch, pickup queue ahead
text: You picked up a cup with a name tag that is not yours and the drink tastes much sweeter than you expected. The counter still has a short queue.
explanation: Something you already received does not match what you asked for, and you need a calm fix at the counter. "When Your Café Order Is Wrong" covers describing what you got versus what you wanted.

title: Pickup shelf, sandwich filling mismatch
text: Your sandwich arrived without the filling you chose and you are still at the pickup shelf. The barista calls the next name and glances back at you.
explanation: You are correcting a completed order, not asking about allergens before you buy. "When Your Café Order Is Wrong" fits going back calmly and thanking them when it is fixed.

title: Large-cup order, size looks short
text: You paid for a large hot chocolate but the cup looks smaller than the others on the shelf. You have not left the shop yet.
explanation: The issue is what was handed to you after payment, not a shelf price at a supermarket till. "When Your Café Order Is Wrong" is for speaking up before you walk away.

title: First-visit porch, doorbell footsteps
text: A classmate gave you their address on a folded note and asked you to come over after school. You ring the doorbell and hear footsteps approaching from inside.
explanation: You are arriving at someone's private home for a planned visit, not being seated in a dining room. "Visiting a Friend's Home for the First Time" covers thanking them, following their lead, and asking before using things.

title: Unfamiliar porch, thank-you plant in hand
text: You are on a porch you have never stood on before, holding a small plant as a thank-you gift. A parent opens the door and steps aside into the hallway.
explanation: This is a social visit at home, not settling in to work at a public table. "Visiting a Friend's Home for the First Time" fits arriving on time and noticing how they use their space.

title: Hallway shoes off, bag placement unsure
text: You were asked to leave shoes in the hallway and your host points toward a room where others are already sitting. You are unsure where to put your bag.
explanation: You are settling into someone else's home, not finding your seat in a dark auditorium. "Visiting a Friend's Home for the First Time" includes following their cues and asking before you explore.

title: Cloakroom programme, black-tie seating flow
text: The invitation listed black tie and you are in a cloakroom reading the printed programme. Ushers are directing people toward numbered seats in the hall.
explanation: A scheduled formal gathering with seating and dress expectations is what "Attending a Wedding or Formal Event" prepares you for, including arriving on time and keeping your phone silent.

title: Order sheet in hand, row standing
text: Music started and everyone around you stood up while you hold a small order-of-service booklet. You watch the row ahead to see what happens next.
explanation: You are following group cues at a formal ceremony, not learning office routines on day one. "Attending a Wedding or Formal Event" fits observing when others stand or sit and keeping interactions brief.

title: Early departure need, couple table circuit
text: You need to leave before dessert and the couple is moving between tables with a relative. They pause near you as the room noise rises.
explanation: You are closing out your time at a large formal gathering, not ending a casual hangout in a kitchen. "Attending a Wedding or Formal Event" includes a short congratulations before you go.

title: Temporary badge, fourth-floor desk search
text: Security gave you a temporary badge and a map to the fourth floor. People in lanyards walk past without stopping and you are looking for a reception desk.
explanation: You are starting in a new workplace and need to find where to check in, not navigate a travel hub. "First Day at a New Job" covers introducing yourself and observing more than you speak at first.

title: Team question prompt, workstation still unknown
text: Someone at a desk waves you over and asks which team you are joining. You have names from orientation written down but nobody has shown you your workstation yet.
explanation: This is professional onboarding, not mingling at a social gathering. "First Day at a New Job" fits answering clearly, noting details, and asking one or two focused questions.

title: Late-afternoon pack-up, forms still pending
text: It is late afternoon and colleagues are packing up while you still have forms to complete. You want to acknowledge people before you leave without interrupting too much.
explanation: You are wrapping up your first day at work, not saying goodbye after a home visit. "First Day at a New Job" includes a brief thanks and looking forward to what comes next.

title: Loud living room, snack-table pause
text: Music is loud in a living room full of people you have only met once. You are near the snacks table and one other person is also alone, looking at their phone.
explanation: You are at a busy social gathering where starting a short conversation helps you feel less stuck. "Talking to Someone at a Party When You Don't Know Many People" covers a simple opener and a polite exit.

title: Host stepped away, eyes turn toward you
text: The host introduced you to a small group and then left to answer the door. Everyone turned to you after someone asked how you know the host.
explanation: You need to keep a light exchange going in a group, not follow ceremony seating. "Talking to Someone at a Party When You Don't Know Many People" fits listening, asking a follow-up, and sharing a little about yourself.

title: Slowing chat, ready to move on
text: You have spoken with one person for several minutes and the chat has slowed. They are still smiling but you feel ready to move on.
explanation: Ending one conversation at a gathering is the skill, not planning for festival crowds outdoors. "Talking to Someone at a Party When You Don't Know Many People" includes a natural line before you step away.

title: Box-filled hallway, nearest shop needed
text: Boxes are still stacked in your hallway and the street outside sounds unfamiliar. You want to find the nearest shop without walking too far today.
explanation: You are settling into a new neighbourhood over time, not planning a single trip on a map app. "Moving to a New Area" covers exploring in small steps and building routines that help you feel anchored.

title: Lamppost flyer, two-week indoor stretch
text: A flyer on a lamppost advertises a local walking group on Saturdays. You have been in town two weeks and mostly stayed indoors.
explanation: Finding community connections in your new location is the goal, not a one-off visit to green space. "Moving to a New Area" includes looking for groups linked to your interests when you are ready.

title: Next-door van unload, curbside eye contact
text: Someone is unloading a van next door and you realise you have not spoken to them yet. They look up as you carry recycling to the curb.
explanation: A brief hello to a neighbour supports settling in, not a planned visit inside their home. "Moving to a New Area" fits introducing yourself when you feel ready.

title: Back-row seat, stand-sit sheet guidance
text: You found a seat near the back after reading online that hats should be removed indoors. A printed sheet shows when people stand and sit together.
explanation: You are attending a structured gathering with shared customs, not a private celebration with a reception. "Attending a Religious or Cultural Service" covers arriving early, following others' lead, and staying quietly if unsure.

title: Unfamiliar scents, row-ahead pattern watching
text: Sounds and scents in the room are unfamiliar and people around you move in unison. You stay seated until you see a clear pattern from the row ahead.
explanation: You are participating in a communal ritual space, not browsing exhibits at your own pace. "Attending a Religious or Cultural Service" fits watching what others do before you join in.

title: Exit approach, volunteer water cups
text: The gathering is ending and volunteers are near the door with small cups of water. Someone in a name badge smiles as you approach the exit.
explanation: You are leaving a communal service, not wrapping up a hangout in someone's kitchen. "Attending a Religious or Cultural Service" includes a simple thank-you to a greeter when you go.

title: Front desk lane chart, first-visit prompt
text: You reach the front desk with a membership card and a towel in your bag. A screen lists lane speeds and the receptionist asks if you have been here before.
explanation: You are at the start of a pool visit: paying, lockers, showering, and choosing a lane. "Arriving at a Swimming Pool" covers those first steps before you get in the water.

title: Locker coin ready, glass-door flow
text: Signs point toward changing areas and you are holding a coin for a locker. Other people in flip-flops carry goggles toward glass doors.
explanation: You are still getting ready to enter the pool area, not managing privacy in a cubicle afterward. "Arriving at a Swimming Pool" fits finding changing space and storing belongings safely.

title: Shower gesture, lane-color chart confusion
text: Before the pool door, a staff member gestures toward showers and a wall chart shows colour-coded lanes. You are unsure which lane matches your pace.
explanation: Choosing where to swim comes right after arrival routines, not during a fitness class warm-up. "Arriving at a Swimming Pool" includes reading lane signs and picking the right speed.

title: Lane tap at wall, faster swimmer behind
text: You are swimming lengths and someone faster is close behind you in the same lane. They tap your foot lightly as you reach the wall.
explanation: Sharing a lane safely is part of being in the water, not paying at reception. "Following Pool Rules" covers letting faster swimmers pass and staying on the correct side.

title: Whistle from chair, wet-tile reminder
text: A whistle sounds from a high chair and the person there points at a sign about moving slowly on wet tiles. You were walking quickly because the floor felt cold.
explanation: Poolside safety instructions apply while you are on deck, not while you dress afterward. "Following Pool Rules" includes no running and doing what the lifeguard asks right away.

title: Lane-rope splash, duty staff watching
text: Two children are splashing near the lane rope and water hits your face. The person on duty is watching that end of the pool.
explanation: You are already in the pool and need to follow shared behaviour, not plan a quiet afternoon outdoors. "Following Pool Rules" fits staying in your lane and not splashing others on purpose.

title: Stiff cubicle lock, waiting footsteps outside
text: The cubicle door lock feels stiff and your clothes are on a narrow bench. Someone outside is waiting with a laundry bag and shifting their weight.
explanation: You are getting changed in a shared leisure-centre space, not withdrawing cash or buying a ticket. "Using a Changing Room" covers using a cubicle if you want one and keeping belongings together.

title: Locker floor drips, sink still needed
text: Water drips from your hair onto the floor between lockers and a sign asks people not to leave wet items lying around. You need to get dressed and free the sink.
explanation: Tidying up in the changing area is separate from lane behaviour in the water. "Using a Changing Room" includes drying off, dressing, and leaving the space clear for others.

title: Bench covered in towels, hook search
text: Your bag takes up half a bench while you dry your ears. Another person enters and looks for a hook that is not covered by towels.
explanation: Sharing benches and hooks politely is what this script addresses, not using a shopping-centre cubicle on a bus trip. "Using a Changing Room" fits keeping your items compact and not blocking exits.

title: Store-corner cash machine, queue behind
text: You need notes for a market that only accepts cash and the machine sits in a bright corner of a convenience store. Your card is ready and someone is waiting behind you.
explanation: You are withdrawing cash from a machine, not joining a queue to speak with a bank adviser. "Using an ATM" covers shielding your PIN, taking card and cash in the right order, and putting everything away before you leave.

title: PIN screen prompt, card read failed
text: The screen asks for your PIN and you cover the keypad with your other hand. The machine beeps that your card was not read on the first try.
explanation: This is a banking machine for cash, not a transport ticket screen. "Using an ATM" fits reinserting your card calmly and finishing the withdrawal.

title: Bills out first, card still held
text: Bills slide out but the machine holds your card until you confirm. You hear footsteps approaching the same corner.
explanation: You are completing an ATM transaction, not scanning groceries to pay. "Using an ATM" reminds you to take your card first, then cash and receipt, before you walk away.

title: Ticket dispenser wait, savings folder ready
text: You take a paper ticket from a dispenser and the display shows forty-two while the counter calls thirty-eight. You have forms for opening a savings account in a folder.
explanation: You are waiting for in-person banking help with ID and paperwork, not booking a table by phone. "Visiting the Bank" covers taking a number, stating your task, and keeping receipts.

title: Verification desk chat, move-date forgotten
text: The person behind the glass asks verification questions you did not expect. You have your passport but cannot recall the exact month you moved house.
explanation: Security questions at a counter are part of a bank visit, not a quick machine withdrawal. "Visiting the Bank" includes answering clearly and asking them to repeat or explain if needed.

title: Post-appointment leaflets, next-step confirmation
text: After the appointment you are given leaflets and a reference number to keep. You want to confirm what happens next before you leave the building.
explanation: You finished a banking task at the counter, not picking up a mailed parcel. "Visiting the Bank" fits checking you have the paperwork and understanding the next step.

title: Sealed parcel label, counter scale ready
text: You taped a box shut at home and wrote the destination on a label. At the counter a scale sits beside stacks of prepaid envelopes.
explanation: You are posting a sealed item with postage options, not buying sliced food by weight. "Sending a Package at the Post Office" covers stating you want to send it and keeping your tracking receipt.

title: Delivery options asked, value item concern
text: The clerk offers tracked or standard delivery and you are not sure which you need. Your item is small but valuable and you have the address written clearly.
explanation: Choosing postage is part of sending mail, not opening a bank account. "Sending a Package at the Post Office" fits asking staff to advise and paying before you leave.

title: Label missing return, spare sticker offered
text: You forgot to write the return address on the label and the person behind the counter points to a spare sticker. A line is forming on your left.
explanation: Fixing the label happens while sending post, not checking in for a flight. "Sending a Package at the Post Office" includes writing addresses clearly before you pay.

title: Collection barcode ready, lettered shelves behind
text: Your phone showed a ready-to-collect message and you brought the barcode plus photo ID. Shelves labeled with letters sit behind the glass at the counter.
explanation: You are collecting something that was mailed to you, not ordering fresh food at a counter. "Collecting a Parcel from the Post Office" covers showing ID and checking the box before you leave.

title: Medium box slide, screen signature prompt
text: The clerk slides a medium box across and asks you to sign a handheld screen. You want to look at the corners before you walk out.
explanation: Signing for a delivery is different from withdrawing cash from a machine. "Collecting a Parcel from the Post Office" fits signing if asked and confirming the parcel looks okay.

title: Missing slip, reference code lookup
text: You lost the paper slip but have the email with a reference code. The person at the desk types and studies the monitor.
explanation: You are picking up mail with proof of identity, not returning borrowed books. "Collecting a Parcel from the Post Office" includes saying you are there to collect and showing ID.

title: Staffed lanes full, self-service green light
text: Every staffed lane has a long line and a green light shows on an empty self-service machine. You have six items and a reusable bag on your arm.
explanation: You are scanning and paying at a machine yourself, not waiting for sliced goods at a counter. "Using the Self-Checkout" covers scanning each item, finishing, and taking your receipt.

title: Tin barcode fail, orange light flashing
text: The scanner will not read a barcode on a tin and an orange light is flashing on the screen. A staff member in a high-vis vest is nearby.
explanation: The issue is the machine not reading an item during self-service, not a price mismatch at a staffed till. "Using the Self-Checkout" fits calling for assistance and trying again.

title: Scanning complete, receipt prompt on-screen
text: You finished scanning and the machine asks whether you want a receipt. Your payment card is already in the slot.
explanation: You are completing a supermarket self-pay step, not withdrawing cash. "Using the Self-Checkout" includes selecting pay, taking bags, and keeping your receipt if you want one.

title: Saturday aisle crush, breathing tightening
text: It is Saturday midday and the aisles are full of trolleys brushing past each other. Your list has three items left but your breathing feels tight.
explanation: A busy shop can feel overwhelming before you finish your list. "When the Store Is Very Crowded" covers slower breathing, using a list, and stepping outside if you need to.

title: Overlapping announcements, quiet aisle missing
text: Music and announcements overlap and you cannot find the quiet aisle you used last week. You are standing near the front doors with a half-full basket.
explanation: Coping with noise and density in a shop is the focus, not rushing through a self-scan lane. "When the Store Is Very Crowded" reminds you that you can leave and return later.

title: Trolley bump ripple, doorway decision point
text: Someone bumps your trolley accidentally and apologises, but more people close in behind you. You are deciding whether to stay or step outside.
explanation: The setting is a packed supermarket, not a restaurant where you planned sensory tools. "When the Store Is Very Crowded" fits leaving your basket and getting fresh air if it is too much.

title: Curved glass counter, ticket seventeen showing
text: You stand at a curved glass counter where sliced meats are stacked and a ticket machine shows number seventeen. The person serving looks ready for the next customer.
explanation: You need a specific amount from a staffed food counter, not a drink order at a café. "Asking for Help at the Deli or Bakery Counter" covers waiting your turn and saying what you want clearly.

title: Loaf size choice, knife held waiting
text: You point at a loaf behind the glass but are unsure whether you want a whole one or half. The server lifts a knife and waits for you to speak.
explanation: Choosing how much to buy at the counter is different from disputing a price at the till. "Asking for Help at the Deli or Bakery Counter" fits saying roughly how much you need.

title: Per-kilo label, small recipe amount
text: The label shows price per kilogram and you only need a small amount for one recipe. You hold your hands apart to show roughly how much you mean.
explanation: You are buying by weight at a food counter, not asking a librarian to locate a book. "Asking for Help at the Deli or Bakery Counter" includes checking the amount before it is wrapped.

title: Shelf tag mismatch, till screen higher
text: The shelf tag showed two pounds less than what appeared on the till screen. The person scanning your items pauses with the tin in their hand.
explanation: You are questioning a price difference at checkout, not teaching yourself to scan at a machine. "When an Item Scans at the Wrong Price" covers staying calm and pointing to where you found the item.

title: Aisle photo proof, supervisor needed
text: You photographed the yellow label on the aisle end but the screen still shows full price. A supervisor is needed at the register.
explanation: This is a supermarket pricing check, not paying a restaurant bill after a meal. "When an Item Scans at the Wrong Price" fits asking staff to verify the shelf price.

title: Checkout pause, calmer price mention
text: Your friend says they saw the same product cheaper last week but you are at the checkout now. You want to mention it calmly before you pay.
explanation: You are addressing a till price mismatch, not a wrong drink at a pickup shelf. "When an Item Scans at the Wrong Price" is for speaking up while the item is still being rung up.
